title: A Multiscale Biophysical Reaction-Diffusion Framework Coupling Histological Architecture, Interstitial Transport, and Inflammatory Tension in Solid Tumors: An Exploratory In Silico and Retrospective Multi-Cohort Analysis
abstract: Abstract Background In solid oncology, anatomical TNM staging and somatic mutational profiling provide the cornerstone of clinical risk stratification. Nevertheless, substantial clinical heterogeneity remains unexplained: curatively resected (R0) tumors frequently recur, and targeted adjuvant therapies—such as 36-month adjuvant osimertinib in the landmark ADAURA trial—exhibit a post-discontinuation recurrence rebound where 67.9% of all relapse events occur after planned treatment cessation. Similarly, in desmoplastic colorectal cancer (CMS4 subtype), cytotoxic chemotherapy de-escalation/escalation strategies (investigated in trials such as PEGASUS) confront persistent micrometastatic reservoirs that evade clearance. We hypothesized that post-resection persistence and delayed relapse are modulated by the biophysical coupling between epithelial polarity integrity (“The Seed”) and microenvironmental inflammatory-transport resistance (“The Soil”). Methods We established a multiscale biophysical reaction-diffusion continuum model integrating: 1. Spatial drug penetration across microvascular cords governed by modified cylindrical Bessel functions of the second kind (K0); 2. Interstitial transport limitations driven by elevated interstitial fluid pressure ( I F P ≈ 20 – 35 mmHg) and absent functional lymphatic drainage (Δ P ≈ 0); 3. Plastic drug-tolerant persister (DTP) cell transitions within viable, sub-therapeutic annular niches (p O2 ≥ 1 – 2 mmHg); 4. A hereditary Volterra memory functional of residual cytotoxic immune surveillance (Eimm ( t ) = E0 e− γ ∫ Φ d τ) formalizing cumulative inflammatory damage; 5. An exploratory translational metric—the Host-Tumor Biophysical Index (HTBI)—integrating histopathological polarity, stromal desmoplasia, and systemic inflammatory blood parameters (neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio [NLR] and C-reactive protein [CRP]). In accordance with REMARK reporting recommendations, the framework was evaluated across 3,461 curatively treated cancer patients with clinically indexed records across 11 cohorts (with 3,425 complete matched multi-omic and blood profiles analyzed, strictly excluding 36 TCGA cases lacking paired RNA-seq matrices and 274 incomplete blood records): - Discovery Cohort: 604 curatively resected lung adenocarcinoma patients from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC 2020); - Raw Blood Chemistry Cohort: 1,056 curatively resected surgical patients evaluated via strict complete-case analysis with raw pre-operative complete blood counts (NLR) and serum CRP/Albumin (PLOS ONE open data); - Multi-Cohort Solid Epithelial Cohorts (N = 986 matched RNA-seq / N =1 ,222 clinical): Colorectal (TCGA-COADREAD, N =592), Pancreatic (TCGA-PAAD, N =177), Esophageal (TCGA-ESCA, N =181), Cholangiocarcinoma (TCGA-CHOL, N =36), and External Lung (GSE31210, N = 226); - Inherited Cholangiopathy Model: 18 clinically annotated biliary cases (JAG1, NOTCH2, PKHD1, TJP2); - Proof-by-Contradiction Falsification Controls (N =535): Acute Myeloid Leukemia (TCGA-LAML, N =149), Testicular Germ Cell (TCGA-TGCT, N =133), and Soft-Tissue Sarcoma (TCGA-SARC, N = 253); - External Clinical Trial Anchor: The landmark double-blind randomized CANTOS trial (The Lancet 2017, N =10 ,061). Findings In the complete-case raw laboratory cohort (N =1 ,056), pre-operative biophysical inflammatory tier stratified 5-year overall survival from 69.4% (Low HTBI) to 56.7% (High HTBI) (p =3.81×10−7), maintaining independent prognostic association in multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression adjusting for Pathologic TNM Stage and Histological Grade (Hazard Ratio H R =1.43, 95 %CI:1.14 – 1.81 , p = 0.0022; continuous multivariable H R = 2.20, p = 0.00041). In the MSKCC lung adenocarcinoma discovery cohort (N = 604 , 98 recurrences), continuous decoupled HTBI conferred an adjusted H R = 2.49 ( 95 %CI:1.00 – 6.18 , p = 0.050) (binary adjusted H R =1.89, p = 0.029) after controlling for Pathologic TNM Stage (H R = 2.53 , p < 0.0005), patient sex, and somatic EGFR mutations. Schoenfeld residuals confirmed proportional hazards ( χ2 =3.82 , p = 0.431). 500-fold bootstrap cross-validation showed an incremental discrimination gain (ΔC -index =+ 0.050 , p = 0.044; 2-year A U C = 0.794). In competing risks analysis (Aalen-Johansen cumulative incidence function), HTBI specifically stratified cancer-related recurrence ( p = 0.029), while remaining unstratified for non-cancer competing mortality ( p = 0.680). In proof-by-contradiction negative controls evaluated with genuine empirical RNA-seq expression z-scores lacking solid epithelial boundaries, the model was statistically non-significant as predicted: liquid tumors (TCGA-LAML, N =149 , H R =1.28 , p = 0.246), non-epithelial germline tumors (TCGA-TGCT, N =133 , H R = 2.33 , p = 0.471), and mesenchymal sarcomas (TCGA-SARC, N = 253 , H R = 0.85 , p = 0.413). The continuum model analytically reproduced the empirical 5.46-month median ctDNA-to-imaging lead time (transition from 106 to 108 cells with doubling time T d = 24.6 days), and simulated anti-inflammatory microenvironmental stabilization aligned with the biological feasibility demonstrated in published systemic IL-1β neutralization trials (CANTOS, H R = 0.23 , p = 0.0002). Interpretation The Host-Tumor Biophysical Index demonstrates that combining routine surgical histopathology and standard laboratory inflammatory markers with physical transport mechanics provides independent prognostic stratification in retrospective cohorts. This exploratory framework offers a mechanistic hypothesis for residual tumor dormancy and a quantitative foundation for evaluating microenvironmental decompression and host anti-inflammatory strategies in prospective research settings.

title: Multi-Class Gastric Histopathology Classification Using a Hybrid Swin Transformer–ConvNeXt Model
abstract: Abstract Diagnosing gastric cancer still depends, for the most part, on a pathologist looking at stained tissue slides under a microscope. The disease kills roughly 660{,}000 people every year, and although early detection makes a real difference to survival, manual slide reading is slow and two experts examining the same slide do not always agree. In this work we built a system that tries to ease that burden. We trained a hybrid deep learning model on the Gastric Cancer Histopathology Tissue Image Dataset (GCHTID), pairing a Swin Transformer, which is good at picking up the broad structural layout of a tissue patch, with a ConvNeXt network, which captures the fine local textures where early malignant changes tend to hide. Every image first passes through a simple preprocessing chain of median filtering and CLAHE contrast enhancement, a combination we settled on after comparing several denoising and enhancement options. The ensemble sorts each patch into one of eight classes: tumor tissue (TUM) plus seven benign types-adipose, debris, lymphocytes, mucus, smooth muscle, normal mucosa, and stroma. On held-out data it reached 75.35% test accuracy (88.76% training, 76.99% best validation), beating the single-model baselines we tried, including ViT and EfficientNet-B3. To make the model usable outside a notebook, we wrapped it in a Flask REST API and a small web interface where a user can upload a slide image, see the prediction and its confidence, download a PDF report, and look back through past results. The system is a research prototype rather than a clinical tool, but the results suggest that combining transformer and convolutional features is a workable direction for computer-assisted pathology.

title: Hidden Classifier Collapse in Medical Image Classification: The Impact of Structured Pruning, Data Scarcity, and Post-Pruning Optimization
abstract: Abstract Structured pruning reduces the computational complexity of medical image classifiers but may compromise classification reliability under limited training data, with aggregate accuracy or AUC potentially concealing severe prediction failures. This study investigates hidden classifier collapse following one-shot structured pruning under controlled data scarcity using five MedMNIST v2 datasets, ResNet-18 and ResNet-34 architectures (with ResNet-50 in additional controls), four sparsity levels (70-95\%), and repeated random seeds. Fixed and adaptive post-pruning protocols were compared, jointly varying batch size, learning rate, and optimization update budget, while focused controls examined update count, learning-rate scaling, BatchNorm running-statistic adaptation, optimizer family, and pruning criterion. The protocols showed substantial differences on PneumoniaMNIST and BloodMNIST, sparsity-dependent differences on OrganSMNIST and RetinaMNIST, and no detectable difference on DermaMNIST. Additional optimization updates, learning-rate scaling, and BatchNorm-statistic adaptation each reduced classifier collapse in selected conditions, although no single factor was identified as universally necessary. Conventional accuracy and AUC could remain apparently favorable despite hard-label collapse, whereas balanced accuracy and Matthews correlation coefficient exposed classification failures. The adaptive optimization strategy also showed inconsistent performance across optimizer families. These findings emphasize the importance of class-sensitive evaluation, collapse indicators, and appropriate post-pruning adaptation for assessing the reliability of compressed medical image classifiers.

title: AI-Based Interfacial Contact Area Prediction in 3D Granular Media: Benchmarking Volumetric CNN, GNN, and Classical Surface Meshing
abstract: Abstract Interfacial contact area between contiguous grains governs macroscopic elastic moduli, stress transmission chains, effective thermal and electrical conductivity, and solid-state diffusion rates in three-dimensional (3D) granular media. Standard characterization of X-ray micro-computed tomography (µCT) volumes relies on 3D Euclidean distance transform seeding and marker-controlled watershed segmentation followed by polygonal surface extraction via the Marching-Cubes algorithm (Lorensen & Cline, 1987). However, Cartesian voxelization introduces severe staircase terracing along curved inter-particle boundaries, inflating surface area measurements by 40% to 80%, while local mesh triangulation scales poorly to assemblies containing thousands of grains. Conducted under the supervision of Prof. Mayank Goswami , this study establishes a comparative benchmark of four data-driven surrogate architectures—an interpretable Random Forest ensemble, a 4-block 3D Convolutional Neural Network (3D CNN) operating on 48 3 binary dual-particle patches, a 3-layer bidirectional GraphSAGE Graph Neural Network (GNN) operating on the global contact graph G = (V, E) , and a multimodal Hybrid GNN + CNN fusion architecture—across 250 synthetic 3D granular phantoms (50,800 particles and 48,750 contact interfaces). Across 38 held-out test specimens (7,466 contact interfaces), we evaluate models under both DEM-coupled (known sphere geometry) and blind tomographic (voxel-only, zero metadata) operating regimes. When coupled with exact inter-particle distance and radius attributes, the 3-layer bidirectional GraphSAGE network achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.158 vx 2 , a root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 0.217 vx 2 , a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 1.91% , and R 2 = 0.99999 at an inference latency of 2.89 ms per phantom , while the Random Forest baseline achieves R 2 = 0.99992 and MAE = 0.409 vx 2 . title: Multiple b-value diffusion-weighted imaging for predicting lymphovascular space invasion and evaluating prognostic outcomes in endometrial carcinoma
abstract: Abstract Purpose To systematically compare quantitative parameters derived from multiple diffusion models for preoperative Lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI) assessment and to identify independent imaging predictors of LVSI in EC. Material and methods A total of 113 consecutive patients with EC from hospital were enrolled. 15 diffusion parameters derived from 7 diffusion models, including DWI, diffusion kurtosis imaging (DKI), intravoxel incoherent motion (IVIM), stretched exponential model (SEM), continuous-time random walk (CTRW), fractional order calculus (FROC) and virtual magnetic resonance elastography (vMRE), were calculated and compared. Logistic regression analysis was performed to identify independent predictors of LVSI. The diagnostic performance of individual diffusion parameters and combined models incorporating significant clinical variables was evaluated. Internal validation was performed using 1,000 bootstrap resamples. Kaplan–Meier analysis was used to compare prognostic outcomes. Results Of the 113 patients, 45 were LVSI-positive and 68 were LVSI-negative. Among these diffusion models, the CTRW model achieved the highest AUC of 0.888 (accuracy : 0.850, AICc = 96.3). ADC, α CTRW , and µDiff were identified as independent predictors of LVSI. Incorporating age ( P = 0.003) and menopausal status ( P = 0.005) yielded a combined model with an AUC of 0.910 (accuracy = 0.894, AICc = 100.2). Bootstrap-corrected AUCs were 0.893 and 0.892 for the imaging and combined models, respectively. Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated markedly shorter disease-free survival (DFS) in LVSI-positive patients (log-rank P = 0.016). Conclusion ADC, α CTRW and µDiff were independently associated with LVSI and provided complementary imaging information. Their combination showed promising performance for preoperative LVSI assessment, while LVSI positivity was associated with shorter disease-free survival.

title: A Phase-Aware Fusion Framework via Tri-Phase Enhancement Difference Learning for Benign--Malignant Renal Tumor Classification
abstract: Abstract Preoperative differentiation of benign from malignant renal tumors directly informs treatment decisions. However, fat-poor angiomyolipomas, oncocytomas and some renal cell carcinomas (RCCs) have substantially overlapping CT appearances, making them difficult to distinguish by visual assessment. Here, we present a tri-phase enhancement-difference fusion framework guided by phase-level auxiliary supervision to explicitly model enhancement changes across the precontrast phase (PCP), corticomedullary phase (CMP) and nephrographic phase (NP). The proposed UniRepLKNet-based configuration achieved an AUC of 0.981 ± 0.011 and an F1 score of 0.933 ± 0.022 in the representative-method comparison. Five-seed ablation experiments also assessed the individual and combined contributions of TEDM and PAS to model performance. To our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end framework for renal tumor differentiation that explicitly models three-phase enhancement differences and incorporates phase-level auxiliary supervision during training. This study provides a comparative baseline for multiphase renal tumor differentiation and may inform the development of more efficient phase-aware approaches.

title: Bottleneck Width, Loss Design and the Limits of Skip-Free Convolutional Denoising Autoencoders for Simulated Low-Dose CT
abstract: Abstract Convolutional denoising autoencoders (DAEs) are attractive for computed tomography (CT) because they offer a small model and a compact, reusable latent code, but it is unclear whether a skip-free DAE can compete with feed-forward residual networks. We examine this question on 41 abdominal CT volumes from the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (820 real slices, split by volume) and 300 synthetic multi-material phantoms, corrupted with a two-stage noise model (Poisson photon noise followed by Gaussian read noise). We train convolutional DAEs with bottleneck widths of 8 to 256 channels, a variational variant and a composite MSE+SSIM loss, and compare them with a DnCNN-style network and with Gaussian, median and non-local-means filters on identical held-out volumes. DnCNN reached 44.21 dB PSNR and 0.979 SSIM, against 35.07 dB and 0.938 for the best MSE-trained autoencoder; the noisy input scored 35.56 dB and 0.756. The composite loss raised the autoencoder to 35.65 dB and 0.950. Quality was flat between 32 and 256 channels (PSNR spread 0.22 dB) and dropped only at 16 and 8 channels (− 0.9 and − 2.5 dB relative to width 128). On real slices the width-128 autoencoder lowered PSNR relative to the noisy input in 71% of cases, mainly at thin, high-contrast structures, even though SSIM improved by about 0.12. Latent codes predicted phantom material with 66–84% accuracy (chance 20%) but formed no clusters (silhouette ≈ 0). The autoencoder needed about 34 times less compute per tile than DnCNN, yet was far less accurate. In this setting the reconstruction-through-a-bottleneck design, rather than bottleneck size, appears to limit denoising quality; the role of skip connections remains to be isolated.

title: Shape and Attenuation Cues for Defect-Type Classification in X‑ray CT: A Controlled Synthetic Study with a 3D CNN
abstract: Abstract After a candidate defect has been located in an X-ray computed tomography (CT) volume, an inspector must still decide whether it is a pore, a crack or an inclusion, because each type has different acceptance criteria and root causes. Pores and cracks are voids with near-zero attenuation, whereas inclusions have a distinct, non-zero attenuation, so intensity should help where shape alone is ambiguous. We test this in a controlled synthetic study: 7,500 exactly labelled 3D patches (2,500 per class) generated from 200 simulated scans with partial-volume blur, shading and Poisson–Gaussian noise at three SNR levels, split by scan into training, validation and test sets. A compact 3D CNN (0.88 M parameters) reaches 0.990 test accuracy (0.990 ± 0.002 over five training seeds; 95% CI of the headline run 0.984–0.996). An identical network given only binary masks reaches 0.824 ± 0.015, a drop of 16.6 ± 1.6 points. In the headline run (drop 17.5 points; McNemar exact p ≈ 10⁻⁵⁰) the loss is confined to pore–inclusion confusion, cracks being recognised perfectly, and comes almost entirely from spherical inclusions, whose masks resemble spherical pores. Random Forest and SVM classifiers on shape and intensity features perform similarly (0.988–0.997), so the CNN is competitive rather than superior. All 11 errors of the headline run are either dark inclusions with contrast close to that of a void or pores and cracks of 59–69 voxels, and accuracy did not degrade from SNR 40 to 10. Because the data are synthetic, the results are an upper bound for real scans.

title: Non-invasive Prediction of Molecular and Histopathological Subtypes in Murine and Human Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma Using [18F]FDG PET
abstract: Abstract Purpose This study evaluates the utility of [ 18 F]fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography ([ 18 F]FDG PET) for Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) subtype differentiation across preclinical and clinical settings, and assesses the impact of tracer uptake timing on subtype discrimination. Methods [ 18 F]FDG uptake was investigated in classical (C)-HPAC and quasi-mesenchymal (QM)-PSN1 cells, heterotopic rat (n = 11), orthotopic mouse xenografts (n = 8), and gland-forming (GF)/non-GF tumors from seven genetically engineered mouse models (GEMMs). Retrospective [ 18 F]FDG PET data from 16 PDAC patients were analyzed using subtype classification based on keratin-81 (KRT81+(QM)/KRT81-(non-QM)). Dynamic and static [ 18 F]FDG PET parameters, including standard uptake value (SUV) mean , SUV max , and mean tumor-to-muscle ratio (T/M mean ), were evaluated for subtype discrimination. Results QM tumors showed significantly higher [ 18 F]FDG uptake than C tumors in vitro (50.7 ± 1.03% vs. 19.4 ± 2.37%), in heterotopic (SUV max 6.91 ± 1.14 vs. 2.66 ± 0.28), and orthotopic (SUV max 2.85 ± 0.70 vs. 1.45 ± 0.50) xenografts. Non-GF tumors also showed significantly higher uptake than GF (SUV max 3.94 ± 0.70 vs. 2.53 ± 0.97). Patients showed a similar trend (SUV max 6.33 ± 1.74 vs. 4.95 ± 1.46), with shorter overall survival in QM tumors. Dynamic PET revealed continued tracer accumulation in QM/non-GF tumors throughout the 90-minute acquisition period, whereas C/GF tumors approached a plateau by approximately 60 minutes. T/M mean showed the best classification performance across all models. Conclusion [ 18 F]FDG PET differentiated PDAC subtypes across all preclinical models with a similar but less pronounced trend in patients. Later imaging time points showed enhanced metabolic separation, suggesting potential benefits for improving non-invasive subtype discrimination. Clinical Trial Registration N/A

title: AI-Based 3D Pore Volume and Morphology Prediction
abstract: Abstract X-ray computed tomography can quantify pores inside a material, but noisy and blurred pore boundaries make measurements sensitive to the segmentation procedure. This work evaluates direct regression of pore volume, surface area proxy, sphericity, and elongation from a centered synthetic grayscale crop. We generated 180 independent sphere, ellipsoid, and irregular pore geometries and rendered each under three degradation conditions, yielding 540 crops of size 24 3 . All renderings of each geometry remained in one split. A compact three-dimensional convolutional neural network (CNN) was compared with Otsu thresholding and an Extra Trees regressor using segmentation and intensity features. On 27 held-out geometries at high degradation, volume mean absolute percentage error was 14.76% for the CNN, 67.29% for Otsu, and 3.74% for Extra Trees. Otsu recovered clean discrete volume exactly and had the lowest pooled elongation error. Paired and out-of-domain experiments reveal how size, nearby pores, unresolved features, and sampling affect the results. The contribution is a reproducible synthetic benchmark that identifies conditions under which learned estimation improves on thresholding and conditions where classical measurements remain stronger. Independent industrial scans are needed to assess transfer.

title: A simple index derived from cerebral blood flow SPECT for differentiating Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal lobar degeneration
abstract: Abstract Objective Anti-amyloid-β (Aβ) antibody therapy requires confirmation of Aβ pathology, but cerebrospinal fluid testing is invasive and amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) is costly. Differentiating Alzheimer's disease (AD) from frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) is also essential for treatment planning. We evaluated whether a simple index derived from cerebral blood flow single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT), namely the difference in hypoperfusion between disease-specific and non-specific regions, could differentiate AD from non-AD and FTLD from non-FTLD. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 46 patients who underwent N-isopropyl-p-[123I]iodoamphetamine (123I-IMP) SPECT: 27 with AD (9 with mild cognitive impairment due to AD and 18 with mild AD dementia; 9 amyloid PET-positive), 9 with FTLD, 7 with vascular dementia, and 3 with other diagnoses. Using 10 cortical regions from three-dimensional stereotactic surface projection (3D-SSP), we calculated the mean Z-score of AD-specific regions (parietal lobe, precuneus, and posterior cingulate gyrus; specific AD), that of the remaining 7 regions (outside AD), and their difference. FTLD indices were calculated similarly from FTLD-specific regions (frontal and temporal lobes) and the remaining 8 regions. Groups were compared using the Mann-Whitney U test and receiver operating characteristic analysis. Results The median specific AD − outside AD value was 2.55 in AD and − 1.26 in non-AD (p < 0.001; area under the curve [AUC] 0.836). The AUC was 0.871 for mild cognitive impairment due to AD, 0.819 for mild AD dementia, and 0.895 for amyloid PET-positive AD, whereas specific AD alone yielded AUCs of 0.713–0.760. The median specific FTLD − outside FTLD value was 5.11 in FTLD and 0.185 in non-FTLD (p < 0.001; AUC 0.856); specific FTLD alone yielded an AUC of 0.886. No index correlated with Mini-Mental State Examination scores or medial temporal atrophy. Conclusions The difference in hypoperfusion between disease-specific and non-specific regions differentiated AD and FTLD independently of disease severity. This index can be easily calculated from routine 3D-SSP analysis and may help select candidates for Aβ testing.

title: AI-Based Prediction of Total Porosity Volume Fraction from 3D CT Volumes: A Volumetric Regression Approach
abstract: Abstract Computed Tomography (CT) is a premier non-destructive testing (NDT) modality used for inspecting internal defects, particularly porosity in additive manufacturing and metal castings. The standard industry workflow relies on voxel-wise image segmentation (e.g., Otsu thresholding) to separate void spaces from the solid matrix before calculating the total Porosity Volume Fraction (PVF). However, this segmentation step is highly brittle under severe measurement noise and artifacts, leading to catastrophic miscalculations. In this paper, we propose a direct deep-learning regression approach using a 3D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) equipped with Global Average Pooling (GAP) to predict scalar PVF directly from noisy 3D CT volumes, bypassing segmentation entirely. To validate this hypothesis, we engineered a rigorous synthetic 3D CT dataset containing 500 procedural phantoms with precisely controlled spherical pores and uniformly distributed PVF ranging from 0.1% to 15%. We degraded these volumes with varying levels of Gaussian noise (10 dB, 20 dB, and 30 dB SNR). The 3D CNN was evaluated against classical Otsu thresholding and a Random Forest (RF) machine learning baseline utilizing global intensity statistics. Our results demonstrate that the 3D CNN is exceptionally robust, maintaining a low Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.363 percentage points even under extreme 10 dB noise, where Otsu thresholding catastrophically collapses (MAE of 11.51 pp). Unexpectedly, the RF baseline achieved the lowest overall MAE (0.088 pp). Through a rigorous evidence audit and domain-shift experiment involving a simulated beam-hardening cupping artifact, we dissect this phenomenon, revealing that the RF's superiority is a statistical artifact of the synthetic data's homogenous matrix assumption. This research highlights the viability of segmentation-free volumetric regression for NDT while providing a critical warning regarding 'shortcut learning' in synthetic physics datasets.

The 3D CNN was evaluated against classical Otsu thresholding and a Random Forest (RF) machine learning baseline utilizing global intensity statistics. Our results demonstrate that the 3D CNN is exceptionally robust, maintaining a low Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.363 percentage points even under extreme 10 dB noise, where Otsu thresholding catastrophically collapses (MAE of 11.51 pp). Unexpectedly, the RF baseline achieved the lowest overall MAE (0.088 pp). Through a rigorous evidence audit and domain-shift experiment involving a simulated beam-hardening cupping artifact, we dissect this phenomenon, revealing that the RF's superiority is a statistical artifact of the synthetic data's homogenous matrix assumption. This research highlights the viability of segmentation-free volumetric regression for NDT while providing a critical warning regarding 'shortcut learning' in synthetic physics datasets.

title: Sparse-View CT Reconstruction Using Deep Learning
abstract: Abstract Sparse-view computed tomography (CT) reduces radiation dose and scan time by acquiring few projection angles but filtered back-projection (FBP) of such data suffers from severe streak artefacts because the angular sampling falls far below the Nyquist requirement. We study the post-processing approach in which a residual U-Net removes these artefacts from the FBP image, and test it on five synthetic datasets that differ in object class and physics: head phantoms at normal dose, chest phantoms at ten-fold lower dose, aluminium machined parts, photon-starved titanium components, and aluminium resolution targets. Sinograms at 30, 60 and 90 views are simulated with the Beer-Lambert law, Poisson photon statistics and Gaussian read noise, and the network is compared against FBP and the Simultaneous Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (SART), both with settings tuned on validation data. On 150 held-out test images per dataset, the U-Net achieves the highest peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) in all 15 dataset and view settings, improving on the best classical method by 1.9 to 5.8 dB (paired Wilcoxon test, p < 10⁻²⁰ in every setting), and at 30 views it exceeds the PSNR of 180-view FBP on all five datasets, while running in about 20 ms per image on a CPU. Stress tests show the limits of the approach: networks transfer between similar industrial datasets but degrade or harm images of other object classes, fail when the test data are more sparsely sampled or receive ten times fewer photons than in training, and are outperformed by SART on the unseen Shepp-Logan phantom. A network trained on resolution targets does generalise to a resolution plate taken from laboratory data, improving on SART by 2.7 to 3.4 dB. The code, data and trained models are released for full reproducibility.

title: LowFU-HC: A Multi-Task Learning Method for Fetal Head Circumference Estimation in a Low-Resource Setting
abstract: Abstract Maternal and perinatal mortality remain significant challenges in low-to-middle-income countries, where access to advanced fetal monitoring technologies is limited. Deep learning models have shown promise in automating fetal biometry; however, their deployment is often hindered by computational constraints and limited data availability. This study aims to develop an efficient and accurate method for fetal head circumference (HC) estimation from 2D ultrasound images, specifically designed for resource-limited settings. In this work, we propose LowFU-HC, a multi-task learning approach combined with a modified loss function for fetal head circumference (HC) estimation in 2D ultrasound images that combines head segmentation and fetal ellipse parameter prediction. During inference, only the encoder and regression layers are retained, ensuring efficiency. compared to some state-ofthe-art methods, LowFU-HC achieves an HC error of 2.77 mm, with an inference time of 0.35 seconds on CPU and a memory usage of 370 MB on a 400x400 image. By optimizing model efficiency while maintaining high accuracy, our approach enables reliable HC estimation on CPU-only devices. This makes it a practical solution in low-resource settings, where access to high-performance computing resources is limited.

title: Deep Learning Ring Artifact Removal in Computed Tomography: A Two-Head U-Net Benchmarked Against Classical Radial profile Filtering
abstract: Abstract Ring artifacts, caused by detector pixels whose gain or offset is slightly wrong, appear in reconstructed computed tomography (CT) slices as concentric circles around the rotation centre. They can hide small features and break threshold-based segmentation. Classical ring removal relies on hand-tuned filters, and real scans have no ground truth for measuring how well a method works. This project builds a synthetic CT pipeline (phantom, parallel-beam projection, Poisson noise, detector gain and offset error, filtered back-projection) in which the true ring is known for every image, and trains a two-head U-Net that predicts the ring image, which is subtracted from the input, and a ring mask. On 1000 training, 100 validation and 100 test slices of 256 × 256 pixels, where the test slices come from a phantom family never seen in training, the U-Net raises the peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) from 33.11 dB to 39.54 dB and the structural similarity (SSIM) from 0.868 to 0.957. A radial-profile classical baseline tuned on the validation set gains 0.77 dB on validation but loses 0.56 dB on the unseen family. The U-Net gain depends on ring type, from +13.9 dB for dead_hot rings to +0.4 dB for faint band rings. Training with 100, 500 and 1000 images gives 35.29, 38.42 and 39.54 dB; three random seeds give 39.40 ± 0.15 dB; removing the Dice term from the loss raises PSNR to 39.89 dB but lowers mask Dice from 0.640 to 0.605. The mask head is the weaker output (Dice 0.640 overall, 0.07 on band rings). Because all data are simulated, the sim-to-real gap remains the main open question.

title: Controlled Benchmarking and Robustness Analysis of Classical Machine-Learning Approaches for Synthetic CT Sample Segmentation
abstract: Abstract Reliable delineation of a specimen from its surrounding background is a prerequisite for quantitative analysis of computed tomography (CT) images. This work is positioned as a controlled benchmarking and robustness study of classical machine-learning approaches for binary sample–background segmentation in synthetic CT-like images, rather than as a demonstration of validated industrial CT applicability. Five supervised classifiers—Logistic Regression (LR), Gaussian Naive Bayes (GNB), linear Support Vector Machine (SVM), Decision Tree (DT), and Random Forest (RF)—are compared using a synthetic dataset of 300 grayscale images (256 × 256 pixels) with corresponding binary reference masks. Three pixel-level feature representations are examined: intensity alone; intensity with normalized spatial coordinates; and a five-dimensional representation comprising intensity, two spatial coordinates, local mean, and local standard deviation calculated over a 5 × 5 neighbourhood. The dataset is divided into training, validation, and testing subsets containing 210, 45, and 45 images, respectively. Under the constructed synthetic conditions, the DT classifier using the complete feature set achieves the highest reported mean test accuracy (0.9998), Dice coefficient (0.9997), and intersection over union (IoU; 0.9995). Sensitivity experiments reveal marked performance degradation as additive Gaussian noise increases and image contrast decreases, whereas increasing the training-set size produces only marginal gains. The principal contribution is a controlled comparison of classical pixel-wise classifiers, an assessment of feature-engineering effects, and a robustness analysis under specified synthetic perturbations. The results characterize model behaviour within the defined synthetic data-generating process; they do not establish performance on experimental or industrial XCT data. Validation using independent, representative XCT scans is a necessary subsequent step.

title: MRI Anterograde Fistulography Using Rectally Administered Diluted Gadolinium and 3D LAVA-Flex for Preoperative Evaluation of Anal Fistulas: A Prospective Pilot Study
abstract: Abstract Background Accurate preoperative delineation of internal openings and fistulous tracts is important for planning surgery for anal fistulas. MRI anterograde fistulography (MRI-AFG) combines rectally administered diluted gadolinium, a straining defecation, and three-dimensional liver acquisition with volume acceleration-Flex (3D LAVA-Flex) imaging. Objective To describe the feasibility and preliminary diagnostic performance of MRI-AFG in the preoperative assessment of anal fistulas. Methods In this prospective pilot study, 12 patients underwent conventional MRI and MRI-AFG before surgery in 2026. Surgical findings were the reference standard. Internal openings, fistulous tracts, and Parks classifications were assessed descriptively. Results All 12 patients underwent surgery. Surgery identified 20 internal openings and 28 fistulous tracts. Conventional MRI and MRI-AFG detected 16/20 (80%) and 15/20 (75%) internal openings and 25/28 (89.3%) and 21/28 (75.0%) fistulous tracts, respectively. Correct clock-face position and anal-verge distance were each reported for 11/20 (55%) internal openings on conventional MRI and 15/20 (75%) on MRI-AFG. Both methods agreed with the surgical Parks classification in 11/12 patients (91.7%). MRI-AFG maximum-intensity-projection (MIP) images depicted communications among complex fistulous tracts. Conclusion MRI-AFG may provide complementary information about patent internal openings and tract communications, although conventional MRI detected more openings and tracts in this small cohort. Clinical Impact: MRI-AFG may improve preoperative anatomic mapping in selected patients with complex anal fistulas; larger studies are needed to establish its clinical value.

title: Hybrid Deep Learning Ensemble for Ophthalmic Disease Classification: Integrating CNNs and Vision Transformers
abstract: Abstract Standalone Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Vision Transformers (ViTs) exhibit representational trade-offs between capturing localized microvascular lesions and global contextual dependencies in retinal fundus imaging. To address this limitation, this study presents a novel tri-branch hybrid deep learning ensemble framework for multi-class classification across ten distinct ocular conditions. Retinal fundus photographs (16,242 images across 10 categories) were enhanced using a dual-stage pipeline incorporating CLAHE color space transformation and Fourier domain high-pass filtering. The proposed framework fuses extracted features from two CNN backbones (EfficientNet-B0 and VGG16) and a Vision Transformer (ViT-Base) into a 6,144-dimensional representation. The network was trained using a strategic two-phase transfer learning regimen with differential learning rates and class-weighted cross-entropy loss. Grad-CAM visualizations were utilized for qualitative explainability against clinical landmarks. The hybrid ensemble achieved an overall accuracy of 88.99%, macro-sensitivity of 92.36%, macro-specificity of 98.72%, macro F1-score of 90.95%, and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) of 0.8718. This demonstrates a 10.04% accuracy improvement over standalone deep CNNs and a 34.36% increase over handcrafted feature baselines (GLCM/HOG + SVM). Grad-CAM heatmaps confirmed strong alignment with clinically verified pathological features. Combining local texture representations with global contextual self-attention offers high diagnostic reliability and explainability, establishing a robust decision-support system for broad-coverage ocular screening in resource-constrained settings.

title: Development and External Validation of an MRI-Based Multimodal Fusion Model Incorporating Deep Learning and Radiomics for Non-Invasive Prediction of 21-Gene Recurrence Score in Breast Cancer
abstract: Abstract Background: The 21-gene recurrence score (RS) informs adjuvant therapy decisions in selected patients with hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative early breast cancer. Tissue requirements, costs, and availability can limit testing. We evaluated an MRI-based multimodal fusion model combining clinical variables, handcrafted radiomics, and tri-planar deep-learning representations to predict RS ≥ 18. Methods: This retrospective multicohort study evaluated 447 patients with preoperative dynamic contrast-enhanced breast MRI and either measured or transcriptomic-derived 21-gene RS labels. The development cohort combined Peking University Shenzhen Hospital and Duke-Breast-Cancer-MRI cases (n = 324). Development-cohort performance was evaluated using stratified 5-fold cross-validation out-of-fold predictions, with all data-dependent transformations, feature selection, and model fitting restricted strictly within each training fold. TCGA-BRCA cases with RNA-seq-derived RS labels (n = 123) formed the independent external-validation cohort. Four models were evaluated: clinical, radiomics, deep learning, and feature-level fusion using logistic regression. Performance was assessed using AUC with 5,000-replicate bootstrap 95% CIs, threshold-based classification metrics, average precision, Brier score, calibration, and decision-curve analysis. SHAP explained the feature-level fusion model, and Grad-CAM was applied to the deep-learning model. Results: The proportion of patients with RS ≥ 18 was 153/324 (47.2%) in the development cohort and 58/123 (47.2%) in the external-validation cohort. External-validation AUCs were 0.669 (95% CI, 0.568–0.763) for the clinical model, 0.616 (0.513–0.711) for radiomics, 0.686 (0.590–0.774) for deep learning, and 0.800 (0.722–0.872) for multimodal fusion. The corresponding average precision values were 0.687, 0.552, 0.686, and 0.777. At the fixed probability threshold of 0.472, fusion achieved 69.1% accuracy, 65.5% sensitivity, 72.3% specificity, 67.9% PPV, and 70.1% NPV. Its Brier score was 0.182. Decision-curve analysis suggested potential net benefit across part of the evaluated threshold range. In the SHAP analysis, a tri-planar deep feature had the highest global importance, with contributions from PR status and radiomic features. Conclusion: Multimodal fusion achieved higher observed discrimination than the individual models in an independent cohort with transcriptomic-derived RS labels. This MRI-based framework warrants further evaluation as an adjunct to genomic testing in preoperative workflows.

title: Automatic and precise segmentation of medical ultrasound images based on concurrent multi-scale adaptive attention
abstract: Abstract Many convolutional neural networks have been proposed for medical ultrasound image segmentation. Unfortunately, the convolution operation with fixed receptive fields cannot capture robust target characterizations from complex ul-trasound images. Moreover, severe heterogeneous structures, similar intensity distributions, ambiguous boundaries, and variable morphologies also bring great challenges to the precise segmentation of medical ultrasound images. In this paper, a unique deep U-shaped framework with the concurrent adaptive attention module is constructed for the robust segmentation of medical ultrasound image. The concurrent adaptive attention module designed in this paper includes two branches of adaptive attention: channel feature adaptive and spatial feature adaptative. During the calibration of the two attention branches, they can adaptively select robust characterizations captured from different convolutional kernels and reduce the introduction of irrelevant features. In addition, the design of multiple convolu-tional kernels in this attention module not only attenuates the influence of target morphology on the network but also strengthens the representational power of objective regions. The proposed method achieved the best results on four medical ultrasound datasets, with Dice scores of 0.7944, 0.8053, 0.9383, and 0.9082, respectively. Furthermore, the proposed method produced probability-values less than 0.05 based on the Student’s t-test for all evaluation metrics. The robustness of our approach on medical ultrasound image segmentation task is perfectly demonstrated through the extensive and reliable experimental results with more than ten state-of-the-art deep learning segmentation approaches on four datasets. Moreover, the comparison with several classical and advanced attention modules further evidences the effectiveness of the concurrent adaptive attention module.

title: A Two-Stage Framework Combining U-Net++ Lung Segmentation and DenseNet121 for Multi-Class Classification from Chest X-Ray
abstract: Abstract Chest X-rays (CXRs) are widely used to detect lung diseases, but deep learning classifiers may rely on visual cues outside the lungs rather than relevant clinical features. This study evaluates three lung segmentation models (U-Net, U-Net++, and fine-tuned SAM ViT-B) and four ImageNet-pretrained classifiers (DenseNet121, ResNet50, VGG19, and Xception) using the COVID-19 Radiography Database of 21,165 images. U-Net++ achieved the best segmentation performance, while DenseNet121 performed best in classification. Based on these findings, we developed a two-stage framework that uses U-Net++ to segment the lungs and DenseNet121 to classify the extracted regions as COVID-19, Lung Opacity, Normal, or Viral Pneumonia. The framework was tested on unlabeled DICOM radiographs from a diagnostic center without additional fine-tuning. A medical doctor reviewed 15 cases flagged as low-confidence during an earlier run, revealing disagreements in which abnormal cases were classified as Normal, sometimes with very high confidence. Grad-CAM and insertion/deletion curves were used to examine the image regions influencing the model's predictions. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of integrating lung segmentation and disease classification for native DICOM images while highlighting the need for careful clinical validation beyond benchmark performance.

title: Deterministic and Gaussian Decoder LoRA for Point-Prompted Abdominal CT Segmentation
abstract: Abstract This study examines deterministic low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and Gaussian decoder LoRA with heuristic rank selection for point-prompted abdominal CT segmentation using SAM2. Both approaches were evaluated on a single BTCV split comprising 19 training, five validation, and six test volumes, with one training seed and 2,466 matched positive-point prompts. Across 78 volume–organ pairs, mean Dice scores were 0.5123 for frozen SAM2, 0.8049 for deterministic LoRA, and 0.7982 for Gaussian decoder LoRA. The deterministic model achieved a 0.667-percentage-point advantage under equal volume– organ weighting (descriptive 95% t interval: −0.214 to +1.549), although the difference became −0.019 points under equal prompt weighting. We also investigated whether decoder uncertainty provides additional information for identifying segmentation failures. Adding full-image mutual information (MI) to a failureranking model containing organ identity, predicted area, and entropy produced a negligible change in mean AUROC (−0.0001). Retrospective inference-only analyses showed similarly limited effects from replacing learned decoder standard deviations with fixed values. Adding dropout MI to organ, area, and entropy on 189 deterministic-model failures changed AUROC from 0.8222 to 0.8238. The Gaussian decoder also required substantially more inference time than its deterministic counterpart. Both adaptation strategies improved overlap relative to frozen SAM2, but the available evidence does not establish a consistent advantage for Gaussian decoder adaptation or its uncertainty estimates beyond simpler alternatives.

The deterministic model achieved a 0.667-percentage-point advantage under equal volume– organ weighting (descriptive 95% t interval: −0.214 to +1.549), although the difference became −0.019 points under equal prompt weighting. We also investigated whether decoder uncertainty provides additional information for identifying segmentation failures. Adding full-image mutual information (MI) to a failureranking model containing organ identity, predicted area, and entropy produced a negligible change in mean AUROC (−0.0001). Retrospective inference-only analyses showed similarly limited effects from replacing learned decoder standard deviations with fixed values. Adding dropout MI to organ, area, and entropy on 189 deterministic-model failures changed AUROC from 0.8222 to 0.8238. The Gaussian decoder also required substantially more inference time than its deterministic counterpart. Both adaptation strategies improved overlap relative to frozen SAM2, but the available evidence does not establish a consistent advantage for Gaussian decoder adaptation or its uncertainty estimates beyond simpler alternatives.

title: Neuroimaging Cranial Pathology Delineation through Contrast-Specialized Specialist Routing
abstract: Abstract Purpose Cranial MRI reaches the reading room in whatever contrast combination the scanner, site and protocol produced, and lesion appearance changes with contrast. A department that wants segmentation support must maintain a separate model for each contrast combination, a library that is hard to sustain in routine practice. We evaluated a single deep learning framework that replaces that library with contrast-specialised routing. Materials and methods The framework (OMNIA) keeps one specialist subnetwork for each MR contrast and fuses their predictions at every resolution level through a hierarchical gating network that assigns voxelwise weights. Progressive training protects each specialist's contrast-specific behaviour, and a soft allocation module routes incomplete contrast sets to the specialist channels under an availability prior. The study was retrospective, across nine collections totalling 6,336 annotated volumes, five contrasts and six pathology groups, with a healthy reference collection; six public collections were used for training and internal testing, and three institutional collections were held back for external testing. Results On the seen collections the framework reached a mean Dice of 0.8204, above every universal baseline (0.8007–0.8084) and close to dedicated per-combination pipelines (0.8250), as a single deployable model. On the unseen collections it reached 0.7951, the strongest result among single models. On multi-contrast BraTS 2021 input it scored 0.8334 against 0.8366 for fifteen dedicated models, at about one third of their storage (1.65 GB versus about 4.95 GB). Conclusion Contrast-specialised routing allows one deployable model to approach the accuracy of dedicated per-combination pipelines, on data and contrast combinations beyond those it was trained on.

title: Atanassov Intuitionistic Fuzzy Classification of Brain Tumor Patches in BraTS FLAIR MRI: Accuracy, Hesitation and Explainability
abstract: Abstract The proposed work uses a feature-based Atanassov intuitionistic fuzzy classifier (AIFC) for patch-level whole-tumor detection in FLAIR MRI from BraTS 2020. Each $11\times 11$ patch is described by four intensity moments and a center-referenced maximum deviation, and a trainable layer converts them into membership, non-membership and hesitation degrees before a small multilayer perceptron. Across five patient-level splits of 369 patients, the classifier reached an AUC of $0.979\pm 0.005$ and a Dice score of $0.83\pm 0.02$ on unseen patients, indistinguishable from a plain MLP on the same features. SHAP, LIME and permutation importance consistently show that mean intensity accounts for roughly 83\% to 97\% of the model's importance, and a logistic regression on mean intensity alone comes within about 0.005 AUC and 0.014 F1. Hesitation is lowest inside tumor tissue because it follows mean intensity, and it neither marks the tumor boundary nor flags errors. On this task the intuitionistic layer therefore adds readable parameters but no gain in accuracy or uncertainty, and simple baselines and attribution checks should accompany fuzzy neural classifiers.

title: Measuring lesion–vascular context for diabetic retinopathy grading and retinal phenotyping
abstract: Abstract BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) grades summarise severity but do not quantify the vascular surroundings of individual lesions. We investigated whether measured lesion–vascular context improves lesion-based grading and characterises vascular variation beyond severity. SUBJECTS/METHODS: This cross-sectional secondary analysis of public datasets matched 2,874 APTOS photographs to lesion predictions and AutoMorph vascular measurements (1,724 training, 575 validation, 575 test). Five models trained exclusively on DDR annotations predicted four lesion families. Registered anatomy yielded 24 spatial descriptors and 1,584 lesion–biomarker products. Structured ordinal models, an anatomical graph and six frozen image encoders evaluated grading. Separate grade-adjusted analyses assessed vascular associations and prediction. RESULTS: Structured context increased test quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) from 0.764 to 0.827 (difference 0.063; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.028–0.099). The graph achieved QWK 0.849 and macro area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.924 (QWK difference 0.085; 95% CI 0.050–0.119); both comparisons with lesion-only grading had false-discovery-rate-adjusted 𝑞 < 0.001. Individual contextual additions were not separately supported. Graph sensitivity for proliferative DR was 0.316, compared with 0.605 for structured context. Grade-adjusted analysis supported 103 lesion–biomarker associations, and lesion counts improved prediction of 26/66 vascular measurements, predominantly calibre/width and fractal measures. CONCLUSIONS: Combined lesion–vascular representations improved lesion-only grading and characterised vascular variation within severity categories. The measurements provide inspectable anatomical evidence, but segmentation limitations and classwise errors preclude claims of clinical readiness or prognostic validity.

title: A Novel Temporal Variability-Aware Architecture for Ictal-Interictal Continuum Patterns Classification
abstract: Abstract Harmful brain activity may compromise cerebral function and can culminate in mortality if not addressed appropriately. The global deficit of professionals adept in electroencephalogram (EEG) data analysis exacerbates the difficulty in resolving this issue. There is a pressing need for a reliable and automated system, particularly designed to effectively classify harmful brain activity using both signals and images. In this study, we proposed a novel model that can be used for signal as well as image classification. This study employs EEG recordings obtained from the HMS dataset and MRI scans from the Brain Tumor MRI dataset. The EEG dataset comprises 106,800 unique EEG identification numbers. Our proposed model, EfficientNetZEEGv1, with instability-aware gated TSA, demonstrated exceptional performance by achieving a validation accuracy of 97% and a loss of 0.20. We made some enhancements in the gating mechanism of the model, and our second model EfficientNetZEEGv2, achieved a validation accuracy of 98.74%. We have achieved the highest accuracy, precision, and recall values amongst all studies conducted in the domain of harmful brain activities.

title: Bilateral low-lying soleus and flexor hallucis longus muscle bellies: an incidental MRI finding that mimics posterior ankle and tarsal tunnel pathology
abstract: Abstract Purpose Low-lying muscle bellies of the flexor hallucis longus (FHL) and soleus are anatomical variations that can be overlooked in hindfoot imaging and surgical planning. We report bilateral low-lying soleus and FHL muscle bellies detected on MRI in a young man who presented with left medial ankle and plantar tingling, numbness and mild pain, running-related posterior ankle pain and bilateral posterior ankle swelling, and discuss their anatomical, radiological and surgical relevance. Methods A 25-year-old man under investigation for chronic inflammatory back pain, sacroiliitis and inflammatory arthritis presented with tingling, numbness and mild pain over the medial left ankle and the sole, posterior ankle pain that increased with running, and a sensation of posterior ankle swelling. Tinel's test over the left posterior tibial nerve was positive. MRI of both ankles was performed. Clinical, laboratory and imaging data were reviewed. Written informed consent was obtained. Results On MRI of both ankles the FHL and soleus muscle bellies extended lower than usual, whereas the Achilles tendon, plantar fascia, flexor tendons and peroneal tendons were normal. On the left, at the level of the distal tibiofibular joint, the abnormally low-lying and bulky FHL muscle obliterated the fat plane around the posterior tibial nerve medially and indented the nerve, and its musculotendinous junction reached the distal talus. Routine complete blood count, CRP and ESR were normal, HLA-B27 was negative, and the other laboratory tests were unremarkable Conclusion Low-lying soleus and FHL muscle bellies should be considered in the differential diagnosis of tarsal tunnel syndrome and posterior ankle impingement, should not be mistaken for a mass, edema or tear on MRI performed for inflammatory disease, and should be sought on MRI before FHL tendon transfer or hindfoot endoscopy.

title: Does a Brain-Tumour Segmentation Model Notice When a Weak Telemedicine Link Has Degraded Its Input?
abstract: Abstract A clinic without a specialist may send scans over a slow or lossy link to a hub where AI segments them. We asked whether the model’s own confidence warns when the transfer has damaged the scan. A simulator, validated on phantoms, turns a link and a deadline into what arrives: rate-controlled compression over reliable transport (assumed tiers and LTE traces), messaging-app recompression, and, as a worst case, real- time transport that loses image strips. We trained five U-Nets (one used alone, all five as an ensemble), a Monte Carlo dropout U- Net and nnU-Net on 70 patients of a public glioma MRI dataset, and tested them on 30 held-out patients (1320 transmissions per model). Over reliable transport, mean Dice per condition stayed within 0.027 of clean; for studies sent below 0.3 bits per pixel (down to 0.11), it changed by − 0.011 to − 0.030. Losing strips was harmful. Row interpolation removed 92–99% of the harm under independent loss and 59–83% under bursts. On failures (Dice lost ≥ 0.10 ), confidence in the predicted tumour barely fell, and after temperature scaling every model was still overconfident (ECE 0.099–0.176). Disagreement between test- time-augmentation passes ranked U-Net failures better than U- Net’s confidence did (area under the risk–coverage curve 0.109 against 0.141). Ensemble and nnU-Net confidence did as well as uncertainty; a single ensemble member’s did not. Receiver-side image quality detected transmission damage (AUROC 0.91 for U-Net) but missed patients who were hard before transfer. A combined score did well on both.

title: Implementing Screening Questionnaires and a Fish Bone Diagram-Based Program to Enhance the Ability of DBW Education in Hemodialysis Nurses
abstract: Abstract Background: Dry body weight evaluation to detect high and low hydration status is paramount in daily hemodialysis practice. Our aim is to implement screening questionnaires and fish bone diagram-based program to improve the ability of dry body weight education of hemodialysis nurses. Methods: This pioneer research by four staff members was initially authorized by the medical quality and patient safety talent training project and competition meeting initiated by the administrative units of Taipei City Hospital and then approved by Taipei City Hospital Research Ethics Committee with the case number of TCHIRB-11206015.The study began with screening questionnaires of educational test about dry body weight education. Subsequently, teams composed of nurse faculty were evaluated for three domains of dry body weight evaluation, such as hemodialysis nurse’s knowledge and education skills on dry body weight, body components and body weight assessment equipment and tools. A fish bone diagram for root cause analysis was implemented with improvement of knowledge and skills of dry body weight evaluation of nurse faculty, methods of dry body weight evaluation, equipment for dry body weight evaluation, tools of dry body weight evaluation, environment of dry body weight evaluation, and materials of dry body weight evaluation. Results: Wilcoxon Signed Ranks Test are used to identify statistically significant differences in the scores of between the domain 1 and domain 2, between domain 1 and domain 2A, and between domain 1 and domain 2B. The screening questionnaires revealed. A Fish bone diagram was completed and presented to improve the ability of dry body weight education of hemodialysis nurses with dry body evaluation education sheet, poster and ever scam education software. In addition, suggestions for improving the ability of dry body weight education include inclusion of nutritional staff involvement, post- dialysis cardiac echo for inferior vena diameter, chest ultrasound for B lines, Crit-Line for blood volume monitor, DEXA for body composition evaluation, and selection of topics of food salt and water content, techniques and environment of dry body weight evaluation, bio-impedance, and upper arm anthropometry. Conclusions: Accurate evaluation of dry body weight by clinical evaluation, equipment and tools not only can prevent hemodialysis patients from deterioration of cardiopulmonary function and the chance of emergency dialysis due to high hydration status but also prevent patients from hospitalization due to shock and thrombotic complications due to low hydration status, and therefore reduce their medical costs and improve patient satisfaction and trust in the hospital.

title: M2-US: A Large-scale Multi-domain and Multi-task Ultrasound Image Dataset
abstract: Abstract Ultrasound imaging is widely used across clinical specialties. Artificial Intelligence methods have shown remarkable advantages in ultrasound image analysis in recent decades. However, the development of generalizable Artificial Intelligence methods remains limited by the heterogeneity of ultrasound data and the task-specific design of most existing datasets. Here, we present M2-US, a large-scale multi-domain benchmark for unified multi-task ultrasound image analysis. The dataset consists of 67,620 ultrasound images from public datasets and retrospectively collected clinical cohorts. It covers more than 30 anatomical structures and pathological targets across maternal-fetal, cardiac, vascular, abdominal, pulmonary, breast, thyroid, gynecological, and other clinical applications. M2-US supports four major prediction tasks: segmentation, classification, object detection, and landmark regression, organized into 26 subtasks. The dataset provides predefined training, validation, and test partitions, together with task-specific annotations and standardized metadata linking ultrasound images to their corresponding segmentation masks, class labels, bounding boxes, and landmark coordinates. Baseline experiments using Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) and DINOv3 models show the usability of the dataset and evaluation pipeline across heterogeneous ultrasound tasks. To our knowledge, M2-US is the first large-scale ultrasound benchmark comprising data acquired using approximately 24 scanner models from more than 10 manufacturers and covering over 30 anatomical structures and pathological targets. The benchmark supports four major downstream tasks across segmentation, classification, detection, and regression. Together with our evaluation pipeline, the benchmark enables systematic evaluation of task-specific models, multi-task learning methods, foundation model adaptation, as well as cross-domain generalization in ultrasound image analysis.

title: Pneumonia Detection from Chest X-Rays Using Deep Convolutional Neural Networks with Class Imbalance Mitigation
abstract: Abstract Pneumonia remains a leading cause of mortality worldwide, particularly affecting children and the elderly. Early and accurate diagnosis is critical for effective treatment and improved patient outcomes. Chest X-ray (CXR) imaging is the most common diagnostic tool, but its interpretation can be subjective and time-consuming, leading to inter-observer variability. This paper presents a deep learning-based approach for automated pneumonia detection from chest X-ray images. We employ a pre-trained ResNet-18 architecture fine-tuned on a publicly available dataset directory containing 5,860 entries (5,218 in the training folder, 18 in the original validation folder, and 624 in the test folder) (NORMAL and PNEUMONIA classes). To address the inherent class imbalance in medical imaging datasets, we implement a weighted loss function and a weighted random sampler during training. Our data augmentation pipeline incorporates random cropping, horizontal flipping, rotation, and color jittering to enhance model generalization. Two sequential training passes are recorded: the first yields training accuracy 94.27% and validation accuracy 93.30% (validation loss 0.2519), while the second yields training accuracy 96.74% and validation accuracy 95.11% (validation loss 0.2354) and is saved as the best checkpoint. On the held-out test set, the checkpoint achieves 92.63% accuracy and a binary ROC-AUC of 0.9737. The original validation folder is not used; validation is drawn from a random split of the training folder. These results describe the supplied experiment and do not establish external clinical validity.

title: Risk-Screened Multimodal Attribution for Glioma-like Segmentation: A Phantom-Based Study of Explanation Stability
abstract: Abstract \textbf{Background:} Segmentation performance with complete imaging may conceal sensitivity to sequence loss or contrast changes. \textbf{Objective:} We demonstrate risk-screened multimodal attribution (RSMA), a finite-library audit combining region-specific coalition utilities from independently screened predictors. \textbf{Methods:} A newly implemented simulation generated 320 two-dimensional MRI-like phantoms with four channels and three disjoint lesion regions. Four pixel-level classifiers were fitted on 160 phantoms, screened on 60, and evaluated on 100 held-out phantoms. Exact Shapley values were computed from 16 input subsets; 1,500 paired case bootstrap draws quantified attribution and rank uncertainty. \textbf{Results:} At the specified tolerance, all four candidates were retained and assigned unequal weights. RSMA had expected component-model macro Dice of 0.951 with complete inputs and 0.719 under mean single-channel deletion, versus 0.971 and 0.714 for the full-input baseline. Attribution drift under the specified shift was 0.047 (RSMA), 0.054 (baseline), and 0.046 (uniform pooling). Simultaneous intervals resolved 11 of 18 pairwise orderings. \textbf{Conclusion:} The experiment illustrates a trade-off between segmentation performance and attribution stability. RSMA incurred a full-input Dice cost relative to the validation-selected full-input model, while the mean single-deletion Dice was only modestly higher. The paired interval for shifted Dice relative to that baseline included zero. Uniform pooling produced lower drift, and its missing-input Dice was similar to RSMA. These findings do not support a universal advantage. At the primary tolerance no model was excluded; the comparison therefore primarily illustrates the effect of unequal risk-based weights. The narrower tolerance illustrates how the protocol can also select a strict subset. Model weights should be determined by deployment requirements rather than post hoc preference for an attribution profile.

Simultaneous intervals resolved 11 of 18 pairwise orderings. \textbf{Conclusion:} The experiment illustrates a trade-off between segmentation performance and attribution stability. RSMA incurred a full-input Dice cost relative to the validation-selected full-input model, while the mean single-deletion Dice was only modestly higher. The paired interval for shifted Dice relative to that baseline included zero. Uniform pooling produced lower drift, and its missing-input Dice was similar to RSMA. These findings do not support a universal advantage. At the primary tolerance no model was excluded; the comparison therefore primarily illustrates the effect of unequal risk-based weights. The narrower tolerance illustrates how the protocol can also select a strict subset. Model weights should be determined by deployment requirements rather than post hoc preference for an attribution profile.

title: Federated GANs for Histopathology Synthesis: Label Skew Breaks Conditional Training, and FID Can Miss Large Utility Gaps
abstract: Abstract Federated generative adversarial networks (GANs) have been proposed as a way for hospitals to share synthetic medical images without sharing patient data, but how they fail, and whether standard metrics would reveal the failure, are poorly characterized. We study unconditional and class-conditional GANs trained with federated averaging of the generator across five simulated clients on PathMNIST colorectal histology, under IID data, Dirichlet label skew (α = 0.1) on four independent partitions, and a client with corrupted images, with three seeds per configuration. Under label skew the conditional generator’s loss rises and stalls in all six runs with generator- only averaging, while it falls in every IID control and every unconditional run. Averaging the discriminators as well reduces the loss rise but lowers IID downstream accuracy by 21.6 points at an FID difference of only 1.2, so the two aggregation schemes are indistinguishable by FID yet far apart in utility. We measure utility as the test accuracy of a classifier trained on synthetic images and quantify the floor of this measurement: classifiers trained on content-free labels reach 15.3 ± 7.1% (up to 40.1%) when epochs are selected on labeled validation data, against 11.0% without selection. Against a centralized model given the federation’s total gradient steps, federation costs 54–80 FID points; against one given the same per-model step count, the unconditional GAN still pays 25 points but no cost is detected for the conditional GAN.

title: Deterministic projection selection for Limited-View Computed Tomography
abstract: Abstract In Limited-View Computed Tomography (LVCT), one restricts the number of projection angles (or views) for data reduction, which has many implications, especially in medical domain. In most of the existing works on LVCT, the views are sampled randomly or in equi-spaced manner, which makes the sampling process oblivion to the image reconstruction solvers. Motivated by this gap between the sampling strategy and the image reconstruction solvers, we propose a deterministic way of finding an optimal set of views for LVCT using block-sparse optimization problem. The proposed methodology is tied to a selection of Radon sub-matrix possessing low total coherence which is desired for sparsity-based CT image reconstruction. We demonstrate efficacy of the proposed deterministic LVCT in recovering CT images.

title: A 2.5D Attention-Enhanced Mask R-CNN with Multi-Scale Feature Fusion for Brain Tumor Segmentation from MRI Images
abstract: Abstract Advancements in Image processing technology play a crucial part in evaluating the pre-operative condition of tumor morphological state and hence in biopsy guidance. Neoplasm Segmentation is significant in radiotherapy treatment, progressive monitoring of disease and for stage prediction. Due to a number of circumstances, manual diagnosis is time-consuming; therefore, automatic picture segmentation is required. Image processing frequently involves clinical data from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). In this study, we suggested a Mask Region Convolutional Neural Network (RCNN) using an Inception U-Net architecture to carry out autonomous brain tumor segmentation. This model uses U-NET with Dilated Inception convolution as the Backbone network. Information on both a local and global scale is included in the feature map collected from the backbone network. Our model is experimented with the BraTS 2020 dataset and segmentation is carried out with the glioma portion, including tumor core, enhancing core and whole tumor, which are evaluated with various statistical parameters. Our model produces an accuracy of 96.01% for segmentation, proving the proposed approach overwhelms the comparative models with p<0.05.

title: A Comparative Study of Lightweight Uncertainty-Aware Bayesian CNNs and Ensemble Models for MRI-Based ASD Diagnosis
abstract: Abstract Background: Early and accurate diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is essential for improving clinical outcomes. Although deep learning (DL) has demonstrated strong potential in analyzing structural Magnetic Resonance Imaging (sMRI), most existing frameworks rely on deterministic models that lack uncertainty quantification—an essential component for clinical decision-making—and often involve high computational complexity, limiting real-world applicability. Objective: This study aims to conduct a comprehensive comparative evaluation of three deep learning paradigms to develop a robust and uncertainty-aware framework for ASD diagnosis using multi-orientational MRI data (axial, coronal, and sagittal views). Methods: We systematically evaluated three categories of models: (1) fine-tuned deterministic architectures, including EfficientNetV2B0, EfficientNetB3, and MobileNetV2; (2) ensemble learning strategies, including averaging, majority voting, weighted averaging, and stacked generalization; and (3) lightweight Bayesian convolutional neural networks (CNNs) incorporating Monte Carlo (MC) Dropout and Variational Inference (VI) to estimate predictive uncertainty. This hierarchical framework enables a balanced assessment of diagnostic accuracy and model reliability. Results: Experimental results demonstrate that ensemble models achieved the highest classification performance, with a peak accuracy of 99.51% in the coronal view. Notably, the proposed lightweight Bayesian CNNs delivered competitive performance while providing well-calibrated uncertainty estimates, enabling the identification of ambiguous and out-of-distribution cases. Additionally, Grad-CAM visualizations revealed that model attention is concentrated in clinically relevant regions, particularly the frontal and temporal lobes, supporting the neurobiological plausibility of the predictions. Conclusion: This study highlights that integrating uncertainty quantification into lightweight deep learning architectures enhances both transparency and reliability compared to conventional deterministic approaches.

title: Prompt-Conditioned Channel Attention for Hierarchical Feature Modulation toward Anatomy-Agnostic Segmentation
abstract: Abstract Accurate and anatomically plausible medical image segmentation remains challenging due to low contrast, ambiguous boundaries, interpatient variability, and modality-specific artifacts. Interactive segmentation using spatial prompts has emerged as a promising strategyto guide attention and improve localization, particularly in low-contrast or structurally ambiguous regions. However, existing methodstypically restrict prompt integration to late-stage fusion and lack explicit mechanisms for channel-wise feature modulation, limiting theirability to capture deeper contextual and modality-specific variations across hierarchical representations. To address these limitations, weintroduce Prompt-Conditioned Channel Attention (PCCA), a novel modulation mechanism that enables deep, hierarchical integration ofsemantic prompts within encoder-decoder segmentation networks. PCCA extracts compact channel descriptors from both image and promptfeatures via pooling, projects them into a shared latent space, and fuses them through a gated excitation unit to compute prompt-awarechannel attention weights. These weights perform hierarchical channel-wise attention by adaptively reweighting feature responses atevery network stage, enabling spatially selective and semantically enriched representations. Building on this mechanism, we proposePROMISE-Net (PROmpt Modulated Integration for SEgmentation), instantiated in two architectural variants: a convolutional model(PROMISE-CNN) and a transformer-based model (PROMISE-Txformer). Across ISIC-Lesion, Kvasir-Polyp, CAMUS-Cardiac, andKvasir-Instrument benchmarks, integrating PCCA into PROMISE-CNN yielded relative IoU improvements of 10.4%, 8.7%, 0.8%, and3.4% over baseline U-Net, while PROMISE-Txformer achieved corresponding gains of 7.6%, 23%, 2.1%, and 1.1% over baseline UNETR.These results demonstrate consistent cross-architectural, cross-modal, and cross-anatomical improvements, establishing PCCA coupledPROMISE-Net as a scalable and generalizable framework for prompt-aware feature modulation in medical image segmentation. The codeis available at https://github.com/kamruleee51/PROMISENet.

title: Diagnostic yield of CT angiography for pulmonary embolism in patients with interstitial lung disease admitted for acute respiratory worsening
abstract: Abstract Introduction : Acute respiratory worsening (ARW) in interstitial lung disease (ILD) is a critical clinical event with a broad differential diagnosis. Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a potential trigger, but its frequency, predictors, and prognostic implications in this setting remain poorly defined. Objective : To evaluate the diagnostic yield of CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) for PE, associated clinical features, and outcomes in patients with ILD admitted with ARW. Methods : This retrospective cohort study analyzed ILD patients admitted to a tertiary center (2017–2023) for ARW who underwent CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) within 72 hours. Data were retrieved using the MDClone platform and individual chart review, including demographic, clinical, and laboratory variables. In an exploratory analysis, CTPA results were compared with those of non-ILD patients who underwent CTPA, matched for age, sex, and smoking status. Results : Of 2,564 ILD admissions 439 were due to ARW, and CTPA was performed in 77 (17.5%, 68 unique patients). PE was diagnosed in 14 of these admissions (18.2% diagnostic yield). Individual clinical and laboratory features (tachycardia, hypoxemia, D-dimer, malignancy, and clinical signs of deep vein thrombosis) did not differ significantly between PE-positive and PE-negative admissions, with the exception of smoking status: PE was more frequent among never-smokers compared to current or former smokers (31.3% vs. 9.1%; OR 4.55; 95% CI 1.3–16.2), an association that persisted at the patient level and after adjustment for ILD type and age. At the patient level, the proportion of positive examinations was higher compared to matched controls (20.6% vs. 11.0%, p=0.04). No statistically significant association between PE and short- or long-term survival was detected. Conclusion : Among ILD patients with ARW who were selected for CTPA, approximately one in five had PE. Individual clinical and laboratory features did not reliably distinguish patients with PE, and the association with never-smoking status warrants confirmation. Prospective studies are needed to define the optimal diagnostic strategy for PE in this population.

title: CGMU-Net: A Classification-Guided Cross-Interaction Network for Computer-Assisted Dermoscopy Skin Lesion Segmentation
abstract: Abstract Accurate and effective segmentation of dermoscopic skin lesions is critical for clinical diagnosis. Despite recent advances in deep learning, challenges such as irregular shapes, blurred boundaries, and low contrast remain. To address these issues, we propose CGMU-Net, a classification-guided cross-interaction network. The model integrates a cross-interaction attention fusion module to enhance semantic--boundary feature interaction, a channel-wise feature enhancement module to improve multi-scale consistency, and a classification-guided lesion-aware module to introduce discriminative cues. Experimental results on three public datasets (ISIC 2017, ISIC 2018, and PH2) demonstrate that CGMU-Net achieves Dice scores of 89.21%, 89.91%, and 95.01%, respectively. These results indicate that the proposed method provides accurate and robust lesion segmentation.
