title: Right Ventricular Toxicity After Thoracic Radiotherapy: From Pathophysiological Mechanisms to Multimodality Imaging and Personalized Surveillance.
abstract: Radiotherapy (RT) is a cornerstone of treatment for several thoracic malignancies, most notably breast and lung cancers, and has significantly improved long-term survival. However, rising survivorship has heightened recognition of radiation-induced heart disease as a major contributor to long-term cardiovascular morbidity. While most cardio-oncology research has historically focused on left ventricular dysfunction, the right ventricle (RV) has recently emerged as a potentially vulnerable yet underrecognized target of radiation-related injury. Owing to its anterior position within the thorax, the RV free wall is frequently exposed to substantial radiation doses during thoracic irradiation, particularly when internal mammary nodal irradiation is required. Radiation-induced RV toxicity results from a complex interplay of direct myocardial injury and indirect cardiopulmonary interactions. At the myocardial level, ionizing radiation promotes endothelial dysfunction, microvascular rarefaction, chronic inflammation, and progressive interstitial fibrosis, ultimately impairing RV contractile mechanics. Simultaneously, radiation-induced lung injury contributes to pulmonary vascular remodeling, increased pulmonary vascular resistance, and RV-pulmonary artery uncoupling, further accelerating RV dysfunction. Contemporary multimodality imaging has substantially improved detection of these alterations in their subclinical phase. Advanced echocardiographic techniques, particularly RV free-wall longitudinal strain, enable early identification of mechanical abnormalities before conventional indices become abnormal. Cardiac magnetic resonance provides a highly reproducible assessment of RV volumes and function and offers unique capabilities for myocardial deformation analysis, tissue characterization, and quantification of diffuse fibrosis through extracellular volume mapping. Cardiac computed tomography has emerged as a critical tool for cardiac substructure dosimetry, facilitating personalized RT planning and RV sparing strategies. In parallel, radiomics and artificial intelligence approaches are opening new opportunities for individualized risk prediction and long-term surveillance. This narrative review summarizes the current understanding of the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying radiation-induced RV injury, critically examines the role of multimodality imaging in its detection and monitoring, and proposes an integrated clinical framework to improve early diagnosis, risk stratification, and prevention of RV dysfunction in patients exposed to thoracic RT.

title: The Prognostic Value of Coronary Computed Tomography Angiography Plaque Characteristics to Predict Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Background Coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) provides a non-invasive assessment of plaque morphology and burden, offering prognostic information beyond traditional risk factors. Recent studies suggest that CCTA-derived plaque features such as low-attenuation plaque, positive remodeling, and napkin-ring sign (NRS) may predict major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) independent of stenosis severity. To date, no comprehensive synthesis has evaluated the full spectrum of plaque variables in relation to MACE risk. Our objective was to compare and determine which CCTA plaque characteristics, including severity, composition, high-risk morphology, and disease extent, showed the greatest MACE association. Methods We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis using Medline, Embase, Emcare, Google Scholar and Web of Science databases for articles published between 1946 and September 2025 which reported hazard ratios (HRs) evaluating the association between CCTA plaque characteristics and ≥2-point MACE. Eligible studies included adult patients with suspected or known coronary artery disease (CAD) and ≥1-year follow-up. Pooled HRs were generated using random-effects models. Results 72 studies (n = 143,453) met the inclusion criteria. Obstructive stenosis ≥70% showed a strong association with MACE (HR 5.84, 95% confidence interval (CI) 3.86-8.85), followed by ≥50% stenosis (HR 5.04, 95% CI 3.44-7.39), and non-obstructive plaque remained significant (HR 1.54, 95% CI 1.19-1.98). High-risk plaque (HRP) features, including napkin-ring sign (HR 3.28, 95% CI 2.19-4.91), positive remodeling (HR 3.03, 95% CI 1.64-5.61), spotty calcification (HR 2.30, 95% CI 1.40-3.75) and low-attenuation plaque (HR 2.34, 95% CI 1.87-2.93) were also strongly associated with MACE beyond stenosis severity. Risk progressively increased with multivessel involvement (1-vessel: HR 4.18, 95% CI 1.60-10.93; 2-vessel: HR 7.34, 95% CI 2.15-25.10; 3-vessel: HR 10.91, 95% CI 3.50-33.99). Importantly, considerable between-study heterogeneity and evidence of publication bias were observed in selected analyses, while leave-one-out sensitivity analyses demonstrated stable pooled effect estimates. In the hard MACE subgroup of 25 studies, effect estimates were attenuated but remained directionally consistent, with reduced heterogeneity. These findings demonstrate that beyond luminal narrowing, HRPs and disease extent provide significant prognostic value. Conclusion CCTA-derived plaque characteristics, particularly HRP features and multivessel disease, were consistently associated with MACE across studies. These findings highlight the prognostic value of CCTA and support integrating plaque vulnerability and burden into cardiovascular risk stratification.

title: Advances in Neuroscience in an Age of Rapid Technological and AI Innovation – Towards Integration Across Scales
abstract: Rapid technological innovation and artificial intelligence (AI) have transformed not only the resolution at which the brain can be observed, but also the questions that can be asked, shifting the field from description toward prediction, regulation and generation. Yet progress has largely advanced along parallel trajectories, and findings at one level rarely inform or constrain the next. Here, we review recent advances in three exemplary domains and propose a future-oriented framework for their integration. First, molecular and cellular neurotechnology, including synaptic proteomics, cryo-electron tomography, super-resolution microscopy, optoacoustic and ultrasound imaging, sonogenetics and molecular MRI, resolves neural processes with unprecedented specificity. Second, AI-based decoding of human brain activity yields precise signatures of complex, subjective conscious experiences in naturalistic contexts and is beginning to inform diagnosis, drug evaluation and individualized neuromodulation in mental disorders. Third, large-scale neural recordings, mechanistic whole-brain simulations, neural foundation models and AI surrogate brains are converging toward individualized digital twin brains. We argue that the next level of progress requires integrating these domains into a closed loop of reciprocal constraints, in which molecular measurements inform model parameters, human signatures define and evaluate what models must reproduce, and model predictions prioritize perturbations that can be tested across domains.

title: Enhancing Diagnostic Accuracy in Lung Cancer: Evaluating the Performance of a Cutting-edge Artificial Intelligence Algorithm for Pulmonary Nodule Detection in Chest Radiographs.
abstract: Background Lung cancer remains a major global health challenge, and early diagnosis critically improves outcomes. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to enhance diagnostic accuracy in medical imaging, particularly for thoracic diseases. Objective This study evaluated a cutting-edge AI algorithm for detecting pulmonary nodules in chest radiographs to improve early lung cancer diagnosis. Material and methods In this analytical and experimental investigation, two datasets were used: Group1 (112120 frontal-view chest radiographs labeled for 14 thoracic diseases, including nodules) and Group2 (800 radiographs evenly split into positive and negative cases, with expert consensus labeling). The proprietary AI algorithm is based on CheXNet, a 121-layer convolutional neural network pretrained on ImageNet to initialize weights, enabling transfer learning for superior feature extraction. This model was chosen for its validated performance in thoracic disease detection, particularly in chest X-ray analysis. The datasets were divided into Type A (combining Group1 and Group2) and Type B (using only Group2) to assess performance under different conditions. A five-fold cross-validation was employed. Results The model achieved an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.73 for Type A and 0.782 for Type B. Sensitivity and specificity metrics were 0.736 and 0.592 for Type A, and 0.716 and 0.734 for Type B, respectively. Notably, the algorithm outperformed radiologists in some cases, demonstrating its capability to detect subtle or challenging nodules. Conclusion This AI algorithm shows promise as a clinical decision support tool, especially where access to experienced radiologists is limited. Further research is needed to refine the algorithm and validate use in real-world clinical workflows.

title: Liver Segmentation using Wavelet Coefficients and Level Set Algorithm.
abstract: In Computed Tomography (CT) scan, liver segmentation is crucial for diagnosing liver diseases. However, it faces challenges, such as partial volume effects, similarities in gray levels with adjacent organs, and variability in liver shapes. This technical note introduces a method combining wavelet coefficients and level set algorithms for precise liver segmentation. The proposed method integrates wavelet-based texture features with level set evolution, reducing reliance on pre-trained models and manual parameter tuning, and also demonstrates improved accuracy compared to existing approaches.

title: Machine learning prediction of meningioma grade using preoperative MRI: a large multicenter study.
abstract: Objective Preoperative knowledge of intracranial meningioma grade could significantly enhance surgical planning, but reliable noninvasive prediction remains an unmet clinical need. The aim of this study was to develop and externally validate a machine learning (ML) model incorporating traditional radiomic features, along with novel fractal and topological features, to predict WHO meningioma grade from preoperative MRI using a large multicenter cohort. Methods This retrospective diagnostic study analyzed a cohort of patients in the BraTS Meningioma Challenge. Patient data (n = 909) from 6 academic medical centers were used for model training and internal validation (n = 699) and one-time final external validation (n = 210). Tumors were segmented into three regions and radiomic features extracted across four MRI sequences. Eight different ML algorithms (e.g., based on neural networks, decision trees, clustering, and linear relationships) were tested across a total of 2889 candidate features. The primary outcome was the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) for prediction of binarized WHO grade (1 vs 2 or 3). Results The final model used a support vector machine algorithm comprising 20 features and achieved an AUROC of 0.824 (95% CI 0.755-0.883) on unseen test data, with favorable calibration. Feature importance analysis revealed that topological complexity added complementary predictive value to conventional radiomics features. The final model is publicly available for anyone to use. Conclusions This externally validated ML model accurately predicted meningioma grade using routine preoperative MRI, with the potential to guide surgical decision-making and serve as a basis for future imaging-based brain tumor classifications.

Objective

Preoperative knowledge of intracranial meningioma grade could significantly enhance surgical planning, but reliable noninvasive prediction remains an unmet clinical need. The aim of this study was to develop and externally validate a machine learning (ML) model incorporating traditional radiomic features, along with novel fractal and topological features, to predict WHO meningioma grade from preoperative MRI using a large multicenter cohort.

Methods

This retrospective diagnostic study analyzed a cohort of patients in the BraTS Meningioma Challenge. Patient data (n = 909) from 6 academic medical centers were used for model training and internal validation (n = 699) and one-time final external validation (n = 210). Tumors were segmented into three regions and radiomic features extracted across four MRI sequences. Eight different ML algorithms (e.g., based on neural networks, decision trees, clustering, and linear relationships) were tested across a total of 2889 candidate features. The primary outcome was the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) for prediction of binarized WHO grade (1 vs 2 or 3).

Results

The final model used a support vector machine algorithm comprising 20 features and achieved an AUROC of 0.824 (95% CI 0.755-0.883) on unseen test data, with favorable calibration. Feature importance analysis revealed that topological complexity added complementary predictive value to conventional radiomics features. The final model is publicly available for anyone to use.

Conclusions

This externally validated ML model accurately predicted meningioma grade using routine preoperative MRI, with the potential to guide surgical decision-making and serve as a basis for future imaging-based brain tumor classifications.

title: Radiation-induced versus sporadic cerebral cavernous malformations: comparative analysis of incidence and hemorrhage risk.
abstract: Objective Radiation exposure has emerged as a recognized risk factor for cerebral cavernous malformation (CCM). Radiation-induced CCM (XRT-CCM) may arise months to decades after treatment and may carry higher hemorrhage risk than non-XRT-CCM, though studies remain limited. This study aimed to compare clinical characteristics, hemorrhage rates, and surgical management between XRT-CCM and non-XRT-CCM. Methods A single-institution retrospective cohort study examined patients with MRI-confirmed CCM (1987-2024). All XRT-CCM and non-XRT-CCM patients, regardless of presentation type, were included. The primary outcome was symptomatic hemorrhage following diagnosis, and the secondary outcome was surgical intervention. Analysis included descriptive statistics, group comparisons, hemorrhage incidence, multivariable logistic regression for hemorrhage risk, and Cox regression for hemorrhage-free survival. Results The cohort comprised 612 patients: 16 XRT-CCM and 596 non-XRT-CCM patients. The XRT-CCM group included 11 incidental (68.8%) and 5 non-seizure-associated hemorrhage (31.3%) presenters, while the non-XRT-CCM group included 336 incidental (56.4%), 123 non-seizure-associated hemorrhage (20.6%), and 137 seizure (23.0%) presenters. Demographic characteristics were similar between groups. XRT-CCM patients received radiation at a median age of 11.9 years, with diagnosis a median of 13.5 years later. The mean ± SD radiation dosage was 47.8 ± 15.1 Gy, most commonly for arteriovenous malformations (31%). Multivariable analysis showed that radiation was significantly associated with hemorrhage (OR 5.23, 95% CI 1.35-20.36), while presentation type was not. Hemorrhage incidence was 7.77 per 100 person-years for XRT-CCM patients versus 4.36 for non-XRT-CCM patients (incidence rate ratio 1.78). Surgical intervention rates did not differ significantly between groups (25.0% vs 21.1%), nor did primary surgical indications, with hemorrhage being the most common indication in both XRT-CCM (75.0%) and non-XRT-CCM (43.7%) patients. Conclusions XRT-CCM demonstrated a higher hemorrhage incidence compared to non-XRT-CCM, with radiation exposure significantly associated with symptomatic hemorrhage. However, radiation exposure was not significantly associated with time to hemorrhage on survival analysis. The extended latency from radiation to CCM diagnosis underscores the need for long-term surveillance in patients exposed to cranial irradiation.

title: Posterior fossa decompression in pediatric Chiari malformation type I: a meta-analysis and meta-regression of outcomes with and without duraplasty.
abstract: Objective The role of duraplasty in posterior fossa decompression for pediatric Chiari malformation type I (CM-I) remains controversial. Proponents of posterior fossa decompression with duraplasty (PFDD) argue that it improves CSF flow and syrinx regression, while posterior fossa decompression only (PFDO) is thought to offer a less invasive alternative with fewer complications. The authors investigated whether adding duraplasty provides patient-relevant clinical benefit in children with CM-I. Methods A systematic review and meta-analysis of comparative pediatric studies (PFDD vs PFDO) was conducted according to Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Primary outcomes were overall clinical improvement, syrinx regression, Chicago Chiari Outcome Scale (CCOS) score, complications, and reoperation. Random-effects models, study-level meta-regression, graft-type subgroup analyses, and prespecified sensitivity analyzes were performed, including restriction to rigorously defined congenital CM-I cohorts and studies routinely using intraoperative ultrasound. Formal assessments of risk of bias, publication bias, and certainty of evidence were also conducted. Results Twenty-six studies consisting of 5977 pediatric patients (2641 PFDO, 3336 PFDD) were included. Clinical improvement (70.8% PFDO, 80.0% PFDD; p = 0.13), syrinx improvement (55.4% PFDO, 63.5% PFDD; p = 0.11), CCOS scores (p = 0.39), and reoperation (risk ratio [RR] 1.54, 95% CI 0.93-2.54; p = 0.09) showed no significant intergroup difference. PFDD was associated with substantially higher CSF-related morbidity (RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.28-0.78; p < 0.01) and longer operative time (mean difference [MD] 63.9 minutes) and hospital stay (MD 1.22 days). No consistent differences emerged by graft type. Meta-regression showed that higher cohort-level syrinx prevalence correlated with greater clinical improvement after PFDD (p < 0.05) but not PFDO. Sensitivity analyses restricted to rigorously defined congenital CM-I cohorts and studies routinely performing intraoperative ultrasound reproduced all primary findings. Most studies were retrospective with moderate to serious risk of bias and overall certainty of evidence graded as moderate. No significant publication bias was detected (p = 0.36). Conclusions PFDD and PFDO yielded broadly comparable clinical and radiographic outcomes in pediatric CM-I, although PFDD was associated with higher CSF-related morbidity and greater operative burden. Current evidence does not clearly define patient subgroups that derive additional benefit from duraplasty, and observed differences are likely influenced by underlying cohort heterogeneity. Prospective trials incorporating standardized phenotyping and patient-reported outcomes are needed. Systematic review registration no.: CRD420251112828 (www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/).

title: A proposed classification system for intramedullary spinal cord arteriovenous malformations that informs surgical strategy.
abstract: Objective An anatomical classification system is proposed to characterize spinal arteriovenous malformations (SpAVMs) using preoperative digital subtraction angiography (DSA) and MRI to guide surgical strategy for each SpAVM type. Methods A consecutive, single-surgeon series of 52 intra- and perimedullary SpAVMs resected over 17 years was reviewed. DSA, MRI, intraoperative videography, and digital photography findings were analyzed to classify SpAVMs into 5 types on the basis of arterial supply (anterior spinal artery, posterior spinal artery, or both), depth within the cord parenchyma (pial or intramedullary), and anatomical location (anterior, posterior, concentric [entirely intramedullary], or eccentric [intramedullary and presenting to or through the pial surface]). Results SpAVMs were classified into 5 types as follows: type 1, posterior pial (11/52, 21%); type 2, anterior pial (11/52, 21%); type 3, anterior intramedullary (7/52, 13%); type 4, concentric intramedullary (4/52, 8%); and type 5, eccentric extra- and intramedullary (17/52, 33%). Two SpAVMs were unclassifiable. Extramedullary resection was used with types 1 and 2 pial SpAVMs (20/21, 95%) and all 17 eccentric type 5 SpAVMs. Cord rotation was applied for types 2 (8/11, 73%) and 5 (13/17, 76%). Midline myelotomy was used with all type 3 (7/7) and type 4 (4/4) SpAVMs, whereas perinidal myelotomy was used with type 5 SpAVMs (14/17, 82%). Intramedullary resection was used with all type 3 (n = 7) and type 4 (n = 4) SpAVMs and most type 5 SpAVMs (14/17, 82%). In situ occlusion was used for holomedullary SpAVMs. Algorithms recommended by the classification system were applied in 86% of cases, resulting in complete SpAVM resection or angiographic obliteration in 83% of patients (43/52). At the last follow-up, 33 (65%) surviving patients were intact or had mild motor or sensory deficits (McCormick grade 1 or 2); 18 (35%) patients had moderate or severe deficits or quadriplegia/paraplegia (McCormick grade ≥ 3). Overall, 3 of 51 (6%) patients experienced deterioration relative to preoperative baseline to dependent status (McCormick grade ≥ 3). Conclusions The proposed classification system clarifies the SpAVM pathology and guides the application of surgical techniques, thereby defining surgical strategies for each SpAVM type. This classification delineates intra- and perimedullary SpAVMs by expansion from 2 to 5 categories. The proposed classification system differentiates the spectrum of SpAVM pathoanatomy, guiding resection technique by type-specific algorithms. The classification does not predict surgical risk, patient outcome, or natural history.

title: Intraoperative artificial intelligence for brain tumor surgery: from tissue diagnosis to real-time surgical guidance.
abstract: The 2021 WHO CNS tumor classification marked a fundamental shift in neuro-oncology: molecular markers rather than histological appearance now define glioma diagnosis and guide treatment. Yet, in clinical practice the molecular information that matters most to a surgeon-IDH status, 1p/19q codeletion, and methylation class-typically arrives days to weeks after the operation it was meant to inform. Artificial intelligence (AI) is beginning to close that gap. Over the past several years, a growing body of work has demonstrated that AI models can extract diagnostically relevant molecular and histological information from data sources available in the operating room, in real time, at the point of surgical decision-making. In this review, the authors provide a comprehensive overview of state-of-the-art intraoperative AI models available to neurosurgeons during brain tumor resections. They examine AI-augmented approaches to established intraoperative techniques, such as cryosection and fluorescence-guided surgery, before turning to novel technologies including nanopore sequencing and stimulated Raman histology (SRH). The authors conclude by discussing barriers to widespread clinical adoption and what lies ahead for this field. For cryosection, models such as LGNet and the Cryosection Histopathology Assessment and Review Machine (CHARM) have demonstrated strong performance on intraoperative discrimination of primary CNS lymphoma and molecular subtyping of glioma, respectively, with CHARM achieving areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.88-0.93 across glioma subtypes. In fluorescence-guided surgery, hyperspectral imaging combined with machine learning has enabled classification of tumor type, grade, and IDH mutation based on the 5-aminolevulinic acid (5-ALA) signal with up to 93% accuracy, extracting molecular information from a modality already present in the operating room. For nanopore-based methylation classification, ensemble models such as Rapid Nanopore Brain Intraoperative Classification (ROBIN) have achieved 90% concordance with the final diagnosis prospectively in under 2 hours. In SRH, foundation models for infiltration detection now outperform FLAIR, contrast enhancement, and 5-ALA fluorescence in identifying tumor margins, while molecular classification models have achieved over 90% glioma subtype accuracy in multi-institutional cohorts. At the single-cell level, morphometric profiling of SRH images has revealed nuclear features distinguishing IDH-mutant from IDH-wildtype tumors, opening new avenues for interpretability. Despite this progress, widespread adoption remains limited by the absence of randomized clinical trials demonstrating patient-level benefit. Addressing this gap and realizing the potential of multimodal AI systems that integrate imaging, pathology, and molecular data represent critical next steps for the field.

title: Sequential arterial feeder targeting with microscope-based augmented reality and multimodal navigation for brain arteriovenous malformation resection: an integrated operative workflow in 158 cases.
abstract: Objective Early proximal arterial control is an established principle of brain arteriovenous malformation (bAVM) microsurgery but remains difficult to execute when feeding arteries are deep, obscured, or not apparent at the cortical surface. Herein, the authors describe the longitudinal clinical implementation of a workflow using multimodal navigation and microscope-based augmented reality (AR) to identify and target arterial feeders before substantial nidal dissection in bAVM resections. Methods Case-specific multimodal datasets were assembled according to clinical relevance and availability from CTA, high-resolution structural MRI with thin-slice T2-weighted imaging, MRA, and 3D rotational DSA studies and were fused within standard clinical neuronavigation platforms. All angiographically identifiable arterial feeders were segmented along their surgically relevant courses, prioritized as operative targets, and incorporated into exposure and corridor planning. Targets were displayed intraoperatively using the available navigation configuration, including microscope-based AR as the technology evolved. Functional MRI (fMRI) and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) were coregistered selectively to provide cortical and tractographic context. Consecutive navigation-assisted bAVM resections performed by a single neurosurgeon from 2013 to 2025 were analyzed. Outcomes included angiographic obliteration, perioperative morbidity, mortality, and modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score change relative to baseline. Results Of 192 bAVM resections performed during the study period, 158 consecutive navigation-assisted resections comprised the analytical cohort and included Spetzler-Martin (SM) grades I-V. Complete obliteration on initial angiography after microsurgery was observed in 97.5% of cases (154/158). At a median follow-up of 15 months, 93.0% of patients were functionally independent (mRS score 0-2). An increase in the mRS score relative to baseline occurred in 18.4% of patients, most commonly reflecting minor, nondisabling deficits with preserved independence. Loss of independence attributable to surgery occurred in 3.1% of patients, and the mortality rate was 1.3%. Conclusions Multimodal navigation with microscope-based AR was implemented longitudinally to identify and target arterial feeders before substantial nidal dissection, with selective integration of fMRI and DTI providing cortical and tractographic context for lesions near eloquent anatomy. Across SM grade I-V bAVMs, the workflow was feasible and was associated with high rates of angiographic obliteration and functional independence. By translating preoperative angioarchitecture into a planned sequence of discrete intraoperative arterial targets within their structural and functional context, the featured workflow provides a structured framework for operative planning, execution, and teaching in feeder-directed bAVM microsurgery.

title: CNS metastatic renal cell carcinoma radiologically mimicking nerve sheath tumors: illustrative cases.
abstract: Background Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) shows unpredictable, often delayed metastatic behavior, and CNS involvement carries significant morbidity. Rare metastases to cranial and spinal nerves can masquerade as benign nerve sheath tumors, causing misdiagnosis and treatment delays. Recognizing distinguishing features is essential to guide management. Observations The authors present the cases of 3 patients with pathologically confirmed clear cell RCC metastatic to neural structures, presenting 6-9 years after nephrectomy. The sites included the cervical dorsal root ganglion, cerebellomedullary angle involving lower cranial nerves, and cerebellopontine angle mimicking trigeminal schwannoma. Initial MRI showed well-circumscribed, homogeneously enhancing masses with smooth margins and bony remodeling, favoring nerve sheath tumors. Closer review revealed atypical features including arterial spin labeling hyperperfusion, a susceptibility-weighted hemosiderin rim, vasogenic edema, and interval growth. PET/CT and biopsy confirmed metastatic disease. Management was individualized with radiosurgery, resection, and systemic therapy, achieving durable local control. Lessons Patients with prior RCC warrant a high index of suspicion for metastasis even when imaging suggests a benign nerve sheath tumor. Advanced MRI and PET/CT help identify features atypical for schwannoma and locate the safest biopsy site. When feasible, pathological diagnosis should precede definitive local therapy to inform radiosurgical dose, surgical planning, systemic therapy, and prognosis. https://thejns.org/doi/10.3171/CASE26518.

Closer review revealed atypical features including arterial spin labeling hyperperfusion, a susceptibility-weighted hemosiderin rim, vasogenic edema, and interval growth. PET/CT and biopsy confirmed metastatic disease. Management was individualized with radiosurgery, resection, and systemic therapy, achieving durable local control.

Lessons

Patients with prior RCC warrant a high index of suspicion for metastasis even when imaging suggests a benign nerve sheath tumor. Advanced MRI and PET/CT help identify features atypical for schwannoma and locate the safest biopsy site. When feasible, pathological diagnosis should precede definitive local therapy to inform radiosurgical dose, surgical planning, systemic therapy, and prognosis. https://thejns.org/doi/10.3171/CASE26518.

title: Balloon angioplasty for acute posterior communicating artery occlusion due to dissection: illustrative case.
abstract: Background Acute occlusion of the posterior communicating artery (PComA) due to dissection is rare, and the optimal revascularization strategy has not been established. The authors report a case of acute PComA occlusion due to suspected arterial dissection in a patient with a fetal-type posterior cerebral artery (PCA), successfully treated with balloon angioplasty. Observations A 66-year-old woman presented with acute-onset impaired consciousness and left hemiparesis. CT angiography revealed right PComA occlusion associated with a fetal-type PCA. Cerebral angiography performed after intravenous thrombolysis demonstrated transient recanalization of the PComA with severe residual stenosis, followed by reocclusion. Because the lesion appeared stenotic rather than embolic, balloon angioplasty was performed, resulting in favorable antegrade PCA flow restoration. During follow-up, an intimal flap, gradual improvement in stenosis, and vessel wall hyperintensity on volumetric isotropic turbo spin-echo acquisition imaging were observed, suggesting spontaneous PComA dissection as the underlying etiology. The modified Rankin Scale score was 2 at 90 days after symptom onset. Lessons Balloon angioplasty may be a feasible revascularization strategy for acute PComA occlusion when arterial dissection is suspected. https://thejns.org/doi/10.3171/CASE26592.

title: Long-term radiation effects following radiotherapy for intracranial dural arteriovenous fistula: illustrative case.
abstract: Background Radiation-induced cavernous malformation (CM) and chronic encapsulated intracerebral hematoma (CEIH) are rare but well-described long-term sequelae of radiotherapy. The authors report a case of an intracranial dural arteriovenous fistula (DAVF) that was treated with conventional radiotherapy and subsequently developed these uncommon lesions in chronological order. Observations A 52-year-old woman with a left transverse-sigmoid sinus DAVF underwent traditional radiotherapy at another institution. Following treatment, she developed disabling vertigo. Serial imaging surveillance revealed radiation-induced changes (RICs) in the cerebellum 2 years posttreatment. A de novo CM subsequently emerged within the center of the RIC after a latent period of approximately 3 years. Owing to persistent symptoms, the patient underwent left retrosigmoid craniotomy 4 years after radiotherapy. Although vertigo improved significantly postoperatively, she developed progressive visual impairment 4 years later. Follow-up MRI demonstrated an encapsulated hematoma in the left occipital region within the prior radiation field. A second craniotomy was performed, and histopathological examination confirmed CEIH. Lessons This illustrative case underscores the importance of appropriate treatment selection and highlights the potential for significant adverse effects associated with suboptimal radiotherapy planning. https://thejns.org/doi/10.3171/CASE26598.

title: Primary cauda equina neuroendocrine tumor mimicking myxopapillary ependymoma: illustrative case.
abstract: Background Primary cauda equina neuroendocrine tumors (CENETs) are rare intradural extramedullary neoplasms that were historically termed cauda equina paragangliomas. They may resemble more common cauda equina lesions, including myxopapillary ependymoma and schwannoma, on preoperative imaging. Recent molecular and immunohistochemical studies support CENET as a distinct entity, creating a need for practical diagnostic frameworks that separate primary tumors from metastatic neuroendocrine disease and nonneuroendocrine mimics. Observations A 42-year-old woman presented with progressive nocturnal low back pain, bilateral leg heaviness, lower extremity numbness, and urinary incontinence. MRI demonstrated a 5-cm L1-3 intradural extramedullary mass nearly occupying the spinal canal, with cauda equina compression and prominent surrounding vessels. She underwent urgent L1-3 laminoplasty and microsurgical resection. Intraoperatively, the tumor was extremely vascular, friable, and associated with the filum terminale. Gross-total resection was achieved. Pathology demonstrated a WHO grade 1 primary CENET with neuroendocrine marker expression, CK8/18 positivity, low proliferative index, and no evidence of systemic neuroendocrine malignancy on postoperative staging. Lessons Cauda equina neuroendocrine lesions should be approached as a diagnostic spectrum. Clinical tempo, lesion multiplicity, imaging clues, intraoperative vascularity, and immunohistochemical/molecular workup can help distinguish primary CENET from metastatic neuroendocrine disease and mimics. https://thejns.org/doi/10.3171/CASE26609.

title: Surgical decompression of uveal melanoma with optic chiasmal extension via a modified orbitozygomatic approach: illustrative case.
abstract: Background Uveal melanoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy of adulthood. Perineural spread along the optic nerve to the optic chiasm is exceedingly rare, with only 4 previously published cases. No standard neurosurgical management has been established. Observations A 65-year-old woman presented with progressive right-sided monocular vision loss over 1 year, subsequently developing left temporal hemianopia. MRI demonstrated a 3.3 × 2.9 × 2.2-cm right intraconal mass extending through the orbital apex along the optic nerve to the optic chiasm, with a 2.8 × 1.9 × 1.5-cm suprasellar component. A right modified one-piece orbitozygomatic craniotomy achieved subtotal resection of the suprasellar disease and decompressed the contralateral optic nerve. The patient received combination ipilimumab/nivolumab, 60 Gy in 30 fractions adjuvant orbital radiotherapy, nivolumab/relatlimab (progression), 27 Gy in 3 fractions stereotactic radiosurgery for new intracranial metastases, and salvage temozolomide with bevacizumab. She remained alive with stable disease at 12 months. Lessons To the authors' knowledge, this is the first reported case of uveal melanoma with optic chiasmal extension managed by a modified orbitozygomatic approach. Contralateral visual field deficits in a patient with an ipsilateral orbital mass should prompt dedicated cranial imaging. Multidisciplinary care can achieve meaningful disease control even when first-line immunotherapies fail. https://thejns.org/doi/10.3171/CASE26734.

title: First reported case of intradural extramedullary epithelioid hemangioma of the cauda equina: resection of an extremely rare vascular neoplasm. Illustrative case.
abstract: Background Intradural extramedullary (IDEM) tumors of the cauda equina are most often meningiomas, nerve sheath tumors, and myxopapillary ependymomas; purely vascular IDEM lesions are exceptionally rare. Fewer than 30 IDEM hemangiomas have been reported, mostly cavernous or capillary. Epithelioid hemangioma (EH), a benign vascular neoplasm arising in soft tissue and bone, has not previously been reported at the cauda equina. Observations A 63-year-old male with prior cutaneous melanoma presented with 3 months of progressive left L5-distribution radicular pain. MRI showed a 1.0 × 2.0-cm well-circumscribed IDEM mass at L4-5 with left L5-S1 foraminal stenosis. Under intraoperative ultrasound localization and continuous multimodal neurophysiological monitoring, en bloc gross-total resection was achieved through L4-5 laminectomy. Histopathological analysis revealed a well-circumscribed vascular neoplasm with lobular endothelial architecture and no cytological atypia; immunohistochemical analysis (ERG, CD31, and CD34 positivity; HHV8, inhibin, and melanocytic marker negativity) established the diagnosis of EH. At the 7-week follow-up, gross-total resection was confirmed on postoperative MRI. Lessons To the authors' knowledge, this is the first reported intradural EH at any spinal level. Recognition of epithelioid endothelial morphology combined with a comprehensive vascular and melanocytic immunohistochemistry panel is essential for diagnosis and separates EH from more common intradural vascular differentials. https://thejns.org/doi/abs/10.3171/CASE26857.

title: Quantifying "Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus"-like Brain Morphometry patterns in an Alzheimer's Disease Cohort.
abstract: Background and purpose Idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH) is largely underdiagnosed. It is a potentially treatable contributor to cognitive decline, and cognitive improvement may occur even with comorbid Alzheimer's disease. However, iNPH-related imaging features can overlap with age-related and neurodegenerative atrophy, making differentiation difficult. Automated morphometric profiling of NPH-like patterns in biomarker-defined Alzheimer's disease cohorts has not been systematically explored. This pilot study aimed to quantify iNPH-like brain morphometry in an Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort using deep-learning-based morphometry and automated callosal angle measurement. Materials and methods We included N=30 amyloid-negative reference iNPH patients and N=1003 ADNI participants with structural T1-weighted MRI and CSF biomarkers. Age- and sex-adjusted volumetric z-scores were obtained using a deep-learning-based morphometry algorithm. We derived an iNPH morphometric profile using principal component analysis and Gaussian modeling of the reference iNPH cohort and applied it to the ADNI participants to compute individual iNPH similarity scores. We also automated callosal angle measurement for further clinical representation. We compared scores across cognitive stages and biological Alzheimer's disease groups and evaluated against expert Radscale review. Results iNPH-like morphometry increased with cognitive impairment, with mean differences of 0.03 between cognitively normal and mild cognitive impairment (p=0.06), 0.06 between mild cognitive impairment and dementia (p<0.001), and 0.09 between cognitively normal and dementia groups (p<0.001). Among cognitively impaired participants, scores were higher in biologically-defined Alzheimer's disease patients than biologically-defined non-Alzheimer's disease patients (mean difference=0.08, p<0.001). The iNPH similarity score correlated most strongly with ventricular enlargement features. Automated callosal angle measurements showed high agreement with expert ratings (Gwet's AC1 = 0.939) and angles below 90° occurred in 1.5% of ADNI participants. Conclusions Automated normative morphometric profiling and callosal angle quantification identified heterogeneous iNPH-like structural patterns in the ADNI cohort. These tools provide a scalable approach for characterizing iNPH-like imaging features in dementia cohorts where identifying a potentially treatable contributor to cognitive impairment remains relevant. Further clinical validation remains necessary.

title: Venous Outflow Imaging in Acute Ischemic Stroke: An ASFNR State of Practice.
abstract: Background Venous outflow (VO) imaging describes the egress limb of the cerebral collateral circulation and has been associated with outcome in acute ischemic stroke; its added value beyond arterial collaterals and perfusion measures remains uncertain. More than a dozen VO measures have been proposed on CT and MR techniques used in acute stroke, spanning three physical signals: venous opacification, venous transit and venous oxygenation. They differ in what they measure, in evidence maturity and in readiness for reporting. Methods A writing group reviewed the peer-reviewed studies of cerebral venous drainage measures in acute ischemic stroke. The scope is CT and MRI obtained during routine acute stroke evaluation, excluding measures that require catheter angiography or ultrasound. We describe each measure's acquisition, definition, evidence and technical limitations, and propose a reporting framework based on these features. Key message VO markers are descriptive prognostic measures, not treatment-selection criteria. The cortical vein opacification score (COVES) has the most mature CTA evidence and may be considered when venous timing is adequate, though meta-analyses support an association rather than a threshold; comprehensive venous outflow (CVO) adds the internal cerebral vein. Prolonged venous transit (PVT) adds a temporal dimension read from perfusion, but remains investigational, as do the composite arterial-venous scores, quantitative venous timing and oxygen extraction fraction mapping. Susceptibility signs index deoxygenation and venous blood volume, not drainage. Reporting should name the technique and describe opacification, transit or oxygenation findings in their own terms. The evidence base is predominantly anterior-circulation large-vessel occlusion imaged before thrombectomy.
originalAbstract:
Background

Venous outflow (VO) imaging describes the egress limb of the cerebral collateral circulation and has been associated with outcome in acute ischemic stroke; its added value beyond arterial collaterals and perfusion measures remains uncertain. More than a dozen VO measures have been proposed on CT and MR techniques used in acute stroke, spanning three physical signals: venous opacification, venous transit and venous oxygenation. They differ in what they measure, in evidence maturity and in readiness for reporting.

Methods

A writing group reviewed the peer-reviewed studies of cerebral venous drainage measures in acute ischemic stroke. The scope is CT and MRI obtained during routine acute stroke evaluation, excluding measures that require catheter angiography or ultrasound. We describe each measure's acquisition, definition, evidence and technical limitations, and propose a reporting framework based on these features.

Key message

VO markers are descriptive prognostic measures, not treatment-selection criteria. The cortical vein opacification score (COVES) has the most mature CTA evidence and may be considered when venous timing is adequate, though meta-analyses support an association rather than a threshold; comprehensive venous outflow (CVO) adds the internal cerebral vein. Prolonged venous transit (PVT) adds a temporal dimension read from perfusion, but remains investigational, as do the composite arterial-venous scores, quantitative venous timing and oxygen extraction fraction mapping. Susceptibility signs index deoxygenation and venous blood volume, not drainage. Reporting should name the technique and describe opacification, transit or oxygenation findings in their own terms. The evidence base is predominantly anterior-circulation large-vessel occlusion imaged before thrombectomy.

title: Deep Learning-Accelerated 3D T2 CUBE MRI of the Cochlea at 1.5T and 3T: Sonic DL With AIR Recon DL Versus AIR Recon DL Alone.
abstract: Background and purpose Three-dimensional fast spin-echo MR cisternography (CUBE) of the internal auditory canal (IAC) and cerebellopontine angle (CPA) requires longer acquisition times that can limit clinical throughput. We evaluated whether a deep learning (DL)-based highly accelerated reconstruction technique, Sonic DL`™ (SDL), combined with a commercially available DL denoising reconstruction (AIR™ Recon DL, ARDL), preserves or improves subjective image quality and cochlear anatomy visualization relative to standard CUBE-ARDL while shortening scan time. Materials and methods Consecutive patients underwent brain MRI for suspected IAC pathology at 1.5T and 3T with paired acquisition of standard 3D CUBE-ARDL and an accelerated 3D CUBE-SDL sequence. Both used the same voxel size at 1.5T (0.6x0.6x1.2 mm 3 ) and 3T (0.6x0.6x0.6 mm 3 ). Scan times for CUBE-ARDL versus CUBE-SDL were 2:33 versus 1:41 min at 1.5T and 1:55 versus 1:11 min at 3T. Two independent neuroradiologists blinded to MRI acquisition method scored randomized, de-identified images on a 5-point Likert scale across five domains (overall image quality, noise, sharpness, artifacts, cochlear anatomy visualization). Reader-averaged scores for CUBE-ARDL and CUBE-SDL were compared with paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, with reader-specific and cumulative link mixed model (CLMM) sensitivity analyses and false discovery rate (FDR) adjustment; intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) quantified inter-reader reliability for each technique; Gwet's AC2 and weighted (Conger's) kappa with linear ordinal weights quantified pooled inter-reader agreement. Results After exclusion of 5 training cases per field strength, 49 (1.5T) and 34 (3T) patients were analyzed. CUBE-SDL scored significantly better than CUBE-ARDL for all five domains at both field strengths (all FDR-adjusted P < .001), consistently for each reader and in the CLMM. Inter-reader reliability (ICC) for CUBE-SDL was moderate-to-excellent at 3T (0.63-0.92) and moderate at 1.5T (0.65-0.74), generally exceeding CUBE-ARDL (3T: 0.35-0.61; 1.5T: 0.50-0.71). Pooled inter-reader agreement (Gwet's AC2) ranged from 0.56 to 0.89. Conclusions A combined Sonic DL acceleration with ARDL-denoised reconstruction for 3D T2 CUBE produced significantly higher subjective image quality at both 1.5T and 3T, and, at 3T, higher inter-reader reliability than standard CUBE-ARDL, while shortening acquisition time by 34%-38%. These findings support further evaluation, including diagnostic accuracy studies, of CUBE-SDL as an alternative to CUBE-ARDL.
originalAbstract:
Background and purpose

Three-dimensional fast spin-echo MR cisternography (CUBE) of the internal auditory canal (IAC) and cerebellopontine angle (CPA) requires longer acquisition times that can limit clinical throughput. We evaluated whether a deep learning (DL)-based highly accelerated reconstruction technique, Sonic DL`™ (SDL), combined with a commercially available DL denoising reconstruction (AIR™ Recon DL, ARDL), preserves or improves subjective image quality and cochlear anatomy visualization relative to standard CUBE-ARDL while shortening scan time.

Materials and methods

Consecutive patients underwent brain MRI for suspected IAC pathology at 1.5T and 3T with paired acquisition of standard 3D CUBE-ARDL and an accelerated 3D CUBE-SDL sequence. Both used the same voxel size at 1.5T (0.6x0.6x1.2 mm3) and 3T (0.6x0.6x0.6 mm3). Scan times for CUBE-ARDL versus CUBE-SDL were 2:33 versus 1:41 min at 1.5T and 1:55 versus 1:11 min at 3T. Two independent neuroradiologists blinded to MRI acquisition method scored randomized, de-identified images on a 5-point Likert scale across five domains (overall image quality, noise, sharpness, artifacts, cochlear anatomy visualization). Reader-averaged scores for CUBE-ARDL and CUBE-SDL were compared with paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, with reader-specific and cumulative link mixed model (CLMM) sensitivity analyses and false discovery rate (FDR) adjustment; intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) quantified inter-reader reliability for each technique; Gwet's AC2 and weighted (Conger's) kappa with linear ordinal weights quantified pooled inter-reader agreement.

Results

After exclusion of 5 training cases per field strength, 49 (1.5T) and 34 (3T) patients were analyzed. CUBE-SDL scored significantly better than CUBE-ARDL for all five domains at both field strengths (all FDR-adjusted P < .001), consistently for each reader and in the CLMM. Inter-reader reliability (ICC) for CUBE-SDL was moderate-to-excellent at 3T (0.63-0.92) and moderate at 1.5T (0.65-0.74), generally exceeding CUBE-ARDL (3T: 0.35-0.61; 1.5T: 0.50-0.71). Pooled inter-reader agreement (Gwet's AC2) ranged from 0.56 to 0.89.

Conclusions

A combined Sonic DL acceleration with ARDL-denoised reconstruction for 3D T2 CUBE produced significantly higher subjective image quality at both 1.5T and 3T, and, at 3T, higher inter-reader reliability than standard CUBE-ARDL, while shortening acquisition time by 34%-38%. These findings support further evaluation, including diagnostic accuracy studies, of CUBE-SDL as an alternative to CUBE-ARDL.

title: Diagnostic Performance of Arterial Spin-Labeling MRI in the Presurgical Evaluation of Focal Epilepsy and the Limits of Current Evidence for Predicting Surgical Outcome: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Background and purpose Arterial spin-labeling (ASL) MR imaging is a noninvasive perfusion technique used in presurgical evaluation of focal epilepsy. A 2021 meta-analysis assessed its accuracy for identifying perfusion abnormalities concordant with the epileptogenic zone (EZ) but predated later studies and partly derived specificity from healthy-control true negatives. We re-estimated the diagnostic accuracy of ASL for EZ-concordant perfusion abnormalities with explicit handling of true negatives, and tested whether current data permit a quantitative estimate of the relationship between ASL findings and postsurgical seizure freedom. Materials and methods Following PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-DTA, we searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Scopus from inception to June 2026 for English-language primary studies (≥10 patients) of ASL for EZ localization or surgical-outcome evaluation in focal epilepsy. Random-effects models estimated pooled sensitivity (logit; primary), an exploratory specificity, a logit concordance/detection proportion, and a Freeman-Tukey seizure-free proportion. Because true negatives were absent by design, a joint bivariate/HSROC model was not estimable. Risk of bias used QUADAS-2 and QUIPS; certainty of evidence used a DTA-adapted GRADE approach. Results Fifteen studies were included. The primary analysis (8 studies, 160 patients) yielded a pooled ASL sensitivity for EZ-concordant abnormalities of 0.73 (95% CI, 0.65-0.80; I 2 = 0.0%). The concordance/detection proportion was 0.78 (95% CI, 0.62-0.89; 4 studies), and exploratory specificity 0.37 (95% CI, 0.13-0.71; 5 studies). In the surgical-outcome arm, the pooled seizure-free proportion (Engel I/ILAE 1) was 0.68 (95% CI, 0.58-0.77; 4 studies) and 0.71 (95% CI, 0.56-0.84) in a stricter analysis. Critically, a pooled odds ratio for seizure freedom in ASL-concordant versus ASL-discordant resections could not be computed: the required cross-tabulation was reported in no study. Conclusions ASL has moderate, stable sensitivity for identifying perfusion abnormalities concordant with the anatomo-electro-clinically defined EZ, whereas specificity is not estimable from current single-group designs. ASL-linked surgical cohorts achieve seizure freedom in two-thirds of operated patients, but whether ASL-resection concordance predicts seizure freedom is unquantifiable: a reporting gap, not a null result. Until outcome is reported stratified by ASL-resection concordance, ASL should be used as a localizing adjunct, not a prognostic marker.

title: Association Between Tissue No-Reflow and Prognosis After successful Recanalization in Endovascular Treatment of Intracranial Atherosclerotic Occlusion: A Post Hoc Subgroup Analysis of the ANGEL-REBOOT Trial.
abstract: Background No-reflow after successful endovascular treatment (EVT) predicts poor outcomes in acute ischemic stroke (AIS) due to intracranial atherosclerotic stenosis (ICAS), but its optimal evaluation and prognostic value remain unclear. This study assessed computed tomography perfusion (CTP)-defined no-reflow for predicting outcomes in ICAS-related large vessel occlusion (ICAS-LVO). Methods This retrospective post hoc analysis included patients from the prospective ANGEL-REBOOT trial with anterior circulation ICAS-LVO, successful eTICI 2b/3 recanalization, and postoperative 24-hour CTP. No-reflow was defined as persistent hypoperfusion (Tmax >4s or >6s) after recanalization. Outcomes included 90-day modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score (poor outcome ≥3) and 24-hour National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score. Results In this exploratory post-hoc analysis, the optimal cohort derived cutoff value for Tmax > 4s hypoperfusion volume was 95.8 mL. Among 64 patients, Tmax >4s hypoperfusion volume ≥95.8 mL best predicted poor 90-day outcome (area under the curve [AUC] 0.75). Larger Tmax >4s volumes correlated with worse 90-day mRS scores (P=0.04) and higher 24-hour NIHSS scores (P=0.006). Tmax >6s (cutoff 9.9 mL, AUC 0.690) only predicted higher 24-hour NIHSS score (P=0.001) but not 90-day outcomes (P=0.12). Conclusions Postoperative 24-hour CTP Tmax > 4 s hypoperfusion volume showed a trend toward better prediction of 90-day poor functional outcomes compared with Tmax > 6 s in recanalized ICAS-LVO patients.

title: Half-Dose Gadopiclenol versus Full-Dose Gadobutrol for Hydrops MR Imaging: Comparison in Contralateral Clinically Unaffected Ears.
abstract: Background and purpose Hydrops MR imaging, performed 4 hours after IV gadolinium administration, requires sufficient contrast-agent accumulation in the perilymph to delineate the nonenhancing endolymphatic spaces. The higher relaxivity of gadopiclenol may reduce gadolinium exposure while preserving perilymphatic enhancement and anatomic detail. Clinically unaffected contralateral reference ears provide a standardized reference that minimizes disease-related confounding. We compared half-dose gadopiclenol (0.05 mmol/kg; half the gadolinium dose) with full-dose gadobutrol (0.1 mmol/kg) for hydrops MR imaging. Materials and methods This retrospective study reviewed 90 consecutive patients referred for hydrops MR imaging. Forty-five received gadobutrol (1.0 mmol/mL; 0.1 mmol/kg), and 45 received gadopiclenol (0.5 mmol/mL; 0.05 mmol/kg). Two experienced head and neck radiologists, blinded to clinical findings and contrast agent, independently evaluated the clinically unaffected reference ear. Quantitative endpoints were the signal intensity ratio (SIR) and reference-normalized contrast (RNC); qualitative endpoints were separate delineation of the saccule and utricle and visibility of the 3 semicircular canal ampullae. The prespecified noninferiority margin was 0.5 units, with a sensitivity analysis using 0.25 units. Results Seventy-one patients were included: 37 received gadopiclenol and 34 received gadobutrol. Nineteen were excluded because of motion degradation, suspected bilateral disease, or abnormal audiometric or MR imaging findings in the reference ear. Mean reader-averaged SIR was 8.15 (SD, 1.51) with gadopiclenol and 7.59 (SD, 1.40) with gadobutrol, yielding a mean difference of 0.56 (95% CI, -0.13 to 1.25). Mean reader-averaged RNC was 7.66 (SD, 1.56) and 6.97 (SD, 1.37), respectively, yielding a mean difference of 0.69 (95% CI, 0.00 to 1.39). Both lower confidence limits exceeded the noninferiority boundary of -0.5; noninferiority was maintained using -0.25. Interreader reliability was excellent for SIR (ICC, 0.915; 95% CI, 0.868-0.946) and RNC (ICC, 0.925; 95% CI, 0.882-0.952). Qualitative assessments showed no significant between-group differences. Where estimable, Cohen κ ranged from 0.66 to 1.00; observed agreement was 97.2%-100% for features with nonestimable κ. Conclusions In clinically unaffected reference ears, gadopiclenol at 0.05 mmol/kg provides quantitative perilymphatic enhancement noninferior to that of gadobutrol at 0.1 mmol/kg, with comparable qualitative anatomic delineation. Higher-relaxivity gadopiclenol may therefore reduce gadolinium exposure without compromising reference-ear image quality.

title: ASFNR Clinical State-of-Practice in Neuroimaging of Minor Large Vessel Occlusion Stroke.
abstract: Background Minor ischemic stroke (MIS) with anterior large vessel occlusion (LVO) is a distinct stroke subtype in which mild neurological deficits may mask a substantial volume of threatened but salvageable brain tissue. Despite a baseline NIHSS≤5, nearly one-third of patients experience poor functional outcomes, often due to early neurological deterioration (END). Current evidence and ongoing trials Patients with LVO-MIS were markedly underrepresented in landmark thrombectomy trials, resulting in limited evidence to guide treatment. Retrospective studies have identified imaging biomarkers of END, including proximal occlusion, clot length, collateral status, and perfusion mismatch, but the benefit of endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) remains uncertain. Ongoing randomized controlled trials, including STEP and MOSTE, are expected to define the role of EVT and imaging-based patient selection in this population. Purpose To summarize the current state of neuroimaging in anterior circulation LVO-MIS and provide a practical imaging workflow and reporting checklist for diagnosis, prognostication, and treatment selection. Key points CTA remains the primary modality for LVO detection and collateral assessment, while CT and MR perfusion identify salvageable tissue and predict END beyond baseline NIHSS. MRI further refines infarct core, perfusion deficit, and thrombus characterization. Current AI-based LVO detection tools improve stroke triage but require careful human oversight because proximal M2 and non-terminus ICA occlusions may be missed. Conclusion Pending results from ongoing trials, tissue-based imaging with CTA, CT perfusion, and MR perfusion can complement clinical assessment to improve risk stratification and individualized treatment decisions. Advances in quantitative imaging and artificial intelligence are expected to further enable precision imaging-guided management of LVO-MIS.

title: Conformal Uncertainty for Preoperative MRI Radiomic Glioma Subtyping: Showing When the Model Cannot Separate Subtypes.
abstract: Background and purpose MRI radiomic models predict WHO 2021 glioma subtypes with high AUCs, but reporting only the most probable subtype (argmax) can miss the less common oligodendroglioma. We evaluated whether class-conditional conformal prediction, which sets a separate probability cutoff for each subtype, lets a radiomic model return a set of plausible subtypes for each patient before tissue diagnosis, hypothesizing that it would cover all three subtypes at the target rate at the cost of larger sets. Materials and methods We retrospectively analyzed 1544 patients with preoperative T1, T2, contrast-enhanced T1, and FLAIR MRI from four public datasets. A random forest trained on TCGA and UCSF-PDGM (n=611) was applied unchanged to the Erasmus Glioma Database (EGD, n=404) and UTSW-Glioma (n=529), each split 200 times into a calibration half, used to fit every rule, and a test half. Class-conditional conformal prediction was compared with single-subtype rules, probability sets, abstention, and standard conformal prediction (one shared cutoff). Rules were compared on per-subtype coverage (the share of patients whose set contained the true subtype), mean set size, and the share of patients given a single subtype and its accuracy. Results Per-subtype AUCs were 0.87-0.96 (EGD) and 0.82-0.91 (UTSW-Glioma), yet argmax identified 7 of 73 and 4 of 63 oligodendrogliomas. At the 90% target, only class-conditional conformal prediction reached it for all three subtypes in both cohorts (mean coverage 0.90-0.93, mean set size 1.39 and 1.70). Standard conformal prediction covered 0.51 and 0.37 of oligodendrogliomas, probability sets fell below the target for two subtypes in UTSW-Glioma, and abstention matched on single-subtype calls needed larger sets (1.79 and 2.17). Single-subtype sets, given to 61.8% and 41.7% of patients, were correct in 98.5% and 97.4% when they named glioblastoma but about half the time otherwise. Development-cohort cutoffs fell below the target for glioblastoma (0.84 and 0.79). Conclusions Class-conditional conformal prediction allowed the model to suggest multiple glioma subtypes when uncertain, reducing the risk of excluding the correct diagnosis, particularly oligodendroglioma. With calibration using comparable patient populations, the correct subtype was included at the intended rate. Single-subtype predictions were most reliable for glioblastoma.

title: The Ataxias as an Example of Rare Diseases: Diagnosis, Genetics, and Treatment.
abstract: Background Ataxias are a group of rare diseases. In the European Union, a disease is defined as rare if its prevalence is less than 5 per 10 000 people. Ataxias are rarer than this threshold, although reliable prevalence estimates are largely lacking. The worldwide mean prevalence of autosomal dominant hereditary ataxias is approximately 2.7 per 100 000 people (95% confidence interval [1.5; 4.0/100 000]), and that of autosomal-recessive ataxias is approximately 3.3 per 100 000 people [1.8; 4.9/100 000]. Ataxias include hereditary (genetic), sporadic degenerative, and acquired types. Methods This narrative review is based on the guidelines of the German Society for Neurology ( Deutsche Gesellschaft für Neurologie ) and on other current reviews, supplemented by the findings of targeted PubMed searches. Results In the more common types of hereditary ataxia, a presumptive diagnosis (spot diagnosis) can already be made on the basis of the history, neurological examination, and brain MRI findings and can then be confirmed by genetic testing. These include Friedreich ataxia, the RFC1-CANVAS syndrome (cerebellar ataxia, neuropathy, and vestibular areflexia), and spinocerebellar ataxia types 3 and 27B (SCA3 and SCA27B). When a spot diagnosis is not possible, the diagnosis can often be established by genetic testing (preferably genome-based). Multisystem atrophy of the cerebellar type (MSA-C) arises sporadically. Ataxia with a subacute course suggests an acquired type of ataxia-in particular, immune-mediated ataxias and vitamin B1 deficiency (Wernicke) encephalopathy. Omaveloxolone has been approved for the treatment of Friedreich ataxia. In a phase 2 trial with 103 patients, the clinical severity score (mFARS value, maximum 99 points) improved by a mean of 1.55 points after 48 weeks of treatment, compared with worsening by 0.85 points with placebo. Fampridine is used off-label to treat episodic ataxias, downbeat nystagmus, and SCA27B. Randomized trials have documented the benefit of physiotherapy and regular exercise training for patients with ataxia. Conclusion An increasing number of ataxias can be diagnosed with the improved genetic and immunological diagnostic techniques that are now available. Opportunities for treatment remain limited, but many new therapies are under development, including gene therapy.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Anti-Müllerian Hormone for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Background The 2023 international evidence-based guideline for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) conditionally recommended serum anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) as an alternative to ultrasound for diagnosing polycystic ovarian morphology (PCOM) in adults, marking a significant shift in diagnostic practice. However, the diagnostic accuracy of AMH remains debated, particularly regarding its utility as a standalone test, its application across diverse populations, and its use in adolescents. Methods A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted following PRISMA guidelines. Major electronic databases, including PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library, were searched for diagnostic accuracy studies published until November 2024, and studies evaluating serum AMH against the Rotterdam criteria for PCOS or ultrasound-defined PCOM were included. A bivariate random-effects model was used to pool sensitivity and specificity with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for three key questions: AMH for 1) PCOS diagnosis in adults, 2) PCOM diagnosis in adults, and 3) PCOS diagnosis in adolescents. The Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2 tool was used to assess the risk of bias. Results For adult PCOS diagnosis, 83 studies (n = 33,376) were included, yielding a pooled sensitivity of 0.81 (95% CI, 0.78-0.83) and a specificity of 0.89 (95% CI, 0.86-0.91). For adult PCOM diagnosis, six studies (n = 11,436) provided a pooled sensitivity of 0.79 (95% CI, 0.70-0.86) and a specificity of 0.88 (95% CI, 0.77-0.94). In contrast, the analysis for adolescent PCOS (11 studies, n = 1,090) revealed a significantly lower accuracy, with a pooled sensitivity of 0.66 (95% CI, 0.58-0.73) and a specificity of 0.78 (95% CI, 0.71-0.83). Substantial heterogeneity was observed across all analyses. Conclusion The current, updated meta-analysis confirms that serum AMH is a highly specific and moderately sensitive biomarker for diagnosing PCOM and PCOS in adults, supporting its role as an adjunctive diagnostic tool. However, its utility as a standalone test is limited by significant heterogeneity; in addition, its diagnostic performance is further limited in adolescents, providing evidence against its use in such population. Future efforts must focus on the international standardization of AMH assays and the development of population-specific reference values to enhance its clinical utility.

originalAbstract:
Background

The 2023 international evidence-based guideline for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) conditionally recommended serum anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) as an alternative to ultrasound for diagnosing polycystic ovarian morphology (PCOM) in adults, marking a significant shift in diagnostic practice. However, the diagnostic accuracy of AMH remains debated, particularly regarding its utility as a standalone test, its application across diverse populations, and its use in adolescents.

Methods

A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted following PRISMA guidelines. Major electronic databases, including PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library, were searched for diagnostic accuracy studies published until November 2024, and studies evaluating serum AMH against the Rotterdam criteria for PCOS or ultrasound-defined PCOM were included. A bivariate random-effects model was used to pool sensitivity and specificity with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for three key questions: AMH for 1) PCOS diagnosis in adults, 2) PCOM diagnosis in adults, and 3) PCOS diagnosis in adolescents. The Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2 tool was used to assess the risk of bias.

Results

For adult PCOS diagnosis, 83 studies (n = 33,376) were included, yielding a pooled sensitivity of 0.81 (95% CI, 0.78-0.83) and a specificity of 0.89 (95% CI, 0.86-0.91). For adult PCOM diagnosis, six studies (n = 11,436) provided a pooled sensitivity of 0.79 (95% CI, 0.70-0.86) and a specificity of 0.88 (95% CI, 0.77-0.94). In contrast, the analysis for adolescent PCOS (11 studies, n = 1,090) revealed a significantly lower accuracy, with a pooled sensitivity of 0.66 (95% CI, 0.58-0.73) and a specificity of 0.78 (95% CI, 0.71-0.83). Substantial heterogeneity was observed across all analyses.

Conclusion

The current, updated meta-analysis confirms that serum AMH is a highly specific and moderately sensitive biomarker for diagnosing PCOM and PCOS in adults, supporting its role as an adjunctive diagnostic tool. However, its utility as a standalone test is limited by significant heterogeneity; in addition, its diagnostic performance is further limited in adolescents, providing evidence against its use in such population. Future efforts must focus on the international standardization of AMH assays and the development of population-specific reference values to enhance its clinical utility.

title: Association of CT-Based Sarcopenia, Clinical Frailty, and Nutritional Status With Mortality After Aortic Valve Replacement for Severe Aortic Stenosis.
abstract: Objective This study investigated the association between multiple frailty-related markers-Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS), Controlling Nutritional Status (CONUT) score, and computed tomography (CT)-based sarcopenia-and overall survival after aortic valve replacement (AVR) for severe aortic stenosis (AS), with particular emphasis on the first year after AVR. Materials and methods A total of 407 patients with severe AS who underwent surgical or transcatheter AVR at a tertiary center between November 2020 and December 2022 were retrospectively included. Three frailty-related markers were analyzed: CFS score for functional frailty, CONUT score for nutritional status, and CT-defined sarcopenia for structural muscle depletion. The CONUT score was calculated using serum markers, and sarcopenia was defined according to cohort-specific tertiles of the paravertebral muscle index quantified at the 12th thoracic vertebra (T12) vertebral level using CT. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards analysis was performed to assess the prognostic associations of the Society of Thoracic Surgeons (STS) score and the three frailty-related markers with all-cause mortality after AVR. Results Within 1 year after AVR, 32 patients (7.9%) died. In the overall multivariable analysis, higher CFS scores and CT-defined sarcopenia were independently associated with mortality, with hazard ratios (HRs) of 1.82 (95% confidence interval [CI], 1.40-2.38; P < 0.001) and 2.63 (95% CI, 1.22-5.67; P = 0.014), respectively. The STS score and CONUT scores were not associated with survival, with HRs of 1.00 (95% CI, 0.95-1.06; P = 0.883) and 1.05 (95% CI, 0.90-1.22; P = 0.563), respectively. A significant interaction was observed between the CONUT score and sarcopenia. Conclusion Among patients with severe AS undergoing AVR, higher CFS scores and CT-based sarcopenia were independently associated with survival after adjustment for the STS score. The prognostic association of the CONUT score differed according to sarcopenia status. These findings support the incorporation of functional and structural vulnerabilities into risk assessment for patients undergoing AVR for AS; however, the role of nutritional status requires further investigation.

title: Multi-color space image enhancement with weighted fusion and lightweight deep learning framework for AI-based breast cancer histopathology image classification.
abstract: Introduction Variations in Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) staining, illumination, tissue preparation, and image acquisition affect breast histopathology image analysis, altering nuclear contrast, color consistency, and downstream feature extraction. Separately, prior BreakHis studies have often used image-wise splitting, which can place a patient's images in both training and test sets and inflate performance estimates. Methods To address these two issues, this study introduced a Multi-color Space Image Enhancement (MSIE) approach and evaluates it under strict, leakage-controlled, patient-wise five-fold cross-validation on the BreakHis dataset. MSIE combines H&E color deconvolution, stain normalization, hematoxylin contrast processing with Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE), Hue-Saturation-Value (HSV) space processing, eosin reconstruction, and H&E-weighted fusion. Before model training, the dataset underwent a decoded-pixel Secure Hash Algorithm 256-bit (SHA-256) integrity check, and 125 duplicate images were removed, reducing the dataset from 7,909 to 7,784. The Lightweight Convolutional Neural Network (LCNN) model is trained and tested on MSIE and original RGB images using an identical architecture and patient partitions, and MobileNetV2, ResNet50, DenseNet169, and EfficientNetB0 are evaluated under the same protocol to assess efficiency-accuracy trade-offs across model capacities. Results Performance is assessed at the image and patient levels using accuracy, precision, recall, F1 Score, Receiver Operating Characteristic Area Under the Curve (ROC AUC), and Precision-Recall Area Under the Curve (PR AUC), alongside Fusion-coefficient sensitivity, magnification-specific performance, computational efficiency, Grad-CAM visualization, and independent BACH testing. At the patient level, original RGB achieved an accuracy of 0.8397 ± 0.0325 and F1-score of 0.8789 ± 0.0326, versus a mean accuracy of 0.7522 ± 0.2218 and F1-score of 0.7632 ± 0.2734 for MSIE. MSIE, however, produced a slightly higher mean ROC-AUC (0.9024 ± 0.1274 versus 0.8952 ± 0.1023). Higher-capacity ImageNet-pretrained architectures performed better on MSIE inputs, with EfficientNetB0 achieving the highest mean patient-level accuracy (0.9007 ± 0.0718) and ROC-AUC (0.9707 ± 0.0354). Independent evaluation on the BACH dataset using frozen BreaKHis-trained MSIE-LCNN models yielded an accuracy of 0.7056 and an ROC-AUC of 0.7012, indicating substantial cross-dataset domain shift. Discussion Overall, MSIE provides a stain-aware representation whose downstream benefits are not universal and depend on the classifier architecture, fusion balance, operating point, and dataset domain, thereby supporting leakage-controlled and externally validated assessment of histopathology processing methods rather than claims of immediate clinical translation.

title: Biomechanical effects of different suture pretension levels in suture-bridge repair of supraspinatus tendon tears: a finite element analysis.
abstract: Objective The optimal initial suture pretension during suture-bridge repair of full-thickness supraspinatus tendon tears remains uncertain and is largely determined by the surgeon's experience. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of different suture pretensions on the mechanical environment of the tendon-bone interface and to provide a biomechanical reference for intraoperative tension control. Methods A three-dimensional finite element model of the shoulder joint was reconstructed from computed tomography data of a healthy adult volunteer. A full-thickness supraspinatus tear was simulated and repaired using a double-row suture-bridge configuration. Seven total pretension levels (30-90 N, in 10 N increments) and three shoulder abduction positions (10°, 20°, and 30°) were combined to generate 21 loading conditions. The mean contact pressure, effective contact area, relative interfacial displacement, and tendon-side von Mises stress were analyzed. Results Increasing pretension increased the mean tendon-bone contact pressure at all abduction angles. At 20° of abduction, the mean contact pressure increased from 0.382 MPa to 0.856 MPa. The peak tendon-side von Mises stress also increased with pretension, reaching a maximum of 4.533 MPa in the 30°/90 N condition. The effective contact area changed only slightly at 10° of abduction, decreased from 181.4 mm 2 to 169.5 mm 2 at 20°, and reached relatively high values at 50-60 N at 30°. High-stress regions were mainly concentrated around the medial-row suture perforation sites and expanded as pretension increased. Conclusion Suture pretension improved tendon-bone compression and initial interfacial stability, but higher pretension increased local pressure and tendon stress concentration. Within the tested configurations, 50-60 N represented an intermediate, condition-dependent range rather than a universal clinical target.
