title: Multiphase dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging radiomics nomogram for preoperative differentiation of sinonasal inverted papilloma-associated squamous cell carcinoma from benign inverted papilloma.
abstract: Background Reliable preoperative distinction between sinonasal inverted papilloma-associated squamous cell carcinoma (SNIP-SCC) and benign sinonasal inverted papilloma (SNIP) is important for the planning of treatment. Methods This retrospective study analyzed 304 patients who were pathologically diagnosed with SNIP or SNIP-SCC from two centers. Among them, 214 patients from Center A formed the development cohort, in which model performance was internally evaluated using 20 repetitions of stratified nested five-fold cross-validation; 90 patients from Center B served as the external validation cohort. Radiomics feature descriptors were derived from conventional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI in the early, peak/plateau, and delayed phases. Results Increasing age, convoluted cerebriform pattern mutation, and a washout-type time-signal intensity curve were independently associated with SNIP-SCC. The multiphase contrast-enhanced radiomics model achieved an internally validated area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.870 [95% confidence interval (CI), 0.813-0.921] in the development cohort and an AUC of 0.843 (95% CI, 0.735-0.932) in the external validation cohort. A nomogram integrating the radiomics score with the selected clinical and imaging predictors yielded AUCs of 0.899 (95% CI, 0.853-0.941) and 0.883 (95% CI, 0.755-0.979), with corresponding accuracies of 84.1% and 85.6%, respectively. Conclusion Multiphase dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI radiomics provides complementary information to conventional clinical and imaging assessment and may facilitate preoperative differentiation of SNIP-SCC from benign SNIP.

title: Clinical judgment enhances interim PET interpretation in Hodgkin lymphoma: a real-world monocentric experience.
abstract: Background Interim PET after two cycles of ABVD (PET2) is a strong prognostic tool in Hodgkin lymphoma (HL), yet how clinicians use it to guide treatment in routine practice remains largely unexplored. Methods We retrospectively studied consecutive adults with classical HL treated 2010-2023 at one Italian centre. PET2 was assessed semiquantitatively: Deauville score (DS) 4 was assigned when the SUVmax of the hottest residual lesion exceeded the hepatic SUVmax reference. In PET2-positive patients (DS ≥ 4) the clinician decided whether to intensify (high-dose salvage ± autologous stem cell transplantation, ASCT) or continue. The primary endpoint was complete metabolic response (CMR, DS ≤ 3) at the first PET after PET2 (PETpost). Results Of 373 evaluable PET2, 53 (14%) were positive; 51 were analysed, treatment being modified in 28 (55%) and continued in 23 (45%). CMR at PETpost was more frequent in patients who continued ABVD (15/23, 65% vs. 10/28, 36%; p = 0.036). Residual metabolic activity at PET2 was lower in the continuation group (lesion-to-liver Δ SUV 0.9 vs. 3.5, p = 0.002). In exploratory multivariable analysis the decision to intensify was associated with lesion-to-liver Δ SUV (OR 1.99, p = 0.004) and younger age (OR 0.95, p = 0.033), and was much less frequent from 2015 onwards (OR 0.07, p = 0.009); in the model for CMR the decision was the only variable retained (OR 0.30, p = 0.039). After a median follow-up of 7.9 years, overall survival did not differ (5-year 79.9% vs. 89.3%, p = 0.106), nor the 10-year cumulative incidence of lymphoma-related death (12.7% vs. 7.1%, Gray's test p = 0.76), although patients continuing ABVD received a median of one treatment line and avoided ASCT in 87%. Conclusion In a real-world setting without ultra-specialised PET review, clinicians resolved the grey zone of PET2 by weighting quantitative PET parameters alongside patient characteristics and evidence. This heuristic filter identified patients with borderline positivity responding to ABVD and spared them intensification without a detectable excess of lymphoma-related deaths, supporting the integration of semiquantitative PET parameters and clinical judgment into treatment decisions.

title: From macroscopic screening to microscopic characterization: AI and CLE in small bowel disorders.
abstract: Background Small bowel diseases have long posed a diagnostic challenge in gastroenterology due to their deep anatomical location, tortuous configuration, and nonspecific clinical presentation. Capsule endoscopy (CE) and device-assisted enteroscopy (DAE) have improved small bowel visualization, yet CE reading burden and DAE procedural complexity remain core limitations. Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted endoscopy and confocal laser endomicroscopy (CLE) have emerged as promising solutions. Methods This review narratively synthesizes the current evidence on AI-assisted capsule endoscopy (AI-CE) and AI-assisted device-assisted enteroscopy (AI-DAE) in the diagnosis of small bowel disorders. A critical appraisal approach was adopted to evaluate methodological quality, lesion type coverage, and standardization across studies. A literature search of PubMed was performed up to September 1, 2026, and reference lists of key reviews were screened to identify additional relevant articles. Results AI-CE has accumulated substantial evidence for Tier 1-2 (lesion detection and macroscopic classification), yet its capability does not extend to Tier 3 (microscopic characterization). AI applications in DAE are in early stages, facing challenges of data scarcity and cross-device generalization. CLE enables real-time "optical biopsy" but is constrained by the pharmacological limitation that fluorescein sodium does not stain cell nuclei and the absence of small bowel-specific diagnostic criteria. While AI + CLE has achieved notable progress in other parts of the gastrointestinal tract, the small bowel remains nearly blank. AI-CE has accumulated substantial evidence for Tier 1-2 (lesion detection and macroscopic classification), yet its capability does not extend to Tier 3 (microscopic characterization). title: Spectral CT material decomposition for non-invasive quantitative assessment of metabolic and elemental abnormalities in liver cirrhosis: a narrative review.
abstract: Metabolic and elemental abnormalities caused by chronic liver disease are frequently underestimated in the clinical assessment of liver cirrhosis, despite their impact on disease progression and prognosis. Spectral computed tomography (CT) exploits energy-dependent differences in X-ray attenuation to achieve non-invasive, single-scan quantitative detection of liver components, overcoming the limitation of conventional imaging, which can only evaluate morphology. This narrative review summarizes recent advances and technical limitations of spectral CT material decomposition for metabolic and elemental assessment in liver cirrhosis. Virtual iron content (VIC) can quantify hepatic iron deposition and, in selected populations, is associated with fibrosis severity, although its role as an independent fibrosis-staging tool remains to be established. Liver fat content measured by multimaterial decomposition (MMD) agrees well with Magnetic resonance imaging proton density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF), and low-dose scanning may suffice for detection. Currently, liver calcium quantification has only been validated using phantom studies, and relevant clinical research remains scarce; routine spectral CT cannot directly quantify trace elements such as zinc and copper. The fusion of photon counting CT (PCCT) and deep learning algorithms is expected to eventually overcome the technical bottleneck of trace element quantification. In summary, spectral CT promotes the imaging assessment of liver cirrhosis from morphological characterization to metabolic quantification. Combining new hardware and artificial intelligence can improve detection efficiency; further technical and multicenter clinical validation is required before clinical translation.

title: Hepatorenal index and an exploratory combined model for identifying moderate-to-severe histologic steatosis in patients with liver injury of undetermined etiology.
abstract: Background Liver biopsy is the reference standard for grading hepatic steatosis, but its invasiveness limits routine use. We evaluated the hepatorenal index (HRI), derived from routine two-dimensional grayscale ultrasound images, and an exploratory combined model incorporating HRI with clinical parameters for identifying moderate-to-severe histologic steatosis (S ≥ 2) in patients with liver injury of undetermined etiology. Methods This retrospective single-center cohort included 80 biopsy-referred patients who had undergone same-day grayscale ultrasound, liver stiffness measurement, and liver biopsy. HRI was calculated offline. The exploratory combined model used Firth bias-reduced logistic regression followed by intercept correction, with 1,000-resample bootstrap internal validation. Results The S0, S1, S2, and S3 groups comprised 46, 17, 12, and 5 patients, respectively. Median HRI differed among the S0-S1, S2, and S3 groups (1.02, 1.25, and 1.59; P < 0.001). Body mass index (BMI), prognostic nutritional index (PNI), and HRI were positively associated with S ≥ 2 steatosis, whereas the aspartate aminotransferase-to-platelet ratio index (APRI) was inversely associated. HRI yielded an apparent area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.866 (95% CI, 0.782-0.950). At the data-derived cutoff of >1.05, HRI identified all 17 S ≥ 2 cases, with an apparent sensitivity of 100.00% (95% CI, 80.49%-100.00%) and an apparent specificity of 60.32%. The exploratory combined model yielded an apparent AUROC of 0.942 and a bootstrap optimism-corrected AUROC of 0.927. Conclusion HRI showed promising apparent discrimination and potential rule-out value requiring independent validation. The combined model retained high discrimination after bootstrap correction and may provide a low-cost adjunct where dedicated fat quantification is unavailable, but remains hypothesis-generating pending external validation.

title: Cryptogenic multifocal ulcerous stenosing enteritis diagnosed and managed with intraoperative enteroscopy: a case report.
abstract: Background Cryptogenic multifocal ulcerous stenosing enteritis (CMUSE) is a rare small intestinal disorder characterized by multifocal superficial ulcerations and short-segment circumferential strictures. Because the lesions are discontinuous and confined to the mucosa/submucosa, preoperative assessment of disease extent is often inadequate. Intraoperative enteroscopy may enable direct mucosal visualization and guide segmental resection, yet its role in CMUSE remains inadequately described, and whether it confers any advantage over conventional surgical assessment cannot be established from a single case. Case summary A 58-year-old Han Chinese man presented with recurrent small-bowel obstruction for 20 years. Each episode had resolved with conservative management, but the cause had never been identified. He was admitted to our hospital with recent symptom exacerbation; he had no musculoskeletal or joint disorder and no chronic use of aspirin, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), or over-the-counter analgesics, and his only remote exposure was a 1-2-week course of an over-the-counter analgesic taken two years earlier after operative fixation of a left shoulder fracture. Contrast-enhanced CT enterography revealed localized ileal wall thickening, routine endoscopic examinations were unremarkable. Capsule endoscopy was performed after thorough counseling regarding the risk of retention, with the understanding that retention, should it occur, would confirm and localize obstructive strictures. Two stenosing ulcerations were visualized while the capsule was retained between them. The patient subsequently underwent exploratory laparoscopy. Intraoperative enteroscopy through a limited enterotomy provided direct visualization of the entire small bowel and identified four circumferential strictures, all of which were included in a tailored segmental resection. Histopathology showed superficial ulcerations confined to the mucosa and submucosa with fibrotic stricture formation, consistent with CMUSE. The postoperative course was uneventful, and he remained symptom-free at 10-month follow-up. Conclusion In this patient, intraoperative enteroscopy enabled intraoperative mucosal assessment of the entire small bowel, defined the extent of disease, and guided tailored segmental resection; these observations are limited to a single case and do not establish a bowel-preserving advantage over conventional surgical assessment. Capsule endoscopy in suspected stricturing small-bowel disease requires caution and patency assessment; if retention occurs it may provide localizing information, but this does not justify its use in patients with suspected strictures.

title: Feasibility of patient-specific 3D-printed fragment models for preoperative planning in bicondylar tibial plateau fractures: a retrospective case series.
abstract: Purpose Schatzker type V and VI tibial plateau fractures have complex three-dimensional patterns that complicate surgical planning and coronal alignment restoration. This study assessed the feasibility of patient-specific 3D-printed fragment models for planning combined medial and lateral approaches and described radiographic and functional outcomes. Methods We retrospectively reviewed 22 patients with Schatzker type V or VI fractures treated at Foshan Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine from January 2023 to July 2024. Preoperative CT data enabled fragment segmentation, color coding, virtual reduction, and fabrication of patient-specific physical models. Posterior tibial slope, medial proximal tibial angle, articular depression, and tibial plateau width were compared pre- and postoperatively. Rasmussen functional and radiological scores and Knee Society Scores were assessed at 3 and 6 months, 1 year, and final follow-up; complications were recorded. Results All 22 patients completed follow-up (mean, 30.73 ± 3.20 months). A mean of 24.41 ± 2.26 tibial fragments were identified and segmented per patient. Mean articular depression decreased from 6.70 ± 3.07 to 1.74 ± 0.48 mm. Posterior tibial slope, medial proximal tibial angle, and tibial plateau width improved significantly after surgery (all P < 0.001). Mean postoperative coronal alignment was within the predefined normal range in both preoperative varus and valgus subgroups. All three scores differed significantly across follow-up (all P < 0.001). At final follow-up, mean Rasmussen functional and Knee Society Scores were 27.18 ± 1.84 and 87.55 ± 4.92, respectively, with excellent-or-good rates of 100% and 95.45%. Mild post-traumatic knee osteoarthritis, superficial infection, and deep-vein thrombosis occurred in 5, 1, and 2 patients, respectively. No secondary varus or valgus deformity was observed. Conclusions In complex bicondylar tibial plateau fractures, patient-specific 3D-printed fragment models provided a practical three-dimensional reference for fragment identification, reduction sequencing, and planning of combined medial and lateral approaches. Satisfactory articular reduction, maintenance of proximal tibial coronal alignment, and favorable functional outcomes at final follow-up were observed in this cohort. These findings support the feasibility of incorporating 3D-printed fragment models into preoperative planning for these fractures.

title: Artificial intelligence in radiology education: from AI-supported learning to clinical innovation-a narrative review.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing diagnostic radiology, but education and training have not kept pace. This narrative review brings together current evidence on AI-supported learning in radiology education and how such learning can move into clinical innovation. Surveys from different countries point to the same gap: in a 25-country international survey of radiographers, radiologists, and students, only 10.3% had received formal AI training; in one national survey of Turkish residents, 84.5% had received none. The review maps competency frameworks and curriculum models that define AI literacy and support staged integration into residency. It also assesses AI as a teaching tool, including AI-assisted case-based learning, computer-aided diagnosis training, precision-education knowledge recommenders, and virtual, augmented, and extended reality. Controlled and randomized studies show measurable gains: computer-aided diagnosis training raised resident scores above self-study controls (mean score 52 vs. 38 on a 100-point scale), while an AI-based knowledge recommender shortened reporting time by 162 s per case and relative improvement in graded reporting accuracy scores of 14% (95% CI 8.1-19.8%). Large language models are promising but limited: GPT-4 approaches board-style examination performance (80.6%) yet remains poor at image-based reasoning (47.8%). The review closes by considering how education can feed clinical innovation, along with algorithmic and automation bias, ethical governance, and future research needs. AI education should therefore span the full continuum-from undergraduate training to continuing professional development-if radiology is to innovate safely, effectively, and equitably.

title: Intraoperative rescue left stellate ganglion block for refractory ventricular arrhythmias following resuscitation from torsades de pointes: a case report.
abstract: Background Congenital long QT syndrome (cLQTS) predisposes patients to torsades de pointes (TdP) under sympathetic stress. Although ultrasound-guided left stellate ganglion block (LSGB) can rapidly achieve cardiac sympathetic blockade, its application in intraoperative rescue has been scarcely documented. Case A 53-year-old woman with clinically suspected cLQTS (QTc 499 ms) developed pulseless TdP during fracture manipulation under general anesthesia. Following restoration of spontaneous circulation, frequent ventricular ectopy and short runs of TdP persisted despite treatment with magnesium sulfate, lidocaine, and esmolol. Following concomitant multimodal antiarrhythmic therapy, LSGB was performed with 5 mL of 0.25% ropivacaine, and a marked reduction of arrhythmias was observed shortly afterwards. No recurrent ventricular arrhythmias were observed during subsequent treatment and follow-up. Conclusions LSGB may be considered as an adjunct to pharmacological therapy when ventricular arrhythmia responds suboptimally and is presumed to be exacerbated by sympathetic stimulation in patients with QT prolongation.

title: HER2 amplification assessment in breast cancer in the HER2-SISH histopathological images using deep learning models.
abstract: Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2 (HER2) status is a critical determinant of breast cancer prognosis and therapeutic strategy. Silver in situ Hybridization (SISH) enables HER2 gene assessment under bright-field microscopy while preserving tissue morphology, rendering it a clinically favoured alternative to fluorescence-based methods. Nevertheless, manual SISH slide interpretation is subjective, time-intensive, and susceptible to inter-observer variability, necessitating robust automated computational solutions. This work presents a systematic comparative evaluation of six deep learning architectures for multiclass HER2-SISH histopathology image classification across three diagnostic categories: Amplified, Non-Amplified, and ROI_Normal. The evaluated architectures span convolutional neural networks (MobileNetV3-Large, DenseNet121), transformer-based models (ViT-Small, DeiT-Small), and novel hybrid CNN-Transformer frameworks (DenseNet121-ViT, DenseNet121-DeiT). All models were trained under five-fold stratified cross-validation with a split-before-augmentation protocol and evaluated on an independent held-out test set over both the original and an augmented version of the publicly available HER2-SISH40x dataset. On the original dataset, DenseNet121 achieved the highest test accuracy of 82.10% with a macro F1-score of 77.33%. After offline rotational augmentation of the training partition, DenseNet121 achieved the best performance with test accuracy of 85.09% and macro F1-score of 80.61%, with ViT-Small (84.47%) and DenseNet121-ViT (83.23%) following closely. Per-class analysis revealed that ROI_Normal was consistently classified with the highest accuracy, whereas Amplified versus Non-Amplified discrimination remained the principal challenge across all evaluated models.

title: Multi-tissue segmentation of knee MRI based on U-Net and conditional generative adversarial networks.
abstract: Objective This study aimed to systematically compare the performance of U-Net and a conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN) for multi-tissue segmentation of knee magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) using the public SKI10 dataset, and to investigate the effects of loss functions, discriminator receptive fields, and normalization strategies on model performance through ablation experiments. Methods The segmentation targets included the femur, femoral cartilage, tibia, and tibial cartilage, with the background incorporated as an additional class to formulate a five-class segmentation task. All MRI images and labels were read from the original. mhd files and two-dimensional slices were extracted along the sagittal direction. Images were resized to 512 × 512 pixels and standardized using z-score normalization, whereas labels were resized with nearest-neighbor interpolation to preserve categorical encoding. Training and test sets were split at the MRI-volume level to prevent information leakage caused by adjacent slices from the same volume being assigned to different subsets. U-Net was used as the supervised baseline model, and a cGAN segmentation framework consisting of a U-Net-style generator and a discriminator was constructed. Evaluation metrics included the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) and the 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95). Qualitative segmentation, error heatmaps, boundary comparison, per-class win rate, Bland-Altman agreement analysis, boundary DSC, false-positive/false-negative composition, surface-distance distributions, and training dynamics were further analyzed. A sub-selection of 10 of the 70 training volumes was used as a validation set for checkpoint selection; the 30 test volumes were accessed only at final evaluation and were never used for training, model selection, or hyperparameter optimisation. Results Baseline comparison showed that U-Net and cGAN exhibited complementary behavior in knee MRI multi-tissue segmentation. The mean DSC across the four anatomical structures was significantly higher for cGAN than for U-Net (0.8061 ± 0.0542 vs. 0.8035 ± 0.0520; P < 0.001). In contrast, the mean HD95 was lower for cGAN than for U-Net (4.02 ± 1.18 mm vs. 5.38 ± 1.44 mm), indicating better boundary-distance control and local contour fitting. Structure-specific analysis showed that segmentation of osseous structures was more stable than that of cartilage structures, and model differences were concentrated mainly in thin-layer tissues such as femoral and tibial cartilage. Loss-function ablation showed that L2 and Smooth L1 losses improved DSC and reduced HD95 in U-Net, with Smooth L1 being more favorable for boundary-distance control. In the cGAN framework, the L1 pixel-wise loss yielded the most stable performance. Discriminator receptive-field ablation showed that PixelGAN achieved the best overall performance, indicating that larger PatchGAN receptive fields do not necessarily improve segmentation of medical label maps. Comparison of normalization strategies showed that BatchNorm achieved higher DSC than InstanceNorm in both U-Net and cGAN PixelGAN. Conclusion U-Net and cGAN showed complementary strengths in knee MRI multi-tissue segmentation. U-Net provided better regional overlap and cartilage continuity, whereas cGAN PixelGAN achieved lower boundary errors. These findings support task-specific selection of segmentation architectures and discriminator configurations. However, as the results were based on a single predefined volume-level split of the SKI10 dataset, they require confirmation through repeated splits, cross-validation, and external multicenter validation.

title: MRI-derived radiogenomic surrogate of a hypoxia-angiogenesis-EMT transcriptional state in nasopharyngeal carcinoma: multicenter external validation.
abstract: Background This study aimed to develop a pretreatment MRI-derived radiogenomic surrogate of a prespecified hypoxia-angiogenesis-epithelial-mesenchymal transition transcriptional state and to evaluate its associations with treatment response and survival in nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Methods This multicenter observational study integrated patient-derived public transcriptomic datasets, experimental CNE2/CNE2-IR radioresistance models, a prospective RNA-sequencing cohort of 49 patients with paired contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI and RNA data, and two independent clinical cohorts (n = 532 and n = 118). HAE-CAS was the equal-weight mean of three within-cohort standardized module scores. Treatment response was assessed approximately 3 months after chemoradiotherapy according to RECIST version 1.1 using nasopharyngeal MRI, nasopharyngoscopy, and clinical evaluation. Rad-HAE used a five-feature Gaussian ridge model and was evaluated with 20 repetitions of five-fold nested cross-validation; response and survival outcomes were excluded from model development. Results Among 49 response-evaluable RNA-sequenced patients, 17 had complete response (CR) and 32 had partial response (PR); no stable or progressive disease occurred. HAE-CAS was higher in PR than CR (rank-biserial correlation = 0.365, P = 0.035). In GSE102349, continuous HAE-CAS was not significantly associated with progression-free survival (HR per 1-SD increase = 1.20, 95% CI 0.74-1.95; P = 0.465), whereas the median-dichotomized comparison was exploratory (log-rank P = 0.024). Aggregated out-of-fold Rad-HAE correlated with HAE-CAS (Spearman rho = 0.637, P < 0.001) and discriminated PR from CR among 49 paired response-evaluable patients (AUC = 0.846, 95% CI 0.732-0.943). In two independent clinical cohorts, higher Rad-HAE was associated with shorter progression-free and overall survival. Conclusion Pretreatment CE-T1WI radiomics was associated with interpatient variation in a prespecified composite HAE transcriptional state. Rad-HAE represents an imaging-based surrogate associated with the composite HAE transcriptional state and does not directly quantify individual biological processes.

title: CT-derived nested habitats score for preoperative IASLC grading in lung adenocarcinoma: cross-center validation and radiogenomic analysis.
abstract: Introduction The 2020 International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer (IASLC) grading system integrates the predominant histologic pattern and the proportion of high-grade patterns, but preoperative CT assessment is limited by spatial averaging of heterogeneous tumor components. We aimed to develop a CT-derived nested habitats score (NHS) that recursively identifies grade-associated intratumoral CT subregions, evaluate its cross-center performance for preoperative IASLC grading, and explore its transcriptomic correlates. Methods This retrospective two-center study included 650 patients with surgically resected lung adenocarcinoma. Center 1 formed the development cohort (n = 390); Center 2 was stratified 1:1 into validation (n = 130) and locked test (n = 130) cohorts, both from the same external institution. The prespecified primary task was pathologic IASLC Grade 1 versus Grade 2/3. NHS was generated using five-fold out-of-fold estimation in development data. Clinical-radiological, whole-tumor radiomics, NHS, and integrated models were compared, with algorithm selection confined to validation before one-time test evaluation. An independent TCGA-LUAD/TCIA CT-RNA cohort (n = 88) underwent exploratory WGCNA and Hallmark gene-set enrichment analysis. Results The development/validation/test cohorts contained 41/14/14 Grade 1, 293/101/96 Grade 2, and 56/15/20 Grade 3 tumors. The selected random-forest integrated model yielded AUCs of 0.871 (95% CI, 0.784-0.936) in validation and 0.866 (95% CI, 0.784-0.935) in testing. NHS alone yielded AUCs of 0.828 and 0.854, compared with 0.620 and 0.497 for the clinical-radiological model and 0.703 and 0.775 for whole-tumor radiomics. NHS accounted for 76.3% of mean absolute SHAP contribution; removing NHS reduced AUC by 0.251 (95% CI, 0.079-0.439) in validation and 0.369 (95% CI, 0.200-0.553) in testing. Brier scores for NHS and the integrated model (0.074-0.077) were below the non-informative reference (0.096), but calibration slopes exceeded 1, and decision curves showed no net benefit over treating all patients as Grade 2/3 at low-to-intermediate thresholds. Exploratory radiogenomics showed nominal NHS-associated coexpression modules and enrichment of WNT/beta-catenin, E2F, G2M-checkpoint, and immune-related programs. Discussion NHS discriminated IASLC Grade 1 from Grade 2/3 tumors, retained stable performance in two held-out cohorts from a second institution, and contributed most of the integrated model's discrimination. The transcriptomic associations are hypothesis-generating, and recalibration and prospective multicenter evaluation are required before clinical application.

title: Multimodal MRI and blood-based epigenomic and protein-based multiomics profiling in mild neurocognitive disorder: a single-center cross-sectional observational study protocol.
abstract: Introduction Mild neurocognitive disorder (mild NCD) is a clinically relevant stage of cognitive decline with heterogeneous clinical trajectories that remain poorly characterized, limiting efforts to identify early markers of disease progression. It may be associated with structural, functional, metabolic, CSF-related, and molecular features of the brain. This single-center, single-group, cross-sectional observational study aims to characterize multimodal imaging, cognitive, emotional, and blood-based molecular profiles in adults with mild NCD and to explore imaging-molecular associations for future hypothesis generation. Methods and analysis Sixty participants aged 50-85 years who meet DSM-5 criteria for mild NCD and satisfy MoCA-K and Short-form Geriatric Depression Scale screening criteria will be enrolled at Daejeon Korean Medicine Hospital of Daejeon University. Neuropsychological assessments will include the K-MMSE, SNSB-II, and ADAS-K-cog, and emotional response measures will be obtained using the emotional stimulus response test, which includes an emotion-inducing video, facial response recording, and self-report ratings. Blood-based multiomics assessments will include targeted plasma protein and cytokine profiling, APOE genotyping, and genome-wide DNA methylation profiling. Multimodal brain MRI will be performed at the Korea Basic Science Institute and will include structural MRI, resting-state and task-based functional MRI, magnetic resonance spectroscopy, and intravoxel incoherent motion imaging to deliver CSF-related indices. The main descriptive variables will consist of MRI-derived structural, functional, metabolic, and CSF-related indices. Secondary exploratory analyses will examine associations between MRI-derived indices, cognitive performance, emotional response measures, and blood-based molecular markers. Discussion Although this single-group, cross-sectional study cannot establish causality or directly validate diagnostic or predictive markers, it will characterize multimodal profiles in mild NCD and explore common imaging, cognitive, emotional, and blood-based molecular patterns. These findings will be interpreted as hypothesis-generating and may help prioritize candidate biomarkers for future longitudinal and comparative studies. title: Prediction of multi-stage Alzheimer's disease progression based on surface-based morphometry and machine learning.
abstract: Background Early identification of individuals at high risk of progression from normal cognition (NC) to mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and from MCI to Alzheimer's disease (AD) is crucial for timely intervention. However, predictive models that simultaneously address multiple transition stages along the AD continuum remain limited. Objective To develop and validate machine learning models and nomograms based on surface-based morphometry (SBM) features, neuropsychological assessments, and plasma biomarkers for predicting disease progression in early mild cognitive impairment (EMCI), late mild cognitive impairment (LMCI), and NC populations. Methods This longitudinal study included 406 participants from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database. SBM features, including sulcal depth, gyrification index, and fractal dimension, were extracted from 3D T1-weighted MRI. Multiple machine learning classifiers (support vector machine, linear discriminant analysis, LASSO, and Gaussian process) were employed to construct predictive models. An R score generated from the optimal machine learning model was combined with clinical predictors via logistic regression to build the nomogram. Model performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves. Results The study included 406 participants: 150 with EMCI, 67 with LMCI, and 189 with NC. The conversion rates to the next stage were 20.7% for EMCI-to-AD, 49.3% for LMCI-to-AD, and 26.5% for NC-to-MCI. The SBM-based machine learning models yielded AUCs of 0.769, 0.750, and 0.640 for predicting conversion from EMCI to AD, LMCI to AD, and NC to MCI, respectively, in the validation set. The integrated nomogram incorporating the R score and clinical predictors significantly improved predictive performance, achieving validation AUCs of 0.91 (EMCI to AD), 0.74 (LMCI to AD), and 0.73 (NC to MCI). Independent predictors for the different transition stages included the R score, tau protein (P-tau181), Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio, age, and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score, with variation across stages. Conclusion Integrating the SBM-derived R score with clinical and biomarker data through a nomogram provides a clinically interpretable tool for predicting multi-stage AD progression. This strategy may facilitate early risk stratification and the development of individualized intervention plans.

The study included 406 participants: 150 with EMCI, 67 with LMCI, and 189 with NC. The conversion rates to the next stage were 20.7% for EMCI-to-AD, 49.3% for LMCI-to-AD, and 26.5% for NC-to-MCI. The SBM-based machine learning models yielded AUCs of 0.769, 0.750, and 0.640 for predicting conversion from EMCI to AD, LMCI to AD, and NC to MCI, respectively, in the validation set. The integrated nomogram incorporating the R score and clinical predictors significantly improved predictive performance, achieving validation AUCs of 0.91 (EMCI to AD), 0.74 (LMCI to AD), and 0.73 (NC to MCI). Independent predictors for the different transition stages included the R score, tau protein (P-tau181), Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio, age, and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score, with variation across stages.

Conclusion

Integrating the SBM-derived R score with clinical and biomarker data through a nomogram provides a clinically interpretable tool for predicting multi-stage AD progression. This strategy may facilitate early risk stratification and the development of individualized intervention plans.

title: Brain structural and functional alterations in patients following cardiopulmonary bypass: a short-term longitudinal fMRI study.
abstract: Objective While cross-sectional studies have identified brain abnormalities after cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB), the early dynamic trajectory of these alterations from the preoperative state remains to be fully characterized. This longitudinal study investigates the within-subject evolution of brain structure and function following CPB. Methods Sixty-eight patients undergoing CPB were scanned twice (preoperatively and 15 days post-surgery) using resting-state fMRI and T1-weighted MRI. We assessed changes in regional homogeneity (ReHo) for local neural activity, graph-based network topology, and surface-based morphometry (SBM). Results Comparison of pre- and postoperative scans revealed a coordinated pattern of brain reorganization. Functionally, ReHo decreased within default mode network (DMN) hubs, specifically the posterior cingulate cortex and right angular gyrus, while increasing in fronto-parietal network (FPN) regions (bilateral inferior frontal gyri) and the right temporal lobe. Network analysis showed altered functional segregation (reduced clustering coefficient and local efficiency) alongside enhanced integration (increased global efficiency), raising the possibility of network-level reorganization. Structurally, these functional shifts paralleled gray matter loss, cortical thinning, and sulcal shallowing in fronto-temporal regions and the right precuneus, accompanied by reduced cortical complexity (fractal dimension, gyrification index) in temporal, frontal, and occipital areas. Conclusion This longitudinal study provides preliminary evidence suggesting that CPB is associated with dynamic and coordinated remodeling of brain structure and function. The DMN-FPN imbalance and right temporal lobe alteration may represent candidate neural correlates for future investigations into postoperative cognitive dysfunction.

title: Decoding glioblastoma recurrence: harnessing radiomics and machine learning for early prediction.
abstract: Objective This study aimed to analyze postoperative periresidual FLAIR hyperintensity and assess radiomic features from periresidual enhancing and non-enhancing subregions for predicting early GBM recurrence (pre-CRT RANO criteria). We also evaluated the incremental prognostic value of multi-subregion radiomic signatures over conventional clinical and MRI features. Methods Adult patients with surgically confirmed GBM were retrospectively enrolled and randomly split into training ( n = 128) and test ( n = 56) cohorts at a 7:3 ratio. Postoperative pre-radiotherapy CE-T1WI and FLAIR images were fused to semi-automatically delineate periresidual enhancing (ROI-1) and non-enhancing hyperintense (ROI-2) regions using 3D Slicer. Radiomic features were extracted from both subregions and their fusion area. LASSO regression was used to select optimal features related to early recurrence from ROI-1, ROI-2, and combined subregion datasets. Five machine learning algorithms (DT, LR, NB, SVM, XGBoost) were applied to build radiomic prediction models. To evaluate the incremental value of radiomic signatures, a clinical/MRI-only baseline model was constructed using conventional clinical and morphological MRI features. Multivariate logistic regression was performed to identify independent clinical and MRI predictors. A quantitative Rad-score was generated based on the optimal combined radiomic features, and an integrated radiomics-clinical model with a predictive nomogram was established by incorporating the Rad-score and independent clinical/MRI variables. Ten-fold cross-validation was used for internal validation. Model performance was comprehensively assessed using ROC curves, calibration curves, and decision curve analysis in terms of discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility. Results A logistic regression analysis of 184 GBM cases found subventricular zone involvement [HR 4.868 (1.657-14.308), p = 0.004] and partial resection [HR 3.640 (1.341-9.883), p = 0.011] as predictors of early recurrence. The baseline model achieved an AUC of 0.701. Among five models using ROI-1 features, XGBoost performed best with validation AUC of 0.663. For ROI-2, the DT model excelled with 0.713. Combining ROI-1 and ROI-2, XGBoost achieved 0.752. Integrating radiomics with clinical and MRI data, XGBoost reached 0.817. DCA indicated the combined model had the highest clinical effectiveness. DCA showed that a threshold probability of 0.1 to 0.6 yields a net gain. Conclusion In-depth analysis of the enhanced and non-enhanced regions, within the FLAIR hyperintense surrounding the residual cavity of GBM before pre-CRT using ML, has revealed certain value for the early prediction of GBM recurrence. Furthermore, a combined model incorporating radiomic features, clinical and conventional MRI attributes enhances the predictive accuracy for survival prognosis.

title: The acute effects of decaffeinated coffee on cognitive function and brain activity: a single-center experience.
abstract: Background Coffee is one of the most widely consumed beverages worldwide and is known for its beneficial effects on various diseases, which is often attributed to caffeine. However, other bioactive compounds in coffee also play an important role. The aim of this study was to investigate the acute effects of decaffeinated coffee. Methods Thirty-one healthy adults participated in the study. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI), cognitive-behavioral tests, self-report scales, and physiological measures were completed at baseline and 30 min post-drink. Based on rs-fMRI, we used static and dynamic amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (ALFF), fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (fALFF), and regional homogeneity (ReHo) to observe changes in spontaneous brain activity following acute decaffeinated coffee intake. Definitions of static- (s-) and dynamic- (d-) prefixes for resting-state metrics: Static indices (sALFF, sfALFF, sReHo) were calculated across the entire resting-state time course without sliding-window segmentation, representing the mean level of spontaneous brain activity during the whole scan session. Dynamic indices (dALFF, dfALFF, dReHo) were derived via a sliding-window approach: ALFF, fALFF or ReHo was computed within each successive window, and the standard deviation of these window-wise values was taken as the final dynamic metric, reflecting the temporal variability of regional spontaneous neural activity. Results After consumption, participants showed significantly faster reaction times in the 1-back ( p = 0.002), 2-back ( p = 0.023), Continuous Performance Test ( p = 0.003), and Finger Tapping Task ( p = 0.009). At the neural level, the participants showed significantly higher sfALFF in the fusiform gyrus (FFG) and inferior temporal gyrus (ITG) and significantly lower sReHo in the medial orbital of the superior frontal gyrus (PFCventmed) after consuming decaffeinated coffee compared with before, with no significant differences in sALFF. The sfALFF values in the FFG were significantly negatively correlated with RTs on Continuous Performance Test (CPT). Dynamic analysis revealed significantly lower dALFF values in the FFG and cerebellum, and significantly higher dALFF and dReHo values in the supplementary motor area (SMA). No brain regions showed significant differences in dfALFF after consuming decaffeinated coffee compared with before (GRF-corrected, voxel-level p < 0.01, cluster-level p < 0.05). In addition, diastolic blood pressure significantly increased ( p = 0.004), and headache scores were higher ( p = 0.033), while no significant changes in systolic blood pressure or heart rate were observed. Conclusion These results suggest that decaffeinated coffee may affects cognitive performance and brain activity, providing insights into the effects of non-caffeine components of coffee and their underlying mechanisms. As an initial exploratory study, it provides a foundation for future research. Randomized, placebo-controlled trials with long-term assessments are now needed to validate and extend these findings.

title: Quantified standardized individualized small craniotomy vs. conventional large craniotomy for cerebral herniation secondary to acute supratentorial epidural hematoma: a propensity score-matched study for emergency and battlefield trauma care.
abstract: Background Acute supratentorial epidural hematoma (EDH) with uncal transtentorial herniation is a fatal emergency for civilian and battlefield trauma. Conventional large craniotomy causes excessive surgical damage inconsistent with damage control surgery (DCS). Current minimally invasive EDH approaches lack standardized bone window metrics, rarely enroll patients with definite brain herniation, and lack battlefield-adapted evidence. This 1:1 propensity score-matched (PSM) study compared perioperative trauma and long-term neurological outcomes between a stratified quantitative small craniotomy and traditional decompressive surgery. Methods This single-center retrospective cohort included patients with isolated acute EDH and preoperative uncal herniation (2012-2018). Confounders such as age, admission GCS, hematoma volume and anisocoria were balanced via PSM. A five-step CT-guided quantified small craniotomy workflow with tiered 4.0-6.0 cm bone windows was applied. Primary outcomes were operative time and intraoperative blood loss; secondary outcomes covered reoperation risk, hematoma clearance, soft tissue complications, wound healing and 6-month GOS. Results Twenty-two matched pairs (44 patients) were analyzed. Small craniotomy was associated with a 31.1% reduction in operative duration and 71.7% reduction in intraoperative blood loss (both p < 0.001). It lowered persistent scalp numbness and accelerated suture removal (both p < 0.05). No reoperations occurred in either group. No statistically significant intergroup differences in residual hematoma, clearance efficiency and 6-month neurological recovery were detected, although the cohort size limits our capacity to exclude small-to-moderate clinically meaningful differences. Subgroup exploratory analyses are reported in Supplementary Table S1. Conclusion CT-guided quantified individualized small craniotomy represents a DCS-compliant minimally-invasive surgical option for patients with herniated acute EDH in this selected cohort. No statistically significant between-group differences in hematoma evacuation efficacy or 6-month neurological functional recovery were detected, though our analysis is limited by modest sample size and cannot definitively rule-out small-to-moderate clinically meaningful differences between procedures. The procedure was associated with reduced surgical trauma metrics. This standardized rapid decompression protocol possesses hypothetical translational value for civilian emergency treatment and resource-limited casualty-care scenarios.

title: Explainable volumetric deep learning from contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI for preoperative IDH prediction in adult-type diffuse gliomas: a two-center study.
abstract: Objective To evaluate contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI (CE-T1WI) models for preoperative prediction of isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutation status in adult-type diffuse gliomas and explore phenotype associations of influential latent features. Methods This retrospective study included 462 patients. Center 1 provided training ( n = 259) and internal-test ( n = 65) cohorts, and Center 2 provided external validation ( n = 138). Five input-architecture combinations and six classifiers were evaluated against an interpretable logistic benchmark combining age and Visually Accessible Rembrandt Images (VASARI) descriptors. For each architecture, the classifier with the highest observed external area under the curve (AUC) was selected for reporting. Performance was assessed using discrimination, calibration, decision curves, and 100 downstream refits with fixed deep features. Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) and phenotype association analyses examined influential latent features and their relationships with clinical and imaging phenotypes. Results Region-of-interest (ROI)-constrained three-dimensional vision Transformer (3D ViT) with a support vector machine (SVM) achieved an external AUC of 0.929 (95% CI, 0.885-0.973), accuracy of 0.848, sensitivity of 0.838, specificity of 0.857, and Brier score of 0.106. The age-VASARI benchmark achieved an external AUC of 0.782. Across downstream refits, the ROI-constrained model had a mean external AUC of 0.930 and the smallest mean training-minus-external AUC difference (0.019). The same 10 features formed the highest-importance SHAP set across cohorts, with different rank orders. Feature_546 correlated with age ( r = 0.461), postoperative Ki-67 ( r = 0.562), and enhancement quality ( r = 0.678; all adjusted p < 0.001). Conclusion ROI-constrained volumetric learning from CE-T1WI showed promising cross-center IDH discrimination using one routine MRI sequence. Influential latent features were associated with postoperative Ki-67 and recognizable imaging phenotypes. SHAP attribution and these exploratory associations provide complementary perspectives on model behavior in preoperative IDH assessment.

title: Normative references of corpus callosum across lifespan and application in neurological and neuroimmunological disorders.
abstract: Background The corpus callosum (CC) is the largest white matter structure and is often affected in neurological and neuroimmunological disorders. However, previous studies mainly used group-level comparisons. This limits patient-level magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) assessment. Methods In this multicenter retrospective study, 3D T 1 -weighted MRI data from 24,305 healthy controls aged 4-85 years were used to construct age-,sex-, and estimated total intracranial volume (eTIV)- adjusted normative references for the whole CC and five subregions. Deviation scores were calculated and applied to 4,081 patients with multiple sclerosis (MS, n = 573), neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD, n = 389), mild cognitive impairment (MCI, n = 308), Alzheimer's disease (AD, n = 623), Parkinson's disease (PD, n = 1,285), and cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD, n = 903). Classification, clinical correlation, and prognostic analyses were performed as exploratory applications. Results The volume of CC subregions peaked from early adulthood (central, 26.0 years) to midlife (posterior, 47.2 years; anterior, 47.5 years), forming a "centre-to-periphery" pattern. MS showed negative deviations mainly in central and mid-anterior regions (Cohen's d = -0.28 to -0.30, p FDR<0.001), while CSVD and AD showed widespread negative deviations ( d = -0.13 to -0.49). NMOSD, MCI, and PD showed relatively small or regionally limited deviations. Deviation score based classification performance ranged from AUC = 0.598-0.775. Exploratory analyses identified weak correlations between deviation scores and processing speed in MS (Spearman's ρ up to 0.22, p < 0.05) and cognition in CSVD ( ρ = 0.12-0.19, p < 0.05) and AD ( ρ = 0.10-0.16, p < 0.05). None survived FDR correction. Baseline deviation-based risk groups stratified subsequent relapse and disability outcomes in MS and NMOSD ( p < 0.001). An exploratory comparison suggested a nominal difference in baseline CC deviation burden between MCI converters and non-converters to AD. Conclusion Lifespan normative references of the CC provide a quantitative framework for characterizing individual structural deviations across neurological and neuroimmunological disorders. Exploratory clinical analyses suggest potential applications that require further validation.

title: Multimodal brain lesion classification approach through MRI radiomics and OCR-recovered MRS metabolites with explainable AI.
abstract: This work presents a multimodal machine learning pipeline for brain lesion classification, fusing structural radiomic features from multi-sequence MRI (T2-FLAIR, T1-contrast) with metabolic features recovered from Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy (MRS) screenshots via a custom Optical Character Recognition (OCR) pipeline. The study draws on a clinical cohort of 55 patients (17 non-neoplastic, 38 neoplastic). MRI radiomics span first-order intensity statistics, Grey-Level Co-occurrence Matrix (GLCM) texture, morphological shape, and contrast-enhancement ratios, while MRS metabolites (Cho, Cr, NAA, and their ratios) are lifted from rendered spectra through Tesseract OCR with multi-region cropping and Lanczos upsampling. Features are evaluated under a leakage-controlled Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV) protocol with in-fold imputation, feature selection and normalization, using the classifier's default decision threshold. The primary, bias-corrected performance estimate comes from nested LOOCV, in which classifier family and feature count are chosen using training data only: the multimodal pipeline reaches 82.0% accuracy. The best fixed configuration (Random Forest, k = 3) reaches 85.5% accuracy (47/55) and AUC = 0.82, but because it is selected on the same data it is scored on, it is reported as an exploratory, optimistic figure. The comparison model, which uses MRI-derived features without OCR-recovered metabolites, reaches 78.2% at its own best configuration, so the best-configuration gain is +7.3 percentage points and the nested estimate exceeds that baseline by +3.8 points. The two strongest discriminators are log NAA ( F = 16.01) and log Cho ( F = 12.89). The best-configuration result holds under 1,000-permutation testing (random-label mean 55.0%) and McNemar's exact test ( p = 0.05, borderline). At N = 55, and with diagnostic labels that themselves drew on MRS, these results stand as proof-of-concept: OCR-recovered MRS metabolites are informative for reproducing expert diagnostic judgment beyond what MRI-derived features supply alone.

title: Reclassification of acute inflammatory myelopathies in the antibody era: from AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG to double-seronegative disease.
abstract: Acute inflammatory myelopathy refers to a heterogeneous group of acute or subacute spinal cord syndromes characterized by clinical features suggestive of inflammatory involvement. Although these diseases have overlapping clinical manifestations, their underlying mechanisms, disease progression, and classification systems remain heterogeneous. The discovery of AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG has driven a shift from a "syndrome-based nomenclature" to a "disease-specific classification," allowing some patients previously classified as transverse myelitis or seronegative NMOSD to be reclassified as more specific disease entities. However, AQP4-IgG/MOG-IgG double-negative cases remain highly heterogeneous, including double-negative NMOSD, multiple sclerosis (MS), other immune-mediated myelopathies, and non-inflammatory mimics. Additionally, testing conditions may also affect whether a patient is classified as seronegative. This narrative review examines the roles of antibody stratification, MRI, and cerebrospinal fluid in the classification of acute inflammatory myelopathy, focusing on the disease composition of double-negative cases and longitudinal reclassification. Existing evidence supports interpreting double-seronegative status as a serological classification state rather than an independent disease entity. Some patients initially unclassified may be reclassified into specific disease categories during longitudinal follow-up.

title: An EMG-driven virtual reality platform for physiology-based motor interaction: technical and functional validation.
abstract: Harnessing experience-dependent neuroplasticity has become a central goal of modern neurorehabilitation. Immersive virtual reality (VR) has emerged as a promising tool, enabling task-oriented training in ecologically valid scenarios that are difficult to reproduce in conventional clinical settings. Despite these advances, interaction in most existing VR rehabilitation systems remains primarily mediated by external interfaces, such as motion tracking or handheld controllers, rather than by the user's own physiological motor activity. Consequently, rehabilitation often fails to directly engage the physiological motor commands that naturally drive voluntary movement. We present and validate an integrated VR-electromyography (VR-EMG) platform that enables closed-loop, physiology-driven interaction between users and immersive virtual environments. The platform combines a standalone VR architecture with wearable EMG systems, online EMG decoding, and cloud-based performance monitoring within a unified framework. A standardized motor-command interface enables different EMG acquisition systems to control both anthropomorphic and non-anthropomorphic virtual effectors without modifying the decoding strategy or rehabilitation scenarios, providing a flexible framework for diverse applications. The platform was validated through complementary technical and functional evaluations performed on the two supported EMG acquisition systems. Technical validation assessed signal quality, gesture classification accuracy, communication latency, and system reliability. Functional validation was conducted in individuals with upper-limb amputation and able-bodied controls while performing object-interaction tasks across multiple immersive virtual scenarios. The platform demonstrated stable closed-loop operation, reliable gesture recognition, and the ability to quantify objective performance metrics, including task score, completion time, gesture classification errors, precision errors, correctly recognized gestures, and user-reported workload. Findings demonstrate the feasibility, technical reliability, and functional versatility of the proposed platform by providing a physiology-driven framework for immersive motor interaction that is compatible with different EMG acquisition systems and dissociates motor control from the morphology of the controlled virtual effector. Because the two systems were used for different components of the validation, we do not establish equivalence in their performance. By integrating online EMG decoding, VR, and quantitative performance monitoring, the platform offers a tool for future applications in rehabilitation, prosthetic training, and studies using functional magnetic resonance imaging and high-density electroencephalography to address whether training with the platform induces changes in functional brain organization.

title: The effect of pretreatment CT-assessed low skeletal muscle mass and treatment-related muscle mass loss on prognosis in patients with bone and soft tissue sarcomas: an updated meta-analysis.
abstract: Objective Sarcopenia has been recognized as an important biomarker of adverse clinical outcomes across a wide range of malignancies. However, existing evidence regarding the impact of low skeletal muscle mass on the prognosis of bone and soft tissue sarcomas remains inconsistent. This study aimed to perform an updated meta-analysis to comprehensively evaluate the effects of pretreatment CT-assessed low skeletal muscle mass and treatment-related skeletal muscle mass loss on clinical outcomes in patients with bone and soft tissue sarcomas. Methods A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library to identify studies investigating the associations between baseline low skeletal muscle mass, treatment-related muscle mass loss, and clinical outcomes in patients with bone and soft tissue sarcomas. The outcomes were overall survival (OS), disease-related survival outcomes and postoperative complications (PC). The quality of included studies was assessed using the Quality In Prognostic Studies (QUIPS) tool. This meta-analysis was registered in PROSPERO (CRD42025640369) and conducted in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines. Results Eighteen studies involving 1,684 patients were included. The results showed that low skeletal muscle mass was significantly associated with inferior OS, with a pooled hazard ratio of 1.72 [95% confidence interval (CI) 1.38-2.13; I 2 = 31.3%; p < 0.001] in the mixed model in 17 studies. In the analysis restricted to multivariable adjusted HRs, pretreatment low skeletal muscle mass was significantly associated with OS (HR = 2.54; 95%CI = 1.86-3.48; p < 0.001) in 7 studies. Pretreatment low skeletal muscle mass was significantly associated with an increased risk of PC [odds ratio (OR) = 1.41; 95%CI = 1.15-1.74; p = 0.001]. In addition, skeletal muscle mass loss significantly was associated with worse OS (HR = 1.61; 95%CI = 1.32-1.96; p < 0.001). Exploratory subgroup analyses showed that the prognostic factor was significantly associated with OS in patients receiving surgical resection (HR = 1.71; 95%CI = 1.33-2.22; p < 0.001) and other treatment (HR = 1.67; 95%CI = 1.09-2.56; p = 0.020). According to the QUIPS assessment, only two studies were at low overall risk of bias, whereas eight were at moderate risk and eight at high risk. GRADE profiling rated the overall certainty of evidence for OS as low, limited by serious risk of bias, inconsistency, and imprecision, but partially offset by large effect sizes and a dose-response gradient. Conclusion Both pretreatment CT-assessed low skeletal muscle mass and muscle mass loss are significantly associated with adverse prognosis in adult patients with bone and soft tissue sarcomas. Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42025640369, CRD42025640369.

title: Ultrasound-based radiomics for phyllodes tumor diagnosis: A comprehensive single-center study with extensive patient cohort.
abstract: Background Accurate differentiation of phyllodes tumor (PT) from breast cancer (BC) and fibroadenoma (FA) is crucial for appropriate clinical management; however, this remains challenging owing to overlapping imaging features. This study aimed to evaluate the potential of ultrasound-based radiomics analysis to distinguish PT from BC and FA. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on the ultrasound images of 651 patients, including 251 with PT, 200 with BC, and 200 with FA. Radiomics features were extracted from the ultrasound images, and machine learning models were developed to differentiate PT from BC and FA. The dataset was divided into training and validation sets, and feature selection was performed using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) algorithms. The performance of the model was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, with the area under the curve (AUC) as the primary metric. Results The radiomics models demonstrated significant discriminative power. For PT vs BC differentiation, Logistic Regression achieved the highest validation performance (AUC = 0.917, accuracy = 86.3%), with shape-based features showing highest importance. For PT vs FA differentiation, seven models achieved excellent performance with AUCs >0.90, led by Multilayer Perceptron (AUC = 0.964, accuracy = 93.2%). Texture-based features were most discriminative for PT vs FA differentiation. Conclusion In this single-center internal-validation study, ultrasound-based radiomics differentiated PT from BC and FA, particularly excelling in PT vs FA differentiation, and may represent a promising adjunctive diagnostic tool that warrants external, multi-center validation.

title: Case Report: Giant vulvar aggressive angiomyxoma in a postmenopausal woman with a decade-long history.
abstract: Background Aggressive angiomyxoma (AAM) is a rare, locally infiltrative mesenchymal tumor that typically arises in the pelvic-perineal region of reproductive-aged women. Its occurrence in postmenopausal women is uncommon and may present diagnostic challenges due to its indolent nature. Case presentation We report a case of a 63-year-old postmenopausal woman with a 10-year history of a gradually enlarging, asymptomatic right vulvar mass. Pelvic Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) revealed a well-circumscribed, lobulated mass. Surgical excision was performed, and the gross specimen measured 15 × 8 × 6 cm. Histopathology confirmed the diagnosis of AAM, with an immunohistochemical profile showing Estrogen Receptor (ER) (+), Progesterone Receptor (PR) (-), and a Ki-67 proliferation index of approximately 10% in hotspot areas. All surgical margins were negative. Conclusion This case demonstrates that AAM can grow insidiously over many years in postmenopausal women, presenting as a large, asymptomatic mass. The atypical features, including a decade-long indolent history, PR negativity and a relatively elevated Ki-67 index, highlight the biological variability of AAM. However, the prognostic significance of these findings remains uncertain and requires further investigation. A high index of suspicion is necessary for vulvar masses with prolonged histories, even after menopause. As a single case report, this report has limited representativeness.

title: CT-based clinical deep learning radiomics nomogram for preoperative differentiation of pyelocaliceal upper tract urothelial carcinoma and xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis.
abstract: Objective This study sought to create a CT-based clinical deep learning radiomics (CDLR) model to noninvasively differentiate between pyelocaliceal upper tract urothelial carcinoma (UTUC) and xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (XGP) preoperatively, aiding in personalized treatment decisions. Methods A retrospective analysis included 161 patients with pathologically confirmed pyelocaliceal UTUC or XGP following surgery. Patients were randomly divided into a training cohort (n=112) and a validation cohort (n=49). Radiomics (Rad) features and deep learning (DL) features were extracted from the corticomedullary phase CT images. Combined with clinical features, and after feature selection, a logistic regression (LR) classifier was employed to construct the clinical model, the deep learning radiomics (DLR) model, and the clinical deep learning radiomics (CDLR) model. Model performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and decision curve analysis (DCA), with interpretability assessed by the shapley additive explanations (SHAP) method. In addition, the diagnostic performance of the models was compared with that of a radiologist with 5 years of experience in abdominal CT diagnosis. Results The CDLR model achieved AUCs of 0.955 in the training cohort and 0.930 in the validation cohort. In the validation cohort, the CDLR model significantly outperformed the radiologist's assessment (AUC: 0.930 vs. 0.695, P = 0.0006) and yielded numerically higher AUCs than the clinical model (0.823) and the DLR model (0.882). DCA indicated that the CDLR model provided the highest net clinical benefit. SHAP analysis demonstrated good model interpretability. Conclusion The CDLR model integrating clinical, Rad, and DL features serves as an effective noninvasive tool for preoperative differentiation of pyelocaliceal UTUC and XGP, offering valuable reference for clinical decision-making.

title: Artificial intelligence and triple negative breast cancer: can pathomics help oncologists?
abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive and heterogeneous subtype of breast cancer with limited targeted therapies and poor prognosis. Recent advances in digital pathology and artificial intelligence (AI) are transforming traditional, qualitative histopathology into quantitative, data-driven analysis. Within computational pathology, pathomics (the extraction of handcrafted, high-dimensional features from digitized histological images) and deep learning (DL)-based whole-slide image analysis have been investigated for the prediction of molecular subtypes, biomarker expression, tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, and treatment response in TNBC. AI models, including DL and multimodal systems integrating histopathology, omics, and clinical data, are being explored for patient stratification, risk assessment, and therapy personalization, encompassing chemotherapy, immunotherapy, PARP inhibitors, and antibody-drug conjugates. By linking spatial tissue architecture with molecular profiles, these approaches may provide new insights into tumor biology and the tumor microenvironment. Most TNBC-specific studies are retrospective, small or single-center, few have been externally validated and, to our knowledge, none has yet demonstrated clinical utility in prospective trials; prediction of biomarkers such as PD-L1 or homologous recombination deficiency from hematoxylin and eosin slides remains investigational and cannot replace validated testing. Despite these challenges, AI-assisted computational pathology is a promising decision-support tool, which complements and does not replace pathologists and oncologists, for enhancing diagnosis, prognosis, and therapeutic decision-making in TNBC.

title: Prospective comparison of CT- and MRI-based tumor delineation based on intraoperative navigation and spatially annotated pathology in locally advanced midfacial squamous cell carcinoma.
abstract: Introduction Precise tumor delineation is critical for navigation-guided surgery and radiotherapy (RT) in locally advanced midfacial squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are both recommended for staging and provide complementary information. However, quantitative comparisons of CT- and MRI-based tumor contours remain scarce, while a spatial comparison with histopathological data has never been performed. Therefore, we prospectively compared gross tumor volumes (GTV) derived from CT and MRI before navigation-guided surgery and correlated the results with spatially annotated pathology. Methods This imaging sub-analysis was conducted within the prospective NAVIGATORR trial (NCT05671458). Fifteen patients with locally advanced midfacial SCC underwent contrast-enhanced CT and 1.5T or 3T MRI (T1w, T2w, DWI) for navigation-based surgery planning. Datasets were rigidly co-registered and an experienced radiologist independently contoured the GTV on CT and MRI while blinded to the other modality. Besides qualitative and volumetric evaluation, spatial agreement was assessed using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) and Hausdorff distance (HD). Tumor contours were correlated with spatially annotated intraoperative biopsy locations and histopathological results. Results Fifteen patients and 109 spatially annotated biopsy locations (19 tumor-positive) were analyzed. MRI was preferred for tumor delineation by the radiologist in all cases, with superior differentiation between tumor and mucosal swelling (73%) and improved soft tissue contrast (67%). MRI based GTVs were significantly larger than CT-based GTVs (median 28.3 ml vs. 16.8 ml; p = 0.02). DSC values demonstrated fair agreement with considerable heterogeneity (median 0.58; IQR 0.47-0.65), and median HD was 16 mm (IQR 12-27 mm). MRI-based contours encompassed numerically more tumor-positive biopsy locations than CT-based contours (6/19 vs. 1/19; clustered McNemar p = 0.20) while including fewer tumor-negative locations (7/90 vs. 10/90; p = 0.53). At patient level, at least one tumor-positive biopsy was located inside the contour in 3/8 (MRI) vs. 1/8 (CT) patients. Discussion GTV delineation differs substantially between MRI and CT in locally advanced midfacial SCC, and the two modalities provide complementary information. These exploratory findings support the complementary use of MRI and CT for tumor visualization. Clinical implications remain to be shown by the primary endpoint analysis of the NAVIGATORR trial.

title: Optical coherence tomography for surgical margin assessment of soft-tissue sarcomas of the extremities and trunk.
abstract: Introduction Incomplete resection of superficial trunk and extremity soft-tissue sarcomas can impact the risk of local recurrence and overall prognosis for patients after surgical resection. Multiple methods have been described for intraoperative surgical margin assessment of soft-tissue sarcomas, including optical coherence tomography (OCT) evaluation of surgical margins. The accuracy of OCT imaging for evaluating the surgical margins of soft-tissue sarcoma has not been reported. The first aim of this study was to determine the OCT imaging features of different tissue types at the surgical margins when compared to histopathology to allow for image interpretation training for observers. The second aim was to determine the diagnostic accuracy of OCT for identification of incomplete margin status for soft-tissue sarcomas of the superficial trunk or extremities. Methods The surgical margins of 20 soft-tissue sarcoma specimens were imaged using OCT following surgical resection. The OCT images from the first five tumors were used to identify features of different tissue types compared to histopathology and create a training presentation. The OCT images from all tumors were then used to create a training set and test set. Seven observers underwent a training session using a training presentation and interpreted a training and test set. Images were graded on a numeric scale from 1 (no tumor present) to 4 (tumor present). The results of the test set were used to evaluate the sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and inter- and intraobserver variability. Results The overall sensitivity and specificity for detection of tumor on the surgical margin were 83.5% [95% confidence interval (CI): 74.6% -89.7%] and 76.8% (95% CI: 68.2% -83.6%), respectively. The overall correct classification rate of the surgical margin was 162/203 (79.8%; 95% CI: 73.8% -84.7%). Discussion Further research is needed in an intraoperative setting with a larger patient population to evaluate the use of OCT to evaluate the surgical margins for soft-tissue sarcomas.

title: Dosimetry-guided morphomic modeling using daily FBCT for automated all-in-one radiotherapy eligibility assessment in postoperative cervical cancer.
abstract: Objective This study aimed to develop an automated decision-making model based on daily fan-beam CT (FBCT) morphomic features to determine whether a treatment fraction is suitable for AIO-RT initiation. Methods A total of 48 postoperative cervical cancer patients with 313 FBCT fractions were retrospectively analyzed. Morphomic features were extracted from bladder, rectum, intrarectal gas, bilateral femoral head, and inter-organ spatial relationships. Feature selection was performed using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO), and predictive models were built using Random Forest (RF) and Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM) under leave-one-patient-out cross-validation. Results Both models achieved consistent discriminative performance (AUC = 0.958 for RF and 0.952 for GBM). Bladder-related morphological features were the dominant predictors, particularly bladder volume and shape-derived descriptors. Spatial features also contributed to classification performance, while rectal gas showed limited but complementary predictive value. Conclusion The proposed FBCT-based morphomic framework can accurately identify unsuitable fractions for AIO-RT before workflow initiation, providing a practical and interpretable decision-support tool for adaptive radiotherapy workflow optimization.

title: Breast cancer metastasis to the thyroid gland: case report.
abstract: Background Distant metastasis is common in highly malignant tumors. However, metastasis to the thyroid gland from extrathyroidal malignancies is extremely rare. Among primary tumors metastasizing to the thyroid, renal cell carcinoma, lung cancer, and head and neck cancer are most frequently reported. Breast cancer, despite its high prevalence, accounts for a disproportionately small fraction of thyroid metastases. Here we present the clinical course of a patient with a history of invasive ductal carcinoma(IDC) who was subsequently found to have thyroid metastasis. Case presentation A 53-year-old female patient had a history of IDC of the breast 10 years ago. She underwent total thyroidectomy due to thyroid nodules with high suspicion of malignancy on PET-CT. Postoperative pathology combined with immunohistochemistry (IHC) confirmed metastasis of breast cancer to the thyroid. Despite receiving endocrine therapy and chemotherapy after surgery, the disease continued to progress, resulting in a poor prognosis. Conclusion Metastases to the thyroid and supraclavicular lymph nodes developing in a patient more than a decade after breast cancer diagnosis present a major diagnostic challenge. A combination of IHC and comprehensive imaging is essential for accurate diagnosis. Understanding the underlying metastatic mechanisms may aid in optimizing surveillance and treatment strategies.

Metastases to the thyroid and supraclavicular lymph nodes developing in a patient more than a decade after breast cancer diagnosis present a major diagnostic challenge. A combination of IHC and comprehensive imaging is essential for accurate diagnosis. Understanding the underlying metastatic mechanisms may aid in optimizing surveillance and treatment strategies.

title: Salivary glands auto-segmentation in head and neck radiotherapy: imaging modalities, models, and clinical relevance.
abstract: Radiotherapy-induced salivary gland injury is a major contributor to xerostomia and impaired quality of life in patients with head and neck cancer, making accurate organ-at-risk delineation clinically important. Deep learning-based auto-segmentation has the potential to improve contouring efficiency and consistency, but reported performance is heterogeneous and its clinical significance is not always clear. This narrative review summarizes current evidence on salivary gland auto-segmentation across computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and prostate-specific membrane antigen positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PSMA PET-CT), with particular emphasis on gland-specific challenges, performance evaluation, and clinical translation. CT has the largest evidence base and remains most relevant to routine radiotherapy planning, whereas MRI provides improved soft-tissue visualization and PSMA PET-CT offers high functional contrast for selected salivary structures. Across modalities, segmentation performance is generally more challenging for smaller structures, particularly the sublingual and tubarial gland regions. Importantly, geometric metrics such as the Dice similarity coefficient do not alone establish clinical acceptability or dosimetric equivalence; evaluation should also consider boundary accuracy, expert correction burden, clinical acceptability, and dosimetric impact. Current evidence is further limited by heterogeneous study designs and reference standards, scarce external validation, and limited evidence linking auto-segmentation directly to treatment-related toxicity or patient outcomes. Future research should prioritize multi-institutional validation, clinically meaningful evaluation, improved segmentation of small glands, and human-in-the-loop integration into adaptive radiotherapy. Overall, auto-segmentation represents a promising tool for salivary gland delineation, but its clinical implementation should be supported by evidence extending beyond geometric accuracy alone.
