title: Uncertainty and Geometric Image-Region Ranking in Artificial Intelligence-Based Panoramic Tooth Segmentation: A Multi-Source External Benchmark.
abstract: Background/Objectives: This retrospective benchmark evaluated scores for selecting regions of panoramic tooth segmentations for review. Methods: Three-member U-Net ensembles trained on UFBA-425 were evaluated on 590 held-out images and subsequently on 329 photographed radiographs. The original mixed-granularity pipeline comparison used the calibrated residual ensemble on 100 pediatric images. Cells in a 2 × 4 grid received regional mutual information (MI) scores but shared one whole-image soft Dice confidence (SDC) value. A lower Dice-risk area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC) indicated better ranking against source masks. Interaction tests, quality subset analyses, and prediction-positive sensitivity analyses were post hoc. Image-key bootstrap intervals may be too narrow for patient-level inference because patient independence was unverified. Results: The primary MI-minus-SDC AURC difference was +0.007 (95% confidence interval -0.033 to +0.041), leaving the comparison inconclusive. Subsequent evaluations were exploratory. Analyses of reference-positive cells (containing reference tooth pixels) received co-principal emphasis after outcomes were known. MI had a higher Dice-risk AURC than the replicated SDC in the pediatric main subset (+0.238) and the local SDC in AKUDENTAL (+0.157 residual, +0.134 ResNet18). When 20% of grid cells were reviewed, the mean maximum pixel probability (MSP) captured more error pixels than MI in seven of ten source/model comparisons, including both AKUDENTAL ensembles. On photographed radiographs, the MSP led by 15.73 percentage points for the residual ensemble and MI by 3.66 for ResNet18. For ResNet18, equal weighting of false-positive and false-negative capture favored MSP by 6.59 points. Conclusions: The primary comparison established neither superiority nor equivalence. Exploratory capture varied by source, model, and error mix.

title: The Impact of MTHFR Gene Polymorphisms on Cerebral Small and Large Vessel Disease, Vascular Cognitive Impairment and Cerebral Volumetric Reduction.
abstract: Objective : The study aims to evaluate the association of methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) C677T and A1298C polymorphisms with cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD), cerebral large vessel disease (CLVD), vascular cognitive impairment (VCI) and global and regional brain volumes. Methods : Clinical, laboratory, neuroimaging, volumetric, cognitive and MTHFR genotyping data were retrospectively collected from 62 patients with CSVD ( n = 40) or CLVD ( n = 22), all carriers of at least one MTHFR variant. Brain volumes were compared between patients with VCI carrying C677T ( n = 30) and patients without VCI ( n = 32). Analyses were repeated in the open-source platform jamovi and p -values were corrected for multiple comparisons with the Holm procedure. Results : The cohort comprised 41 women and 21 men (mean age 56.9 years). The CT and TT genotypes of C677T, the AC and CC genotypes of A1298C, blood pressure, total cholesterol and triglycerides differed between CSVD and CLVD at the unadjusted level ( p < 0.05), but none of these differences remained significant after Holm correction. VCI carriers of C677T showed lower white matter (332.9 ± 25.5 vs. 437.9 ± 35.7 cm 3 ) and gray matter volumes (626.0 ± 45.7 vs. 699.7 ± 51.5 cm 3 ), higher cerebrospinal fluid volume (238.3 ± 42.2 vs. 197.1 ± 24.8 cm 3 ) and reduced hippocampal, amygdalar, thalamic, superior frontal, middle temporal, entorhinal, parahippocampal and middle occipital volumes (all Holm-adjusted p < 0.05). Conclusions : Differences in MTHFR genotype distribution between CSVD and CLVD were not robust to correction for multiple testing, whereas VCI carriers of C677T showed global and selective regional volume loss that withstood correction. MTHFR variants are susceptibility markers rather than direct causes of vascular injury; these associations, which could not be adjusted for comorbid vascular risk factors or for concomitant neurodegenerative pathology, require confirmation in prospective, controlled studies with homocysteine measurements.

title: Imaging the Vascular Component of Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma: From Pathophysiology to Novel Hemodynamic Biomarkers.
abstract: Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide. Intraocular pressure (IOP) is its only validated therapeutic target, yet some patients progress despite controlled IOP, sustaining interest in a vascular contribution. This narrative review summarizes the anatomy and autoregulation of the optic nerve head circulation, the evidence linking low ocular perfusion pressure, impaired autoregulation and endothelial dysfunction to POAG, and the imaging modalities used to assess ocular hemodynamics. Color Doppler imaging consistently shows reduced retrobulbar flow velocities, particularly end-diastolic, and increased resistive indices, whereas OCT angiography shows reduced peripapillary and macular vessel density correlated with structural and functional damage. However, most evidence is cross-sectional and associative, and cannot establish whether hypoperfusion causes or follows retinal ganglion cell loss. No hemodynamic biomarker has been validated for clinical decision-making, and evidence of prognostic value beyond conventional structural and functional assessment remains inconsistent. Laser Doppler holography, a contactless technique providing pulsatile retinal blood flow waveforms, is presented as an emerging tool whose glaucoma-specific evidence is currently limited to a pilot study of four eyes. Vascular biomarkers therefore remain research tools pending standardized acquisition, normative databases and longitudinal validation.

title: Dual-Timepoint <sup>18</sup>F-FDG PET/CT Radiomics for Treatment Response in Breast Cancer: A Two-Center External Validation Study.
abstract: Background: This study investigated the incremental value of radiomic features derived from 18 F-FDG PET/CT over clinicopathological characteristics and conventional PET parameters for predicting and assessing metabolic treatment response in breast cancer, using independent external validation. Materials and Methods: This retrospective, two-center study included 153 patients with metastatic or non-metastatic breast cancer representing different biological subtypes, all of whom underwent systemic treatment and paired pretreatment and post-treatment 18 F-FDG PET/CT. The development cohort comprised 115 patients, while 38 patients from a second institution formed the external validation cohort. The endpoint was complete metabolic response (CMR) of the primary breast tumor. Scenario A examined pretreatment prediction of CMR using baseline variables, whereas Scenario B assessed imaging-defined CMR using post-treatment and longitudinal PET/CT parameters. Models were developed using L1-regularized logistic regression with five-fold stratified cross-validation and evaluated in the external cohort without refitting. Results: Primary-tumor CMR was observed in 14 of 115 patients (12.2%) in the development cohort and 18 of 38 patients (47.4%) in the external cohort. In Scenario A, the multimodal model incorporating radiomics achieved an external validation AUC of 0.747 (95% CI, 0.577-0.887), compared with 0.636 for the model combining clinicopathological variables and conventional PET parameters (ΔAUC = 0.111). Compared with the clinical-only model (AUC = 0.658), the multimodal model improved discrimination by 0.089, although the difference was not statistically significant (DeLong p = 0.146). In Scenario B, conventional post-treatment PET parameters achieved an AUC of 0.986 (95% CI, 0.953-1.000). Adding radiomic features did not improve discrimination (AUC = 0.986). Conclusions: Pretreatment radiomics showed potential additional value for predicting primary-tumor CMR, although the improvement in discrimination was not statistically significant. After treatment, conventional PET parameters provided high discrimination for imaging-defined primary-tumor CMR, with no further improvement from radiomics. These findings require confirmation in larger, prospective cohorts before their clinical application.

In Scenario B, conventional post-treatment PET parameters achieved an AUC of 0.986 (95% CI, 0.953-1.000). Adding radiomic features did not improve discrimination (AUC = 0.986). Conclusions: Pretreatment radiomics showed potential additional value for predicting primary-tumor CMR, although the improvement in discrimination was not statistically significant. After treatment, conventional PET parameters provided high discrimination for imaging-defined primary-tumor CMR, with no further improvement from radiomics. These findings require confirmation in larger, prospective cohorts before their clinical application.

title: Prognostic Association of PET/CT-Defined Low Skeletal Muscle Mass in Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Treated with Second-Line or Later Nivolumab: A Single-Center Retrospective Study.
abstract: Background: Low skeletal muscle mass (LSMM) may be associated with outcomes in patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors. We evaluated CT-defined LSMM and survival in patients treated with second-line or later nivolumab. Methods: This single-center retrospective study included 62 patients with pretreatment 18F-FDG PET/CT. Skeletal muscle index (SMI) was measured at L3, and LSMM was defined as SMI <34.4 cm 2 /m 2 in women and <45.4 cm 2 /m 2 in men. Overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were assessed using Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression analyses. Results: LSMM was present in 32 patients (51.6%). Age ≥65 years (OR = 3.57, 95% CI 1.19-10.75; p = 0.021) and BMI <25 kg/m 2 (OR = 5.67, 95% CI 1.73-18.53; p = 0.003) were associated with LSMM. Median OS was 14.23 versus 22.28 months (log-rank p = 0.049), and median PFS was 6.64 versus 14.42 months ( p = 0.058), for LSMM versus no LSMM. Adjusted HRs for LSMM were 2.08 (95% CI 0.97-4.48; p = 0.062) for OS and 1.87 (95% CI 0.93-3.77; p = 0.078) for PFS. Martin and Prado SMI definitions did not reproduce these survival associations. Continuous SMI was also not associated with OS or PFS in adjusted analyses. Conclusions: The primary binary LSMM definition showed an unfavorable survival pattern, but this was not robust across alternative thresholds or continuous SMI and did not establish an independent prognostic association.

title: Spontaneous Relative T1 Hyperintensity of Vertebral Metastases from Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma: A Retrospective Diagnostic Accuracy Study Using the Spinal Cord as an Internal Standard.
abstract: Background/Objective: To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of spontaneous T1 hyperintensity relative to the spinal cord (signal intensity ratio [SIR] > 1) for identifying vertebral metastases from clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) among vertebral metastases of other origins, and to assess the spinal cord as an internal reference standard, as an alternative to the conventional comparison with paravertebral muscle or the intervertebral disc. Methods: This retrospective, single-centre, case-control diagnostic accuracy study was conducted at University Hospital of Messina, Italy, between January 2017 and December 2023. Patients with vertebral metastases who underwent spine MRI for radiotherapy planning were included: 11 consecutive patients with biopsy-proven ccRCC (14 lesions) and 28 patients with metastases from other solid tumours (41 lesions; convenience sample). The index test was the lesion-to-spinal-cord SIR measured on unenhanced sagittal T1-weighted fast spin-echo images acquired at 1.5 T. Two blinded neuroradiologists independently performed the measurements; lesions were classified as hyperintense relative to the spinal cord using the prespecified threshold of SIR > 1. The flow-void sign was assessed as a secondary finding. Diagnostic accuracy was calculated on a per-lesion basis with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results: At the SIR > 1 threshold, both readers correctly classified 13/14 ccRCC metastases and 38/41 control metastases (13 true positives, 3 false positives, 1 false negative, and 38 true negatives). Sensitivity was 92.9% (95% CI, 68.5-98.7%), specificity was 92.7% (95% CI, 80.6-97.5%), and accuracy was 92.7%. The positive and negative likelihood ratios were 12.7 (95% CI, 4.2-38.1) and 0.077 (95% CI, 0.011-0.51), respectively. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.960 (95% CI, 0.886-1.000) for reader 1 and 0.953 (95% CI, 0.873-1.000) for reader 2. Categorical inter-reader agreement was perfect (55/55, 100%; Cohen's kappa = 1.00). Continuous SIR measurements showed a concordance correlation coefficient of 0.896, a mean inter-reader difference of 0.003 SIR units, and no systematic bias ( p > 0.9). The flow-void sign was present in 7/14 ccRCC lesions; it was not assessed in the control group. The three false-positive lesions originated from thyroid, breast, and lung cancers. Conclusions: In this preliminary series, T1 hyperintensity relative to the spinal cord was frequent in ccRCC vertebral metastases and uncommon in metastases from other tumours. Owing to the case-control design, non-consecutive controls, and small sample size, diagnostic accuracy may have been overestimated; validation in prospective, consecutive, multicentre cohorts is required.

title: Prevalence of Radiographic Errors and Assessment of Diagnostic Image Quality in Panoramic Radiographs: A Retrospective Study.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Panoramic radiography is an important imaging modality for the evaluation of dentoalveolar and maxillofacial structures in dental diagnosis and treatment planning. The diagnostic quality of panoramic images is closely related to appropriate patient preparation and accurate positioning. Positioning errors may adversely affect image quality, leading to misinterpretation and unnecessary repeat examinations. This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic quality of panoramic radiographs, determine the frequency of common positioning errors, and identify error types contributing to diagnostically inadequate images. Methods: In this retrospective cross-sectional study, a total of 5155 panoramic radiographs obtained at Mardin Oral and Dental Health Center were evaluated. Patients were divided into four age groups: ≤20, 21-40, 41-60, and ≥61 years. The assessed errors included failure to position the tongue against the palate, slumped patient position, positioning the patient too far forward or backward, failure to bite on the bite block, patient movement, forward or backward head tilt, head rotation to one side, foreign bodies, exposure errors, lip positioning errors, and missing image sections. Radiographic quality was classified as "excellent," "diagnostically acceptable," or "unacceptable." The distribution of error types according to age and sex was evaluated using the chi-square test, with p < 0.05 considered statistically significant. Results: At least one error was detected in 40.1% of the panoramic radiographs. The most frequent errors were failure to position the tongue against the palate (10.3%) and head rotation to one side (9.7%). Of the radiographs, 3.6% were classified as excellent, 95.7% as diagnostically acceptable, and 0.6% as unacceptable. The overall error rate was highest in the ≥61-year age group (53.8%) and lowest in the ≤20 year age group (31%), with a significant increase with age ( p < 0.05). No significant association was found between sex and overall error frequency ( p > 0.05), although significant sex-related differences were observed for some specific error types. Conclusions: Patient preparation and positioning errors may affect the diagnostic quality of panoramic radiographs. Accurate positioning, effective patient communication, and consideration of age-specific error patterns may contribute to improving image quality.

title: Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance for Lifelong Surveillance in Congenital Heart Disease: From Childhood to Adulthood.
abstract: Advances in paediatric cardiology, surgery and catheter intervention have enabled most children with congenital heart disease (CHD) to reach adulthood, yet transfer to adult congenital heart disease (ACHD) care remains a period at risk of discontinuity and of delayed recognition of residual lesions, ventricular dysfunction, arrhythmias and aortopathy. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) provides radiation-free, reproducible assessment of anatomy, ventricular volumes and function, flow, shunts and myocardial tissue. This narrative review examines CMR as a tool for continuous longitudinal surveillance from childhood into adult life. Its role is not to replace echocardiography but to answer questions that echocardiography cannot resolve reliably and to provide serially comparable measurements, particularly after tetralogy of Fallot repair, in systemic right ventricles, in Fontan circulation and in coarctation of the aorta. We describe lesion-specific protocols, standardised phase-contrast acquisition and ventricular contouring that permit valid serial comparison, and the clinical, electrocardiographic, biochemical (NT-proBNP) and echocardiographic triggers that prompt earlier CMR or allow it to be deferred. CMR timing should therefore follow the lesion and the patient's trajectory rather than chronological age, with transfer regarded as one point on a continuous surveillance pathway. Limitations include examination duration, arrhythmia, device artefacts, contrast considerations and limited access to congenital imaging expertise.

title: OBESUS (OBESity UltraSound): A Multiorgan Bedside Ultrasound Framework for Obesity Phenotyping.
abstract: Obesity is a heterogeneous chronic disease in which cardiometabolic and functional risks are influenced not only by total body fat but also by adipose tissue distribution, ectopic lipid accumulation in non-adipose tissues, and alterations in skeletal muscle composition. Traditional anthropometric measurements, such as body mass index and waist circumference, fail to capture these biological differences. Point-of-care ultrasound provides a portable, radiation-free, repeatable, and widely available bedside tool for assessing multiple adipose and muscular compartments, yet a broadly standardized framework integrating these measurements into a multiorgan obesity phenotype remains lacking. We propose OBESUS (OBESity UltraSound), a pragmatic multiorgan point-of-care ultrasound framework for structured obesity phenotyping. To facilitate competency-based and stepwise implementation, OBESUS comprises two complementary tiers: OBESUS-Core evaluates abdominal subcutaneous adiposity, preperitoneal fat thickness, hepatic steatosis, and rectus femoris muscle echogenicity, whereas OBESUS-Plus incorporates epicardial and perirenal adipose tissue as additional regional adipose tissue depots of cardiorenal relevance. Rather than generating a numerical score, the framework integrates these findings into four non-mutually exclusive ultrasound-derived phenotypes: metabolic, increased muscle echogenicity, epicardial adiposity, and perirenal adiposity. This narrative review describes the conceptual basis, standardized acquisition methodology, pragmatic reference thresholds, and potential clinical applications of OBESUS. The framework is intended to provide a foundation for prospective evaluation of its reproducibility, clinical validity, prognostic significance and potential utility for longitudinal monitoring.

title: Visual Acuity Relative to Central Subfield Thickness and Its Association with Optical Coherence Tomography Structural Biomarkers in Diabetic Macular Edema: A Cross-Sectional Study.
abstract: Background/Objectives : Central subfield thickness (CST) correlates only modestly with visual acuity in diabetic macular edema (DME). We described an exploratory CST-normalized index of visual loss (CIVL) and evaluated the association of optical coherence tomography (OCT) structural biomarkers with visual acuity after accounting for CST. Methods : This retrospective cross-sectional study included 243 eyes of 243 patients with type 2 diabetes (150 without macular edema, 93 with DME; one eye per patient, randomly selected in the DME group). Best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA, logMAR), CST, disorganization of the retinal inner layers (DRIL), ellipsoid zone (EZ) disruption, intraretinal fluid (IRF), subretinal fluid (SRF) and epiretinal membrane (ERM) were assessed on spectral-domain OCT. CIVL was calculated as (logMAR × 300)/CST. Within the DME group, a base regression model of BCVA including CST, age and sex was compared with a model additionally including the five biomarkers. Results : Median CIVL was 0.00 (interquartile range 0.00-0.00) in non-edematous eyes and 0.40 (0.26-0.59) in DME eyes ( p < 0.001). Within the DME group, EZ disruption (β = 0.195; 95% CI 0.105-0.285), SRF (β = 0.287; 95% CI 0.152-0.422) and IRF (β = 0.120; 95% CI 0.031-0.210) were associated with worse BCVA independently of CST, age and sex, whereas DRIL was not ( p = 0.285); the association with ERM (β = 0.105; p = 0.020) was not robust in sensitivity analyses. Adding the biomarkers increased the explained variance in BCVA from 36.9% to 66.8% (ΔR 2 = 0.299; p < 0.001; optimism-corrected R 2 = 0.599). Conclusions : In DME, EZ disruption and intraretinal and subretinal fluid were associated with worse visual acuity at a given CST. CIVL is an exploratory descriptive index whose clinical and prognostic value requires longitudinal validation.

title: More than a Second Pair of Eyes: Artificial Intelligence Across the Breast Imaging Pathway.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from stand-alone accuracy studies to prospective deployment across breast screening, risk prediction, multimodal diagnosis, treatment response, and workflow support. The goal of this narrative review is to determine which AI applications have demonstrated clinical benefit, which remain technically promising, and what safeguards are required for implementation. We synthesize randomized trials, prospective cohorts, real-world implementations, external validations, systematic reviews, and guidance identified in PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus through 30 June 2026. In screening, AI-supported mammography can increase cancer detection and reduce reading workload, but effects depend on whether AI is used as concurrent support, an independent reader, triage, or partial autonomy; autonomous workflows may shift work and cost downstream through additional recalls. MASAI met its prespecified noninferiority criterion for interval cancer, but this should not be interpreted as proof of equivalence or mortality benefit. Image-based risk models often discriminate better than density or conventional clinical models, although prospective benefit from AI-guided allocation to supplemental imaging has not yet been demonstrated. Evidence for contrast-enhanced mammography (CEM), MRI, ultrasound, radiomics, and multimodal models is less mature and limited by external validation, domain shift, missing data, operator dependence, and uncertain incremental value beyond clinicopathological factors. Ungrounded large language models and opaque foundation models are not suitable for autonomous clinical advice. Current evidence therefore supports controlled, task-specific integration rather than radiologist replacement; real clinical benefit depends on governance of the whole AI-enabled pathway, including local validation, human factors, downstream resource use, statistical stopping rules, and fallback procedures.

title: Artificial Intelligence Techniques in Endodontics for Dental Students: Development and Preliminary Technical Assessment of an ERFNet-Based Panoramic Radiograph Interpretation Prototype.
abstract: Background/Objectives : Automated interpretation of panoramic radiographs could provide visual support during dental training, but technical feasibility should not be confused with proven diagnostic accuracy or educational benefit. This study describes the development and preliminary technical assessment of sTUDent Dental Assistant, an educational software prototype. Materials and Methods : The original artificial neural network software was developed and tested using a computer equipped with an AMD Ryzen 7 5800H 3.20Ghz processor (Advanced Micro Devices, California, USA) and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3070 graphics processing unit (NVIDIA Corporation, California, USA). The system was implemented in Python version 3.11, and no additional hardware accelerators were employed. A collection of 1480 panoramic radiographs was screened, and 1000 were retained for annotation after 480 exclusions. Images were acquired with a KAVO OP 3DPRO system, converted from DICOM to 8-bit images, normalized and cropped. The prototype uses an ERFNet for semantic segmentation, followed by morphological and region-based post-processing. Eleven dental categories were specified. Results : The application produces color-coded localization overlays and PDF reports. A supplied class-wise count table permits descriptive calculation of precision, recall and F1. Conclusions : This work demonstrates an implemented educational-oriented image-analysis workflow, not clinically validated pathology detection or demonstrated educational effectiveness. Reproducible independent evaluation and student-based assessment remain necessary in future.

title: Explainable AI for Acute Ischemic Stroke Neuroimaging: A Critical Review of SHAP and Grad-CAM Applications and Their Methodological Limitations.
abstract: In the triage of acute ischemic stroke (AIS), rapid non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT), computed tomography angiography (CTA), and diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (DWI) guide intravenous thrombolysis and endovascular thrombectomy (EVT). Machine learning and deep learning models have reported high discrimination for ischemic lesion detection, malignant cerebral edema (MCE), and 90-day modified Rankin Scale (mRS) outcomes. However, opaque model architectures hinder clinical interpretation. Materials and Scope: This critical review is based on a structured PubMed/MEDLINE query (1 January 2021 to 15 August 2026). Among 34 candidate records, two were excluded during initial screening, and two were unretrievable, yielding 30 fully appraised primary prediction studies (24 acute-AIS core studies and six adjacent neurovascular models). Eight acute-AIS studies were prioritized for detailed main-text comparison, while the remaining 22 studies were comprehensively retained in supplementary synthesis. All 30 available models underwent dual evaluation: prediction-model risk of bias via PROBAST+AI and an independent eight-dimension XAI validity appraisal. Overall risk of bias was High in 93.3% (28/30; driven primarily by Domain 4, analysis) and Unclear in 6.7% (2/30; Li et al. and Huang H. et al.); no study was rated Low. Multicollinearity and Attribution Sensitivity: In radiomic and hemodynamic modeling, strong dependence among interdependent imaging predictors (e.g., ASPECTS, core infarct volume, Tmax > 6 s hypoperfusion volume, and white matter hyperintensities) complicates feature-level SHAP interpretation. Interventional or other marginal-reference formulations can break the dependence between observed and integrated-out features and may evaluate combinations that are poorly supported by the empirical joint distribution. Consequently, individual-feature attributions may be sensitive to the explainer formulation and background/reference distribution and should not be interpreted as unique biological or causal effects. Coarse Saliency and Modality Bias: Grad-CAM generates spatially coarse attribution maps due to convolutional downsampling, making it susceptible to skull-base CT beam-hardening artifacts and MRI susceptibility artifacts. Furthermore, unimodal Grad-CAM architectures inherently fail to contextualize non-imaging clinical covariates (e.g., baseline NIHSS, onset-to-door time). Validation-stage Discrimination and Calibration: Across multicenter studies, cross-cohort discrimination is heterogeneous rather than uniformly attenuated. Cao et al. showed marked internal-to-external attenuation (AUC 0.918 to 0.755), whereas Huang L. et al. (0.78 to 0.88) and Li et al. (0.84 to 0.86) showed preserved or improved external discrimination. Training/development, internal validation, and independent external-validation stages must be distinguished. Calibration and uncertainty quantification (UQ) require separate evaluation; explanation maps alone do not establish reliable clinical probabilities. XAI must transition from descriptive post hoc visualizations into validated clinical decision support. Safe translation requires explicit reporting and sensitivity analysis of feature-dependence handling, quantitative saliency validation (e.g., lesion-mask intersection-over-union [IoU] or Pointing Game hit rates against expert anatomical segmentations, alongside deletion/insertion fidelity curves), multi-vendor image harmonization, and uncertainty quantification. Grouped or hierarchical attribution may be considered when appropriate to the intended explanatory target.

title: Improved U-Net for Automated Segmentation of Lung Ultrasound Findings and Assistance with Lesion Assessment in Children with Community-Acquired Pneumonia.
abstract: Objectives : To evaluate an improved U-Net for automatic segmentation of lung ultrasound (LUS) findings in pediatric community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) and its effect on sonographers' contouring performance and efficiency. Methods : This prospective study included 1994 images from 441 children: 1019 with consolidation, 767 with B-lines, and 208 with pleural effusion. The patient-level development and internal held-out set comprised 353 children (1575 images) and 88 children (419 images), respectively. The model used a ResNet34 encoder, dense atrous convolution, residual multi-kernel pooling, and weighted binary cross-entropy losses for multiscale segmentation deep supervision. We evaluated six model configurations by five-fold cross-validation and on an internal held-out test set. The complete model was also compared with sonographers, and two less-experienced readers repeated contouring with model assistance. Image-level paired differences were analyzed using 50,000 patient-cluster bootstrap replicates and within-family Holm adjustment. Results : Development-set Dice similarity coefficients (DSCs) for consolidation, B-lines, and pleural effusion were 0.8411 ± 0.0107, 0.7698 ± 0.0142, and 0.7730 ± 0.0187, respectively; internal held-out set DSCs were 0.8159 ± 0.0134, 0.7467 ± 0.0178, and 0.7498 ± 0.0234. The improved model had higher DSC, intersection over union, and boundary F1 scores and lower 95th-percentile Hausdorff distances than baseline U-Net for all three findings. It exceeded both less-experienced sonographers but remained below senior sonographers. With assistance, both less-experienced readers improved DSC across all findings and exceeded the standalone model in DSC, and reduced mean per-image processing time by 38.3% and 35.8%, respectively. Conclusions : The improved U-Net segmented consolidation, B-lines, and pleural effusion on LUS images from children with CAP and outperformed baseline U-Net on segmentation metrics. Model assistance improved lesion contouring performance in both less-experienced sonographers. These findings highlight the potential of the model as an AI-assisted tool to facilitate lesion delineation and improve the efficiency of LUS assessment in pediatric CAP and may help reduce reliance on operator experience during contouring.

title: SAM3-SemiSkin: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation with Heterogeneous Decoders for Semi-Supervised Dermoscopic and Brain-MRI Segmentation.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Reliable pixel-level segmentation is needed when lesion boundaries are faint, irregular or affected by acquisition artefacts, yet dense annotation is costly. We investigated whether heterogeneous decoders remain complementary when they share a frozen foundation-model representation, and separated this architectural effect from the contribution of unlabelled training. Methods: SAM3-SemiSkin combines a frozen SAM3 image encoder, bottleneck adapters, and convolutional neural network (CNN) and Transformer decoders. Agreement-weighted soft targets provide mutual supervision, supplemented by frequency and morphological objectives; colour compactness is restricted to dermoscopy. Evaluation included ISIC-2018 benchmarks, controls that retain the shared frozen SAM3 encoder and identical adapter stack, component analyses, zero-shot prompt controls, robustness perturbations, and two-dimensional TCGA-LGG brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). MRI data were partitioned by patient and evaluated slice-wise. Training and validation annotation budgets were counted separately. Results: On ISIC-2018, three-seed test means were 0.886/0.811 for mDice/mIoU at nominal 10% training labels and 0.894/0.825 at 30%. In a separate seed-42 checkpoint audit, the epochs with maximal validation mDice were 45 and 40; train/validation/test mDice were 0.964/0.929/0.882 and 0.974/0.942/0.891, respectively. The 30%-label complete ablation reached 0.893/0.827, exceeding a supervised single-CNN reference by 4.1 percentage points (pp) in mDice. Three-seed paired contrasts were 1.53±0.42 pp for heterogeneous versus homogeneous decoders and 0.63±0.38 pp for adding unlabelled objectives. Matched controls and zero-shot prompt evaluations contextualize these gains. At 30% labels, the MRI benchmark yielded mDice 0.833±0.007 and mIoU 0.740±0.007. Approximately 2.2% of the complete model parameters were trainable. Conclusions: The results support parameter-efficient adaptation with heterogeneous decoding as an integrated design for the tested dermoscopic and MRI tasks. The smaller unlabelled-training contrast and competitive matched controls limit the contribution attributable to the particular pseudo-label objective.

title: Baseline Prostate Volume and the Magnitude and Durability of the Volumetric Response After Prostatic Artery Embolization: A Retrospective Ultrasound-Based Time-to-Event Analysis.
abstract: Background/Objectives : Whether the magnitude and durability of prostate volume reduction after prostatic artery embolization (PAE) depend on baseline gland size is unclear. Methods : Retrospective single-operator study at two institutions (2015-2024): 164 of 177 consecutive men treated by PAE for benign prostatic hyperplasia with evaluable transrectal ultrasound volumetry were stratified as small (30-65 mL, n = 53), medium (>65-100 mL, n = 70) or large (>100 mL, n = 41); median follow-up was 12.8 months. The primary endpoint was relative volume reduction at nadir. Durability was analysed in a 6-month landmark cohort of early responders ( n = 87), with regrowth to ≥80% of baseline as an interval-censored event (Turnbull estimator; Cox regression on midpoint-imputed event times). Results : Median reduction at nadir was 41.7%, 40.1% and 39.1% in small, medium and large glands ( p = 0.39); 10 patients (6.1%) never fell below 80% of baseline. Regrowth occurred in 27 of 87 landmark patients; the probability of sustained reduction 24 months after the landmark was 0.76 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.61-0.88). Baseline volume was not significantly associated with durability (hazard ratio 0.97 per 10 mL, 95% CI 0.86-1.10), consistently across sensitivity analyses and after adjustment for 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor pretreatment, which was more than twice as common in large glands; in an exploratory analysis, deeper reduction by the landmark was associated with longer durability. Conclusions : No association between baseline volume and the magnitude or durability of the volumetric response was detected, but the confidence intervals are wide and do not exclude a clinically relevant effect. The durability estimates are conditional on an early volumetric response and continued follow-up and should not be generalised to the entire treated population; residual confounding by medical therapy cannot be excluded, and the findings concern prostate volume, not clinical efficacy.

title: Massive Transfusion-Associated Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome After Liver Transplantation: A Case Report and Retrospective Estimate of the Sodium Load.
abstract: A 67-year-old woman with acute-on-chronic liver failure and profound preoperative hyponatraemia (central-laboratory serum sodium 116 mmol/L preoperatively; 120.3 mmol/L on the first intraoperative blood gas) underwent emergency living-donor liver transplantation complicated by an estimated blood loss of 6200 mL. Resuscitation comprised 20 units of packed red blood cells (PRBC), 12 units of fresh frozen plasma (FFP), 34 units of cryoprecipitate, three units of apheresis platelets, approximately 7.7 L of crystalloid and albumin, 60 mL of 7% sodium bicarbonate and 70 mEq of potassium chloride, with no hypertonic saline. Serum sodium measured on the operating-room blood gas analyser rose from 120.3 to 132.5 mmol/L over 7 h (+12.2 mmol/L), and by 18 mmol/L between the preoperative central-laboratory value and arrival in the intensive care unit, exceeding the 8-10 mmol/L per 24 h limit recommended by the European Renal Best Practice guideline. She developed dysarthria and dysphagia after extubation on postoperative day (POD) 6 and severe tetraparesis with decreased consciousness on POD 7. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) on POD 7 (rapid protocol) reported no pontine lesion, whereas MRI on POD 19 showed T2 hyperintensity in the central pons and both thalami, consistent with osmotic demyelination syndrome with extrapontine involvement. A simple pooled Adrogué-Madias calculation, with its assumptions stated, estimated the sodium contributed by the infused products at roughly +10 to +17 mmol/L, the same order of magnitude as the observed rise. This case illustrates that blood products, isotonic crystalloids and sodium bicarbonate together can deliver a substantial sodium load during massive transfusion, that the load can be estimated approximately, and that an early MRI without a reported pontine lesion does not exclude osmotic demyelination.

title: Silent but Aggressive: A Case of Cervical Large-Cell Neuroendocrine Carcinoma with Repeatedly Normal Cytology in a 22-Year-Old Postpartum Patient.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Neuroendocrine carcinoma of the cervix (NECC) is a rare, aggressive variant of cervical cancer (approximately 1-1.5% of cases), and large-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma (LCNEC) is an even rarer subtype. Diagnosis is often delayed because symptoms are non-specific and cytology may fail to detect the disease. We report this case to highlight the diagnostic challenge posed by LCNEC in a young patient with repeatedly normal cytology. Methods: We describe the diagnostic work-up and multimodal management of a 22-year-old woman who presented with post-coital bleeding nine months after her second full-term vaginal delivery. Results: Two Babeș-Papanicolaou smears obtained three months apart were negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy. Persistent bleeding prompted a loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP), which revealed a poorly differentiated (high-grade) LCNEC. Clinical examination and MRI showed proximal parametrial involvement and a left external iliac lymph node metastasis (FIGO 2018 stage IIIC1r, cT2bN1M0). The patient received definitive chemoradiotherapy (external beam radiotherapy with a simultaneous integrated boost and high-dose-rate brachytherapy) with six cycles of platinum-etoposide chemotherapy (two concurrent, four adjuvant), achieving a complete response with no evidence of disease approximately three years after treatment. Conclusions: This report illustrates that cytology can be repeatedly negative in NECC and that persistent symptoms or a visible cervical lesion warrant histological evaluation. Given its aggressive clinical course, LCNEC requires the rapid initiation of combined local and systemic therapy.

Persistent bleeding prompted a loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP), which revealed a poorly differentiated (high-grade) LCNEC. Clinical examination and MRI showed proximal parametrial involvement and a left external iliac lymph node metastasis (FIGO 2018 stage IIIC1r, cT2bN1M0). The patient received definitive chemoradiotherapy (external beam radiotherapy with a simultaneous integrated boost and high-dose-rate brachytherapy) with six cycles of platinum-etoposide chemotherapy (two concurrent, four adjuvant), achieving a complete response with no evidence of disease approximately three years after treatment. Conclusions: This report illustrates that cytology can be repeatedly negative in NECC and that persistent symptoms or a visible cervical lesion warrant histological evaluation. Given its aggressive clinical course, LCNEC requires the rapid initiation of combined local and systemic therapy.

title: Association Between Plasma Homocysteine Levels and Peripapillary Vessel Density in Patients with Pseudoexfoliation Syndrome Without Glaucoma.
abstract: Background/Objectives : The relationship between circulating homocysteine (Hcy) and ocular microvascular alterations in pseudoexfoliation syndrome (PXS) remains unclear. This study evaluated the association between plasma Hcy concentrations and peripapillary vessel density (VD) in patients with PXS without clinically evident glaucoma and controls. Methods : This single-center, cross-sectional observational study with prospective recruitment included three groups: patients with PXS and Hcy < 15 µmol/L, patients with PXS and Hcy ≥ 15 µmol/L, and controls without PXS. Fasting plasma Hcy was measured using chemiluminescent immunoassay. Peripapillary VD was quantified from optical coherence tomography angiography images using ImageJ (version 1.54, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, USA). Generalized estimating equations accounted for inter-eye correlation and assessed associations adjusted for age, intraocular pressure, and PXS status. PXS-only and single-eye sensitivity analyses were performed. Results : VD analyses included 71 eyes from 60 participants. Mean peripapillary VD was 62.3 ± 7.2%, 54.1 ± 6.4%, and 66.3 ± 6.3% in the respective groups (overall p < 0.001). In the full cohort, each 1 µmol/L increase in Hcy was associated with a 0.30-percentage-point decrease in VD (95% CI, -0.57 to -0.03; p = 0.029). Associations remained inverse but were not statistically significant in the PXS-only analysis (B = -0.25; p = 0.114) or single-eye sensitivity analysis (B = -0.28; p = 0.077). Global retinal nerve fiber layer thickness did not differ significantly among groups. Conclusions : Higher plasma Hcy was associated with lower peripapillary VD in the full cohort, but evidence within PXS remained inconclusive. These exploratory cross-sectional findings do not establish causality or prognostic value and require confirmation in larger longitudinal studies.

title: AI-Assisted Follow-Up MRI Interpretation in Multiple Sclerosis: Radiology Residents' Diagnostic Confidence and Performance.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are becoming increasingly utilised in everyday radiological practice. Evaluating follow-up magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of patients with multiple sclerosis (MS) is challenging. The aim of this study was to assess changes in confidence among four participating radiology residents when evaluating follow-up MRIs of MS patients using Pixyl.Neuro.MS ® software. Methods: This retrospective study included 78 MS patients. Previous and new FLAIR images were independently analysed by four residents, first without AI and then in an immediate AI-assisted second reading using Pixyl.Neuro.MS ® , a deep-learning lesion-segmentation software. Readers recorded their findings and confidence after each reading and rated the impact and usefulness of AI. The reference standard was defined by a consensus reading of a neuroradiologist and a radiology resident (15 and 4 years of experience). Paired analyses and patient-level bootstrap confidence intervals were used; bootstrap inference was conditional on the four readers. Results: The reference standard identified 24 patients with new lesions. Mean accuracy across readers increased from 84.62% to 90.71% (difference, 6.09 percentage points; 95% bootstrap confidence interval [CI], 2.24-10.26). Only Reader 3 showed a significant accuracy increase after Holm adjustment ( p = 0.025). No accuracy comparison with routine reports was significant after adjustment. Confidence increased for all readers (all Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). Perceived usefulness did not differ significantly between lesion-burden groups. All readers predominantly rated the impact of AI as positive. The second-reading phase was shorter by a mean of 59.35 s (95% bootstrap CI, 51.39-67.07). Conclusions: In these four residents, the AI-assisted second reading was associated with higher confidence and average accuracy. The immediate sequential design prevents separation of AI contributions from familiarity and order effects, and the shorter second-reading phase does not establish an overall workflow time saving.

title: From Diagnostic Imaging to Surgical Management: Patient-Specific Three-Dimensional Modelling in Gynaecological Cancer-A Scoping Review.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Patient-specific three-dimensional (3D) models may clarify complex anatomy in gynaecological cancer surgery. This scoping review mapped applications of virtual and printed models, and examined their reported contributions to surgical planning and outcomes. Methods: The review followed Joanna Briggs Institute guidance along with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews. PubMed, Scopus and Embase were searched on 4 March 2026 for English- or Spanish-language reports. Following a broad gynaecological search, an oncology-focused synthesis examined patient-specific models linked to surgical anatomy or planning. Eligibility assessment and data charting were each performed independently by two reviewers. Findings were synthesised descriptively without formal risk-of-bias appraisal or quantitative pooling. Results: Fourteen studies published between 2016 and 2026 were included: nine evaluated virtual models and five incorporated physical printing. Evidence comprised comparative observational studies, small feasibility or prospective studies, and case reports. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging were the main imaging sources. Applications included tumour mapping, depiction of neural and vascular anatomy, and planning complex or recurrent tumour resections. Some comparative studies reported shorter operative times and lower blood losses, whereas others found improved anatomical assessments without significant perioperative differences. Any additional advantage of printing over virtual visualisation remained uncertain. Interpretation was limited by small samples, heterogeneous methods, subjective evaluations, and one mixed malignant and non-malignant cohort. Conclusions: Patient-specific 3D modelling may assist planning in selected complex gynaecological oncology procedures. Evidence of improved clinical outcomes remains insufficient. Prospective comparative evaluations should establish appropriate indications, and determine whether additional anatomical information produces meaningful patient benefit.

title: Effects of Topical Products Used on the Facial Region on Intraoral Radiographic Image Parameters: An Exploratory In Vitro PSP Study.
abstract: Background/Objectives: This exploratory in vitro study evaluated the effects of topical facial products on quantitative pixel-level parameters of intraoral radiographic images under different exposure conditions using a photostimulable phosphor (PSP) system. Methods: Six groups were tested: inorganic sunscreen, organic sunscreen, BB cream, CC cream, silver (Ag) sulfadiazine 1%, and an untreated control. To isolate the individual radiographic signature of each formulation from anatomical confounders, the products were applied at a dose of 2 mg/cm 2 to a homogeneous silicone soft-tissue phantom and imaged under three protocols (60 kVp/7 mA/0.080 s, pediatric anterior; 60 kVp/7 mA/0.160 s, adult anterior; 63 kVp/6 mA/0.200 s, adult posterior) with three independent acquisitions per group and protocol (54 images). Six parameters were measured in ImageJ: brightness, uniformity, signal-to-noise ratio, histogram clipping, noise, and uniformity index. Data were analyzed by two-way ANOVA with Dunnett post hoc testing and Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) correction. Results: Compared to the control, the BB cream showed significant differences in uniformity (higher SD), noise (higher), and uniformity index (higher; i.e., greater uniformity among the ROI means); the CC cream showed significant differences in histogram clipping (higher), noise (higher), and uniformity index (higher) (all BH-adjusted p ≤ 0.011). Silver sulfadiazine increased histogram clipping (BH-adjusted p = 0.002), while the inorganic sunscreen altered the uniformity index (BH-adjusted p = 0.042). The organic sunscreen did not differ from the control in the primary analysis. Neither exposure protocol nor the group-by-protocol interaction reached significance, although the study was powered only for large effects and exposure dependence cannot be excluded. Conclusions: Products containing metal oxides or silver sulfadiazine produced formulation-specific changes in quantitative imaging parameters, whereas the organic sunscreen tested in this study showed no significant difference from the control. This study did not test whether the observed differences are clinically visible or whether software processing can render them visible. The findings serve as a reference for subsequent research involving anatomical phantoms and observer-based studies.

title: Patent Foramen Ovale and Atrial Septal Defects: A Multimodal Approach to Diagnosis, Prognosis and Closure-A Narrative Review.
abstract: Interatrial communications encompass anatomically and clinically distinct entities, ranging from patent foramen ovale (PFO), resulting from incomplete postnatal septal fusion, to atrial septal defects (ASDs) and extraseptal communications associated with congenital malformations. This narrative review synthesizes the literature, integrating embryology, anatomical classification, multimodality imaging and clinical evidence to support diagnosis, prognostic assessment and closure. Particular attention is given to distinguishing true secundum septal defects from ostium primum defects within the atrioventricular septal defect spectrum, sinus venosus communications and coronary sinus unroofing. Transthoracic echocardiography provides the initial anatomical and haemodynamic assessment; contrast echocardiography and transcranial Doppler assess right-to-left shunting, while transoesophageal and three-dimensional echocardiography define morphology, surrounding structures and procedural feasibility. Cardiac computed tomography complements these techniques by mapping complex malformations and pulmonary or systemic venous connections. In patients with otherwise unexplained ischaemic stroke, PFO causal attribution requires integration of clinical characteristics, neuroimaging findings and shunt features following investigation of competing mechanisms. Large right-to-left shunts and atrial septal aneurysm have the strongest evidence for identifying patients who derive greater benefit from closure, while additional geometric and biomechanical markers remain incompletely validated. ASD management depends primarily on shunt burden, right-heart remodelling and pulmonary vascular status, with paradoxical embolism providing an additional indication for closure when haemodynamically safe. Platypnoea-orthodeoxia, decompression sickness and migraine require indication-specific assessment; evidence does not support routine closure for migraine alone. The proposed diagnostic and decision algorithms organize these complementary assessments into a practical framework for individualized multidisciplinary management while remaining subject to prospective validation.

title: Quantifying [<sup>18</sup>F]FDG Uptake in the Liver, Spleen, Aorta, Bone Marrow, and Superior Vena Cava Using TotalSegmentator on [<sup>18</sup>F]PET/CT Imaging.
abstract: Background/Objectives : The measurement of radiotracer uptake in specific organs has potential clinical implications. However, manual delineation is time-consuming. We aimed to evaluate the agreement between manual delineation and automatic segmentation by the artificial intelligence model TotalSegmentator for extraction of standard uptake values (SUVs) from [18F]FDG-PET/CT scans for the aorta, spleen, lumbar spine bone marrow, liver, and superior vena cava. Methods : The aorta, spleen, lumbar spine bone marrow, liver, and superior vena cava were segmented manually by trained physicians and automatically by the TotalSegmentator version 2.4 software, and the correlations between SUV values obtained were assessed. Results : We found good agreement between manually and automatically obtained SUVmean values for the aorta (manual/TotalSegmentator: 2.10/2.11), spleen (2.00/1.95), liver (2.53/2.37), lumbar spine bone marrow (1.88/1.85), and superior vena cava (2.02/1.88) with high correlation coefficients across all organs, ranging from 0.93 to 0.99 and high intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) of 0.81-0.99. title: Mandibular Metastasis Mimicking Medication-Related Osteonecrosis of the Jaw: A Diagnostic Challenge.
abstract: Background : Metastatic tumors in the oral cavity are exceptionally rare, comprising only 1% to 1.5% of all oral malignancies. These metastases typically indicate widespread disease and are seen in patients with advanced-stage cancer. The primary cancers most commonly metastasizing to the oral cavity include those of the breast, lung, kidney, bone, and colon. Case report : We present the case of a 78-year-old male with advanced prostate adenocarcinoma who developed severe jaw pain, swelling, and increased tooth mobility in the right mandibular region. Despite undergoing various treatments for metastatic prostate cancer, including chemotherapy and zoledronic acid, the patient experienced persistent symptoms for six months. The clinical presentation initially raised suspicion of medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ). However, the initial panoramic radiograph revealed no apparent pathological changes in the mandibular bone, whereas skeletal scintigraphy demonstrated increased radiotracer uptake in the affected mandibular region, suggesting metastatic involvement. Clinically, the metastasis presented as an exophytic soft-tissue lesion involving the mandibular gingiva. Histopathological examination revealed a poorly differentiated carcinoma, and immunohistochemical staining for NKX3.1 supported its prostatic origin. Palliative radiotherapy alleviated the jaw pain, but the patient died two months after the diagnosis. Conclusions : This case highlights the diagnostic challenge of distinguishing mandibular metastasis from MRONJ in patients receiving long-term antiresorptive therapy. It underscores the importance of histopathological examination of atypical mandibular lesions, particularly when clinical and radiographic findings do not fully support the diagnosis of MRONJ, to avoid diagnostic delay and ensure appropriate patient management.

title: A Genetic Approach to Characterize Macrocephalies: The Experience of SETD2 -Related Overgrowth Syndrome.
abstract: Background Macrocephaly may encompass a broad array of clinical conditions, but no decisional algorithms exist for its assessment and management. The clinician-geneticist alliance in the specific context of overgrowth syndromes may be of interest for shaping a proper diagnostic path. At present, the literature regarding a genetic link of macrocephaly with pathogenic SETD2 variants is limited. Case presentation We report a young man with macrocephaly first noted in infancy, confirmed in every stage of his life, combined with speech delay and moderate learning disability. He came to our first evaluation due to macrocrania and a history of cognitive and behavioral impairment. Brain magnetic resonance was performed after this first visit, confirming macrocephaly and revealing type I Arnold-Chiari malformation, but neither hydrocephalus nor pituitary abnormalities. Genetic testing evaluating different genes involved in overgrowth syndromes revealed the novel variant c.7039C>T (p.Gln2347*) in the SETD2 gene, leading us to diagnose Luscan-Lumish syndrome, an autosomal dominant intellectual developmental disorder associated with protean overgrowth manifestations, including macrocephaly and dysmorphic features. Case-based Review of the Literature and Discussion: An extremely heterogeneous group of disorders with a wide range of etiologies, neurodevelopmental outcomes, and radiologic characteristics may be associated with individuals with macrocephaly. After initial clinical and neuroimaging assessment, a coherent diagnostic work-up should be customized for each case of macrocephaly to clarify an underlying condition and delineate prognosis. Genetic investigation should be considered mandatory in deciphering the inner architecture of macrocephalies and explaining any associated abnormalities that may cause either growth anomaly in se or its concurrent symptoms. Conclusions A standard recognized classification system integrating clinical, neuroimaging, developmental biological criteria and molecular/genetic assessment of macrocephaly is not currently available; however, future investigations on patients with macrocephaly will help in understanding SETD2 -related disorders and provide accurate genetic counseling for more targeted management strategies.

title: Deep Learning-Based Classification of Mandibular Growth-Rotation Phenotypes from Lateral Cephalometric Radiographs: A Comparative Evaluation of Convolutional Neural Networks.
abstract: Background/Objectives: The cross-sectional classification of mandibular growth-rotation morphology is relevant to orthodontic diagnosis and treatment planning, but conventional structural assessment is observer-dependent. This study developed and internally evaluated deep learning models for classifying existing clockwise and counterclockwise mandibular growth-rotation phenotypes on lateral cephalometric radiographs; it did not forecast future longitudinal growth. Methods: Eight hundred untreated radiographs from individuals aged 9-20 years were labelled by consensus using Björk and Skieller morphological indicators (clockwise, n = 376; counterclockwise, n = 424). A stratified 80:20 training-validation split was used. ResNet50, InceptionV3, and VGG16 were fine-tuned after Gaussian noise reduction, min-max normalisation, and limited geometric augmentation. Results: VGG16 showed the most favourable validation accuracy-loss profile. The archived aggregate confusion matrix ( n = 800) yielded an apparent accuracy of 81.13% (95% CI, 78.38-83.75) and balanced accuracy of 81.32% (95% CI, 78.62-83.96); recall was 84.57% for clockwise and 78.07% for counterclockwise phenotypes. Because the matrix included the complete labelled cohort, these values are descriptive apparent performance and not an independent test estimate. Conclusions: VGG16 can classify cross-sectional mandibular growth-rotation phenotypes with promising apparent performance. External, longitudinal, and observer-benchmark validation is required before clinical use.

title: Anatomical Proximity Between the Retromolar Canal and Mandibular Third Molars on Cone-Beam CT: A Retrospective Study.
abstract: Background/Objectives : The retromolar canal (RMC) and retromolar foramen (RMF) are anatomical variations in the posterior mandible that may lie close to mandibular third molars and may contain neurovascular structures. This study aimed to characterize RMC/RMF-third-molar proximity on cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT), with close proximity defined a priori as a minimum distance < 2 mm. Methods : This retrospective CBCT study included 100 adults (200 hemimandibles). RMC/RMF morphology and morphometry, Pell and Gregory class and position, and Winter angulation were assessed. Generalized estimating equations accounted for within-patient clustering, and inter-observer reliability was quantified. Results : RMCs were identified in 41/200 hemimandibles (20.5%; patient-clustered 95% CI, 14.9-27.6%) and 32/100 patients (32.0%; 95% CI, 23.7-41.7%). Among RMC-positive hemimandibles that also contained a third molar (n = 26), 8 showed a minimum RMC/RMF-third-molar distance < 2 mm (30.8%; patient-clustered 95% CI, 14.9-52.9%). When all hemimandibles containing a third molar were considered (n = 121), the same close-proximity configuration was present in 8 (6.6%). No statistically significant association was detected between RMC presence and third-molar presence, Pell and Gregory class or position, or Winter angulation. Inter-observer agreement was high (κ = 0.757-0.951; ICC = 0.960-0.995). Conclusions : Close RMC/RMF-third-molar proximity occurred in a substantial subset of RMC-positive sites, although precision was limited. The findings suggest that direct assessment of the RMC/RMF may offer complementary anatomical information beyond conventional impaction classifications; this hypothesis requires confirmation in larger prospective studies.

title: CBCT-Based Volumetric Assessment of Tooth Roots in the Context of Alveolar Ridge Preservation.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Alveolar ridge preservation (ARP) is commonly performed following tooth extraction to minimize post-extraction dimensional changes. However, limited information is available regarding root-volume variations among different tooth types. This study aimed to assess the root volumes of maxillary and mandibular teeth using cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) and to compare the measured root volumes with commonly available graft-material package volumes in the context of ARP. Methods: CBCT scans from 53 patients meeting the eligibility criteria were retrospectively evaluated. Fourteen teeth per scan were assessed using a split-mouth approach, resulting in a total of 742 teeth. Root boundaries were identified by two trained and calibrated dentists, and root volumes were calculated using OsiriX MD v13.0.3 software. Statistical comparisons were performed using paired and independent t -tests. Results: Root volumes varied according to tooth type and arch. The maxillary first molar demonstrated the highest mean root volume (0.55 ± 0.10 cm 3 ), whereas the mandibular central incisor demonstrated the lowest (0.11 ± 0.02 cm 3 ). Maxillary teeth showed significantly greater root volumes than their mandibular counterparts. Gender-related differences were limited to the maxillary second premolar and mandibular second molar and were considered of limited clinical relevance. For illustrative comparison, the measured root volumes were considered in relation to commonly available graft-material package volumes, including 0.25 and 0.50 cc; these comparisons do not represent clinically validated graft requirements. Conclusions: This study provides CBCT-derived reference root-volume values for different tooth types and demonstrates variations according to tooth type and arch. Comparison of these measurements with commonly available graft-material package volumes may provide a descriptive volumetric reference in the context of ARP. However, root volume does not directly represent post-extraction socket volume or the quantity of graft material required clinically. Therefore, these comparisons should not be interpreted as recommendations for graft quantity, and prospective clinical studies comparing root volume with actual socket volume and graft utilization are required before clinical application.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Detection of Tumor Calcification in Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma: Emerging Opportunities in Computational Oral Pathology and Biomineralization Research.
abstract: Objective: Tumor-associated calcification is increasingly recognized as a potentially relevant feature of the tumor microenvironment across multiple malignancies; however, its significance in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) remains poorly understood and is frequently overlooked during routine histopathologic assessment. This perspective examines the potential of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted computational pathology to improve the detection, quantification, and spatial characterization of tumor-associated calcification in OSCC and discusses its potential as an emerging histopathologic research phenotype and candidate biomarker requiring further validation. Design: A narrative synthesis of the current literature was undertaken to evaluate the biological mechanisms underlying tumor-associated calcification in OSCC, recent advances in biomineralization research, and the application of AI and computational pathology in digital histopathology. Current evidence was integrated to propose future AI-based workflows for objective calcification assessment and to identify opportunities for investigating its potential biological and clinical relevance. Results: Current evidence indicates that calcification has been reported or proposed in vascular, stromal, necrotic, and extracellular matrix-associated contexts in OSCC and related pathological settings; however, the prevalence, biological mechanisms, and reproducibility of these patterns in OSCC remain insufficiently characterized. Potential associations with hypoxia, chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, and osteogenic-like cellular reprogramming are supported primarily by evidence from broader biomineralization, vascular calcification, and other tumor contexts rather than by calcification-specific mechanistic studies in OSCC. Advances in whole-slide imaging, deep learning, and computational pathology have enabled automated tissue segmentation, feature extraction, and quantitative histopathologic analysis. However, their application to the systematic detection and spatial characterization of calcification in OSCC remains limited. AI-assisted analysis could facilitate objective identification, quantification, and spatial mapping of mineralized structures, providing a conceptual research framework for investigating tumor heterogeneity and microenvironmental remodeling. Conclusions: Integrating computational pathology with biomineralization research may improve the characterization of tumor-associated calcification in OSCC and provide a methodological basis for investigating quantitative digital phenotypes. At present, evidence is insufficient to establish calcification as a validated diagnostic, prognostic, or predictive biomarker in OSCC. Future multidisciplinary studies combining AI, spatial pathology, molecular profiling, and clinical validation are required to determine its biological and clinical significance and to establish whether calcification-associated features have reproducible biomarker potential.
originalAbstract: Objective: Tumor-associated calcification is increasingly recognized as a potentially relevant feature of the tumor microenvironment across multiple malignancies; however, its significance in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) remains poorly understood and is frequently overlooked during routine histopathologic assessment. This perspective examines the potential of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted computational pathology to improve the detection, quantification, and spatial characterization of tumor-associated calcification in OSCC and discusses its potential as an emerging histopathologic research phenotype and candidate biomarker requiring further validation. Design: A narrative synthesis of the current literature was undertaken to evaluate the biological mechanisms underlying tumor-associated calcification in OSCC, recent advances in biomineralization research, and the application of AI and computational pathology in digital histopathology. Current evidence was integrated to propose future AI-based workflows for objective calcification assessment and to identify opportunities for investigating its potential biological and clinical relevance. Results: Current evidence indicates that calcification has been reported or proposed in vascular, stromal, necrotic, and extracellular matrix-associated contexts in OSCC and related pathological settings; however, the prevalence, biological mechanisms, and reproducibility of these patterns in OSCC remain insufficiently characterized. Potential associations with hypoxia, chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, and osteogenic-like cellular reprogramming are supported primarily by evidence from broader biomineralization, vascular calcification, and other tumor contexts rather than by calcification-specific mechanistic studies in OSCC. Advances in whole-slide imaging, deep learning, and computational pathology have enabled automated tissue segmentation, feature extraction, and quantitative histopathologic analysis. However, their application to the systematic detection and spatial characterization of calcification in OSCC remains limited. AI-assisted analysis could facilitate objective identification, quantification, and spatial mapping of mineralized structures, providing a conceptual research framework for investigating tumor heterogeneity and microenvironmental remodeling. Conclusions: Integrating computational pathology with biomineralization research may improve the characterization of tumor-associated calcification in OSCC and provide a methodological basis for investigating quantitative digital phenotypes. At present, evidence is insufficient to establish calcification as a validated diagnostic, prognostic, or predictive biomarker in OSCC. Future multidisciplinary studies combining AI, spatial pathology, molecular profiling, and clinical validation are required to determine its biological and clinical significance and to establish whether calcification-associated features have reproducible biomarker potential.

title: Autogenous Tooth Sticky Bone Graft for Maxillary Radicular Cyst Defects: A Retrospective Case Series.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Radicular cysts (RCs) in the maxillary anterior aesthetic zone can cause substantial buccal bone loss and complicate implant rehabilitation. This retrospective case series evaluated autogenous tooth sticky bone (ATSB) from impacted third molars, covered with concentrated growth factor (CGF) membranes, for reconstructing these defects before delayed implant placement. Methods: Twenty patients with maxillary anterior RC-associated defects and ≥2 nonfunctional impacted third molars were treated under general anesthesia. ATSB was prepared chairside from partially demineralized dentin matrix (425-850 μm) and autogenous fibrin glue, placed after cyst enucleation, and covered with two CGF membranes. Implants were placed after 4 months. Clinical records, panoramic radiographs, and cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) scans were reviewed. Results: The cohort comprised 12 males and 8 females (mean age, 31 years; range, 20-40). All donor and recipient sites healed uneventfully, without recorded infection or graft failure. Four-month CBCT showed increased radiopacity and trabecular-like structures within the defects. All implants achieved primary stability (implant stability quotient > 70) and showed radiographic findings consistent with osseointegration at 3 months; definitive restorations were recorded as functionally and aesthetically acceptable. Conclusions: In selected patients, ATSB with CGF membrane coverage may be a feasible option for post-enucleation reconstruction and delayed implant rehabilitation without an additional bone-harvesting site. Controlled studies with volumetric, histological, and long-term assessment are needed.

title: Sources of Error in Static Computer-Assisted Implant Surgery: A Critical Review of Error Propagation Through the Digital Workflow.
abstract: Static computer-assisted implant surgery (sCAIS) relies on a chain of digital, manufacturing, and clinical steps to transfer the virtually planned implant position to the patient. Although static surgical guides improve implant placement accuracy compared with freehand techniques, clinically relevant deviations persist, and existing systematic reviews mainly report the final planned-versus-placed discrepancy, while evidence on individual workflow stages remains dispersed across several disciplines. This critical review synthesizes quantitative evidence on stage-specific sources of dimensional and angular inaccuracy across the complete workflow, including cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) and intraoral data acquisition, image registration and segmentation, virtual implant planning, guide design, additive manufacturing, washing, post-curing, sleeve installation, sterilization, guide seating, and drilling. Reported stage-specific discrepancies are generally in the submillimeter range, commonly from several hundredths to several tenths of a millimeter, whereas final clinical deviations are larger, with pooled mean deviations of approximately 1.2 mm at the implant entry point, 1.4 mm at the apex, and 3.5° in angulation reported in a consensus meta-analysis. Because these values describe different quantities and differ in magnitude and direction, they cannot be compared directly or summed; their relationship to the final deviation is therefore presented as a conceptual framework rather than a quantitative model. Printer accuracy alone does not determine the accuracy of guided implant surgery. Validated printer-resin and post-processing protocols, appropriate guide design, verification checkpoints at stage transitions, and reliable clinical seating and stabilization are recommended to limit error transfer. Further research is particularly needed to quantify the isolated contributions of washing, post-curing, sleeve installation, guide movement, and operator-related intraoperative factors.

title: Systemic Health and Endodontic Disease Burden: Influence of Root Canal Treatment Quality on Endodontic Outcomes.
abstract: Background: Systemic health conditions are increasingly prevalent among patients receiving endodontic care and may influence the burden of endodontic disease. This study evaluated the prevalence of systemic health conditions among patients undergoing root canal treatment (RCT), their association with endodontic disease characteristics, and the influence of radiographic quality of root canal treatment (QRCT) on endodontic outcomes (EOs). Methods: This retrospective study reviewed electronic records and radiographs of 2036 patients who underwent RCT by predoctoral students between January 2021 and December 2025. Follow-up data sufficient for EO assessment were available for 590 teeth. Variables included systemic health conditions, tooth type, preoperative periapical status, and QRCT parameters (obturation length, density, taper, coronal seal, and procedural errors). EOs were classified using predefined clinical and radiographic criteria. Associations were analyzed using the Wilcoxon rank-sum, χ 2 , and Fisher exact tests and multivariable logistic regression (α = 0.05). A sensitivity analysis was restricted to follow-up ≥12 months. Results: Systemic health conditions were identified in 57.9% of the overall study population (N = 2036) and in 64.1% of patients with evaluable endodontic outcomes (N = 590). Among patients with evaluable outcomes, mental health disorders (40.3%), hypertension (20.8%), neurological disorders (11.4%), and diabetes mellitus (10.7%) were the most prevalent systemic conditions. Overall treatment success was 86.1%. An exploratory association between mental health disorders and dental caries was observed. Mental health disorders were significantly associated with the presence of dental caries (unadjusted p = 0.049). QRCT was significantly associated with endodontic outcomes ( p < 0.001), with higher success rates in teeth with satisfactory treatment quality (88.4%) than in those with unsatisfactory treatment quality (65.5%). After adjustment for age, gender, tooth type, follow-up duration, preoperative periapical lesion status, and systemic health status, satisfactory QRCT was associated with greater odds of successful outcome (adjusted OR = 3.44; 95% CI, 1.82-6.50; p < 0.001). Longer follow-up was associated with lower odds of success (adjusted OR per 12 months = 0.74; 95% CI, 0.61-0.90; p = 0.003). Conclusions: Systemic health conditions were highly prevalent among patients receiving RCT and were associated with selected disease characteristics. However, satisfactory QRCT was the factor most strongly associated with successful EOs after adjustment for relevant patient and clinical characteristics. Practical Implications: Although systemic health conditions should be considered during patient assessment and treatment planning, achieving high-quality root canal treatment remains critical for optimizing endodontic outcomes and supports continued emphasis on technical excellence in clinical practice and dental education.
